topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Turns & Directions
topic.description: Describe movement and direction, including whole, half, quarter, and three-quarter turns
evidence: Follow instructions to move forward, backward, turn left/right
Demonstrate a whole turn, half turn, and quarter turn with their body
Describe a route using directional language
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a game where they have to turn left or right, do they understand what a quarter turn, half turn, and full turn mean?

pedagogy.summary: This is embodied direction and rotation: children physically move (forward, backward, turn left/right) and demonstrate whole, half and quarter turns with their bodies, then describe routes with directional words. It is a doing skill — a turn is felt as an amount of rotation about a fixed spot, distinct from travelling a distance — and it seeds the dynamic angle-as-turn conception developed later. The main hurdles are confusing turning with moving, under- or over-rotating when there is no target to turn to, and left/right, which is frame-dependent and late-developing.
bestPractices: Turn the WHOLE body on the spot first, marking the start and finish facing, so a turn is felt as rotation rather than travel.
Use fixed reference facings — face the door, now the window — so a 'quarter turn' lands on a checkable target rather than a random amount.
Sequence whole → half → quarter turns, linking a half turn to 'facing the opposite way' and a whole turn to 'facing the same way again'.
Play route and floor-robot games ('give me directions to the door') so children both FOLLOW and GIVE directional instructions.
Anchor left and right on the body (right-hand sticker) before using them in directions, and expect residual errors.
keyRepresentations: The child's own body turning on a spot, with start and finish facings marked by footprints
A programmable floor robot or a marked floor grid for building and walking routes
Quarter / half / three-quarter turn language tied to fixed landmarks to face
A simple route to follow and then to describe
commonMisconceptions: Confusing a turn (rotation on the spot) with moving forward — 'turning' by walking in a curve or stepping sideways
Under- or over-rotating: a 'quarter turn' that is a random amount because it is not referenced to a target facing
Left/right reversed, especially relative to the direction of travel or a facing partner (frame-dependence)
Treating half or quarter of a turn as unrelated to half or quarter of anything else — no sense of a fractional turn amount

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 5–6) learn direction and turning as a doing skill: physically moving forward/backward and turning their whole body through whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, then both following and giving route directions. The core insight is that a turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed spot — felt in the body — distinct from travelling a distance. Main hurdles are confusing turning with moving, under-/over-rotating when there is no target to turn toward, and left/right (which is frame-dependent and matures later). Embodied whole-body movement is the primary teaching medium; a programmable floor-robot or route game is proposed as a companion that can show the result of a turn immediately (a wrong turn visibly misses the goal), though its relative teaching value over embodied movement is not established.

activities.title: Turn your whole body on the spot
feedback: If the child travels across the floor or steps sideways instead of pivoting, mark the spot with a hoop or footprints and require both feet to stay put while turning to face a named target.

If the finish facing is a random amount (not toward the named target), give fixed facings to turn TO — door then window — so a quarter turn lands on a checkable target rather than reteaching the whole idea; the concept may well be held, with only the execution lacking a reference point.
When two quarter turns leave them facing the opposite way, name it: 'two quarter turns make a half turn.'
activities.rationale: Turning the whole body on the spot with marked start/finish facings makes rotation felt as rotation rather than travel, and referencing each turn to a fixed landmark gives the turn amount a checkable target. This dynamic turn experience seeds the later angle-as-turn conception.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should describe position, direction and movement, including whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns.

An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (a start position and the position after the turn); children develop this dynamically by turning — stretching out arms and turning while one arm stays in place — and the dynamic turn conception appears early, with children talking about whole and half turns from Year 1.
learnerActions: Stand on a marked spot (hoop or footprints) with both feet staying put throughout the turn.
Mark your start facing (e.g. 'I'm facing the door'), then make a quarter turn to your right and name your new facing ('now the window').

Go back to your start facing (the door). Make a half turn and check you are facing the opposite way from the start; go back to the start facing, make a whole turn and check you are facing the same way as the start.

Go back to your start facing, then make a three-quarter turn to your right and check where you now face (three quarter-turns to the right from the start, the same facing as one quarter turn to the left).
Make two quarter turns in a row in the same direction (both to the right) and compare: is that the same as one half turn?
activities.intendedInsight: A turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed point, felt in the body — not travelling. A quarter turn lands you on a new facing (about 90° from the start), a half turn faces you the opposite way, a three-quarter turn is three quarter-turns on, and a whole turn returns you to the same facing.

activities.title: Give and follow a route
feedback: If the route is only 'go forward' steps with the turns left out, walk their exact words back to them so they SEE the path miss the bookshelf (or hit a wall), then have them re-give it including the turns.

If they turn the wrong way, reinforce body left/right (e.g. a sticker on the right hand) and keep up exposure; do not drill it as a failure — frame-dependent left/right matures later, especially after they have turned to a new facing or face a partner.
activities.rationale: Both following and producing directions develops directional language as a usable tool; producing a route reveals gaps that imitation hides. Anchoring left/right on the body before using it in directions respects that left/right is frame-dependent and late-developing.
sourceClaims: Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and not mastered until early elementary school; children engage in locating and directional activities (hopscotch, board games moving forward and backward) that build directional understanding.
learnerActions: Follow a spoken route given by an adult or partner: 'go forward two, turn left a quarter, go forward one.'
Then GIVE directions yourself: describe how to walk from here to the bookshelf as a sequence of moves and turns.
Have your listener walk your exact words — if they miss the bookshelf or hit a wall, find the missing or wrong move or turn and re-give the route.
Try describing the route for walking backward from the bookshelf to the start.
activities.intendedInsight: A followable route is a coordinated sequence of moves AND turns with correct directional words — leaving out the turns breaks the path. Giving a route (not just following one) shows the directional words have become a productive tool.

activities.title: Program a robot along a floor grid (companion)
feedback: When the robot misses the goal, point to the arrow's facing after the turn and ask which turn was the wrong amount or direction.
If a quarter turn does not land 90° on, let the child re-enter the command and re-run it so the correction is immediate and visible.
activities.rationale: A programmable route game is proposed as a companion that may give immediate visual feedback on turn direction and amount and capture route-building; it cannot reproduce the proprioceptive feedback of the child's own felt rotation, so it is best paired with, not a replacement for, the child doing the same turns with their own body. No source directly establishes its relative efficacy.
learnerActions: On a floor grid or maze, string commands for a character/robot: 'forward 2', 'turn left a quarter', 'forward 1'.
Aim the robot at a goal; if a turn is the wrong direction or amount, the robot faces the wrong way and misses or runs into a wall.
Watch the start and finish facings shown as an arrow, and adjust so a quarter turn visibly lands the arrow 90° on.
Compare turning-then-walking with walking-then-turning and notice the different results.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'quarter turn' only makes sense as landing on a new facing toward the next target, and the order of turning and walking matters: turn-then-walk is different from walk-then-turn.

constraints: This is a bodily performance skill: assess and teach by watching the child move and listening to the route, not by asking them to explain the procedure.

The child's own felt rotation about a fixed spot is where the idea lives; a screen or floor-robot game does not reproduce proprioceptive turning feedback and should be a companion to embodied movement, not a substitute.

Sequencing a route or picking the picture after a quarter turn can check the idea but does not itself elicit the physical rotation or route production — recognition-only tasks do not demonstrate the doing.

Left/right is frame-dependent and late-developing; expect residual reversal errors, especially after a change of facing or when facing a partner. Reinforce body-anchored left/right and keep exposure rather than drilling errors as failures.
A static picture cannot be turned, so it cannot by itself practise the rotation; use it only as a prompt alongside movement.
When a turn amount drifts, scaffold with a fixed target to turn TO rather than reteaching the concept — the under-/over-rotation is an execution gap, not necessarily a conceptual one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The companion robot activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because no source in the row supports the medium's efficacy; the curriculum and left/right claims are topical only and do not establish that the floor-robot teaches or assesses better than embodied movement.

Activity 2's sourceClaims were reduced to the left/right frame-dependence claim, which directly supports anchoring body left/right and directional activities; the curriculum turns claim was removed there as merely topical to route-giving.

The source framed a static image, 3D avatar, and open dialogue as poorly or marginally suited and asserted that '3D adds nothing' and that a dialogue 'cannot deliver or assess' the skill. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; retained here only as the narrow objective limit that recognition/explanation tasks do not build or demonstrate the physical performance.

The original claim that 'no screen artefact reproduces the proprioceptive feedback of turning your own body' is a reasonable affordance point and is preserved as a scope limit, not as proof that only embodied activity can teach the concept.
The comparison between two quarter turns and a half turn, and between turn-then-walk vs walk-then-turn, is geometrically sound for planar turns and retained as stated.

probeDeeper: Do that quarter turn again but the other way — where do you face now?
Make two quarter turns — where are you facing? Is that the same as a half turn?
Give me the directions again, but for walking backwards from the bookshelf to here.
You turned to your right — if you were facing me, would 'your right' point the same way as 'my right'?
assess.correctAnswer: Rotates on the spot without walking; a quarter turn lands them facing 90° from the start (toward the next target) and a half turn faces them the opposite way; and their route directions are a followable sequence of moves and turns with correct directional words.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Turns' by walking forward in a curve or stepping sideways instead of rotating on the spot
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the spot with a hoop or footprints and require both feet to stay put, turning to face a named target.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: You SEE them travel across the floor rather than pivot in place

errorPatterns.pattern: A 'quarter turn' is a random amount because it is not aimed at a target facing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with fixed facings to turn TO (door then window) rather than reteaching the concept — the idea is held, the execution is unreferenced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finish facing is not 90° / not toward a wall; turn amounts are wobbly and inconsistent

errorPatterns.pattern: Turns the wrong way because left/right is judged from the observer or fixed to a wall, not from the direction they are facing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill this as a failure — reinforce body left/right (sticker) and keep exposure; frame-dependent left/right matures later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: You SEE the wrong-direction turn, especially after they have already turned to a new facing

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes a route as only 'go forward' steps, leaving the turns out, so the path cannot actually be followed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk their exact words back to them so they SEE the missing turn, then have them re-give the route.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When you follow their spoken route exactly, it walks into a wall because the turns are missing

responseLevels.gap: Walks or steps instead of pivoting, turn amounts are random, and left/right is frequently reversed; route directions cannot be followed.
responseLevels.full: Rotates a referenced quarter / half / three-quarter turn on the spot, links two quarter turns to a half turn, and both gives and follows a route as a coordinated sequence of moves and turns with correct directional words, transferring to a new start and goal (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Pivots on the spot and demonstrates a quarter or half turn to a named facing, and follows directional instructions, but turn amounts drift without a target, left/right reverses when the facing changes, or self-given routes omit the turns (multistructural — parts done, not coordinated into a reliable route).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch: 'Stand on this spot facing the door. Make a quarter turn to your right. ... Now make a half turn. ... Now give me directions to walk from here to the bookshelf.' Watch the body rotation and listen to the route — do not ask them to explain the procedure.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who ROTATES on the spot by a referenced amount from one who walks, steps sideways, or turns a random amount; and asking them to GIVE a route (not just follow one) shows whether the directional words are a productive tool. A child can follow 'turn right' by imitation but reveal the gap the moment they must produce a route.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Parallel and perpendicular lines
topic.description: Identify horizontal and vertical lines and pairs of perpendicular and parallel lines
evidence: Point out horizontal and vertical lines in shapes and real-world contexts
Identify a pair of parallel lines (lines that never meet and are always the same distance apart)
Identify perpendicular lines (lines that meet at a right angle)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a set of railway tracks or a window frame, can they point to which lines are parallel (never crossing) and which are perpendicular (meeting at a right angle)?

pedagogy.summary: At Year 3 children learn to see lines by ORIENTATION and RELATIONSHIP rather than as mere marks: horizontal (flat, like the horizon), vertical (upright), parallel (two lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet, however far extended) and perpendicular (two lines that cross at a right angle). The idea rests on the right-angle concept (perpendicular = a right angle between the lines) and on positional language. The characteristic errors treat a non-defining feature as defining — that parallel lines must be equal in length, or must be horizontal/vertical — and confuse the two relationship words with each other, because early examples nearly always show equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs.
bestPractices: Anchor the orientation words to images: horizontal = flat like the horizon or a table top; vertical = straight up like a wall or a standing person
Define parallel by the relationship — always the same distance apart, never meeting even if extended — and TEST by extending the lines or sliding a ruler, not by length or direction
Define perpendicular as meeting at a right angle and check with the corner of a card or a known right angle (links to the right-angle prerequisite)
Show parallel and perpendicular pairs in many orientations and unequal lengths, and in real contexts (railway tracks, window frames, the letter H) so the relationship, not the look, is learned
Separate the two relationship words explicitly and rehearse naming while pointing: these run alongside = parallel; these make a right angle = perpendicular
keyRepresentations: Real-world referents: horizon/table (horizontal), wall/lamppost (vertical), railway tracks (parallel), window corner / plus-sign (perpendicular)
The corner of a card or a set-square as a right-angle checker for perpendicular
A ruler slid between two lines, or the lines extended, to test 'always the same distance / never meet'
Letters and shapes marked up — an H has parallel verticals and a perpendicular cross-bar; a rectangle's sides
commonMisconceptions: Confuses 'horizontal' and 'vertical' (which word is which)
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length
Thinks lines only count as parallel/perpendicular when they are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Confuses 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'

learn.summary: Year 3 learners classify lines by orientation and relationship, not by their look: horizontal (flat like the horizon or a tabletop), vertical (upright like a wall or standing person), parallel (always the same distance apart, never meeting however far extended) and perpendicular (meeting or crossing at a right angle). The core work is replacing appearance-based judgements (that parallel must be equal length, or that only horizontal/vertical pairs count) and separating the two relationship words. The practical test for parallel is extending the lines and checking that the gap between them stays the same; a drawing can only be extended so far, so 'not meeting on the page' supports, but does not by itself prove, 'never meeting'. The practical test for perpendicular is checking the angle where the lines meet against a known right angle, in any orientation.

activities.title: Extend and rotate: what parallel really means
feedback: If a learner says a tilted, unequal pair 'isn't parallel because the lines are different lengths', show parallel pairs of very different lengths and re-test by extending: length is irrelevant, only constant distance / never meeting matters.

If a learner rejects a tilted pair because it is 'slanted/wonky', rotate a pair they already accept as parallel off horizontal so they see the relationship is preserved, then use tilted real examples.
When the extended lines cross, point back to the prediction and connect the outcome: converging means not parallel, however small the lean.
When the right-angle checker reads a tilted cross as perpendicular, name it: these meet at a right angle, so they are perpendicular even though the whole cross is tilted.
activities.rationale: Extending and rotating live lines makes the defining relationship (never meet / same distance apart) observable rather than inferred from appearance, directly targeting the equal-length and orientation-bound errors reinforced by typical equal-length horizontal/vertical examples. An extend-to-edge control, draggable/rotatable lines, an any-orientation right-angle detector, and a labelled gallery of real photos are concrete ways to make the mechanism visible; they are optional illustrations, not required tools — paper, a ruler and a card corner achieve the same tests.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. standard orientation) as if defining, rejecting non-standard examples — the mechanism behind rejecting a tilted parallel pair
learnerActions: Start with two lines on screen or drawn on paper that look 'wonky' and are different lengths; predict aloud whether they will ever cross if extended, and say why before testing.

Extend both lines all the way to the edges (press an EXTEND button, or continue the lines with a ruler across a large sheet), observe whether they meet, and measure the gap between them at several places to see whether it stays the same.

Drag or draw a second pair that looks nearly parallel but leans enough to converge within the page or screen; extend them and watch them cross. Note that a very tiny lean might only cross beyond the edge, and the narrowing gap still shows the lines are not parallel.
Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal and confirm the relationship is kept when tilted.

Use a right-angle checker (the corner of a card, a set-square, or a detector that glows green) on a perpendicular crossing pair tilted to 45 degrees to confirm a right angle is still a right angle whichever way the corner faces.
Label real photos or scenes — railway tracks, ladder rungs, window frames, the letter H — as parallel or perpendicular, including tilted and unequal examples.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallel means staying the same distance apart and never meeting however far extended — not being flat and not being equal in length; and a right angle stays a right angle at any orientation.

activities.title: Anchor and separate the four words
feedback: If a learner calls a right-angle pair 'parallel', re-anchor: parallel lines run alongside and never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle — check the corner with a card.
If a learner points to a vertical line when asked for a horizontal one, re-anchor horizontal to the flat horizon/tabletop and vertical to an upright wall or standing person, then re-ask.
activities.rationale: Early examples almost always show equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs, so the words are learned by association and get swapped; explicit naming-while-pointing and real referents (horizon, wall, tracks, window corner, letter H) separate orientation from relationship. This activity rehearses vocabulary; it supports but does not replace the extend/never-meet work.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method
learnerActions: Point to a horizontal line in the room and a vertical one, naming each and saying a memory hook (horizontal = flat like the horizon; vertical = upright like a wall).
For each pair of lines shown, point and say which relationship it is: 'these run alongside and never meet = parallel'; 'these make a right angle = perpendicular'.
Mark up letters and shapes: find the parallel verticals and the perpendicular cross-bar in an H; mark a rectangle's parallel sides and perpendicular corners.
Deliberately practise cases that are easy to mix up — a right-angle crossing (perpendicular, not parallel) and a vertical line asked for when a horizontal one is shown.
activities.intendedInsight: The four terms name distinct ideas: horizontal/vertical are orientations, parallel/perpendicular are relationships between two lines; naming while pointing keeps them apart.

activities.title: Predict, observe, explain and a sorting check
feedback: Treat the reason the learner gives before testing as diagnostic: a length reason ('one's longer, so not parallel') or a tilt reason ('too slanted') signals an appearance-based rule — respond with extended unequal and rotated examples.
Reinforce the full justification: 'parallel because they stay the same distance apart and would never meet however far extended; their tilt and lengths don't matter.'
activities.rationale: Predicting and justifying before observing exposes whether the learner is applying a length or orientation rule rather than the defining relationship; sorting and matching assess recognition cleanly but test the outcome rather than building the never-meet intuition, so they work best after the manipulation activity. Choosing tilted and rotated items prevents appearance-based guessing from succeeding.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. standard orientation) as if defining, rejecting non-standard examples — the mechanism behind rejecting a tilted parallel pair
learnerActions: Given two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths, predict whether they will ever cross if extended across the room, and give a reason before extending.
Extend them and compare the result to the prediction; explain any surprise.
Sort a set of line-pairs into parallel / perpendicular / neither, including tilted parallel pairs and rotated right-angle crosses chosen so appearance-based answers fail.
Match each word (horizontal, vertical, parallel, perpendicular) to a picture, including non-standard orientations.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer must rest on the relationship (same distance / never meet; meet at a right angle), not on tilt or length; the reason a learner gives before testing reveals which rule they are using.

constraints: Perpendicular depends on the right-angle concept; learners need to recognise or check a right angle (card corner / set-square) first.

Recognition-only formats (sorting, matching, multiple choice) assess the outcome and do not elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals a learner's underlying rule; use them alongside, not instead of, extend/predict tasks. This is a narrow affordance point, not a claim that sorts cannot support classification.

A static reference scene (tap tracks -> 'parallel'; tap a window corner -> 'perpendicular') is a useful poster but cannot be extended or re-tested, so it cannot run the never-meet check; use it as a reference after the interactive work.
Always include tilted and unequal-length examples; equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs alone reinforce the very misconceptions being targeted.

Interactive controls (extend button, drag/rotate, right-angle detector, photo gallery) are illustrative examples of making the test concrete, not mandatory tools; paper, ruler and card corner serve equally.

At this level these are planar page relations and extending to three dimensions is unnecessary here. A flat on-screen or paper diagram represents ideal lines, which have no thickness; the drawn marks are thin, finite approximations, and the 'extend forever / never meet' test reasons about the idealised lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The statutory Year 3 content claim is flagged verified:false in the row and supports only the topic/curriculum scope, not a specific teaching principle; it is retained here as context and was not used as an activity sourceClaim. The two misconception/prototype claims are flagged verified:true; verification status was not re-checked here. The NCETM claim directly covers parallel/perpendicular vocabulary confusion; its use for the horizontal/vertical swap component is by extension.

The legacy 'poor fit' claims that dialogue 'cannot deliver the seeing' and that a third dimension 'adds nothing' were softened to narrowly scoped affordance statements; catalog fit ratings do not establish universal necessity or that one medium cannot teach the concept.

Drawn lines on paper or screen have thickness and finite length, which are approximations of ideal lines; distinguish the idealised line (no thickness, extends without end) from the visible mark, including in child-facing talk about 'extending forever'. Screen edges are finite, so pair on-screen extension with ruler/paper extension to convey 'never meet, however far extended'.

assess.poeTask: Show two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths. Ask the child to PREDICT — 'if we keep extending both lines further and further, will they ever cross?' — and to say WHY before you do it. Then extend both lines to the edges of the page and OBSERVE that they never meet. Ask the child to EXPLAIN the result if they predicted the lines would cross. The reason given before extending is the diagnostic part: a child judging by length or tilt often predicts the lines will meet.
probeDeeper: If we made these two lines much longer, stretching them right across the room, would they ever cross? How do you know?
Point to a horizontal line in the room, and a vertical one. Which is which, and how do you remember?
Here are two lines that make a right angle where they cross — are those parallel or perpendicular?
These two lines lean the same way but one is short and one is long — can they still be parallel?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — they are parallel. They stay exactly the same distance apart all the way along and would never meet, however far you extended them. Their tilt and their different lengths don't matter; parallel is about staying the same distance apart and never meeting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks parallel lines must be the SAME LENGTH — says the tilted unequal pair is not parallel because the lines differ in length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show parallel pairs of very different lengths; define parallel by constant distance / never meeting, tested by extending — length is irrelevant (NCETM).
errorPatterns.distractor: No — the two lines are different lengths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, gives a length reason ('one's longer, so they can't be parallel')

errorPatterns.pattern: Orientation-bound — thinks lines are only parallel/perpendicular when horizontal or vertical, so a tilted parallel pair 'isn't parallel'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal so the child sees the relationship is preserved; use tilted real examples (prototype/imposed-attribute: orientation wrongly treated as defining).
errorPatterns.distractor: No — they are slanted, not straight across or straight up
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' because the lines are 'slanted/wonky', or accepts only flat/upright pairs

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the relationship or orientation words — swaps 'parallel'/'perpendicular', or 'horizontal'/'vertical'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word: parallel = run alongside, never meet; perpendicular = meet at a right angle; horizontal = flat like the horizon, vertical = upright. Rehearse naming while pointing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a right-angle pair 'parallel', or points to a vertical line when asked for a horizontal one

responseLevels.gap: Judges parallel/perpendicular by length or by horizontal/vertical orientation; says the tilted unequal pair isn't parallel; swaps the relationship terms or the horizontal/vertical labels.
responseLevels.full: Says the tilted unequal pair is parallel and justifies by 'same distance apart / never meet, even if extended'; identifies horizontal and vertical lines and perpendicular (right-angle) pairs in any orientation and in real contexts, using the terms correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies parallel/perpendicular and horizontal/vertical in standard (flat/upright, equal-length) cases and can state a definition, but reverts to appearance on tilted or unequal-length pairs, or occasionally mixes the two relationship words.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child two lines that are genuinely parallel but drawn TILTED (diagonal) and of clearly DIFFERENT lengths. Ask: 'Are these two lines parallel?' Then, whatever they say: 'How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The pair is tilted and unequal in length precisely so that a child judging by orientation or length says 'no'. A child holding the relationship (same distance / never meet) says yes and justifies by imagining the lines extended; a child running the same-length or horizontal-only rule says no, exposing the non-defining feature on the reason tier.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Right Angles & Turns
topic.description: Identify right angles; recognise that two right angles make a half-turn, three make three-quarters, and four make a complete turn
evidence: Use a right-angle checker to identify right angles in shapes and the environment
Classify angles as right angles, less than a right angle, or greater than a right angle
Explain that 4 right angles make a full turn (360°)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the corner of a piece of paper, can they tell you that's a right angle — and that spinning all the way round takes four right angles?

pedagogy.summary: The right angle is the benchmark angle of Y3: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. Children learn to identify it with a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) and to classify other angles relative to it — less open or more open. The turn facet is quantitative: two right angles make a half turn, four make a complete turn (360°). The pedagogical goal is that the right angle becomes a reusable UNIT of comparison whose identity is independent of orientation and of arm length.
bestPractices: Make the checker: fold paper (or a circle) twice to build a right-angle tester and have children place it into real corners to test — a concrete, self-checking tool (NCETM 'Monster Right Angle Measurer').
Build right angles from turns: a quarter turn is one right angle, two quarter turns make a half turn (a straight line), four bring you back to the start; link to the four compass points.
Classify by comparison before naming: is this corner more open or less open than my checker? — establishing the less-than / greater-than idea informally ahead of the words acute/obtuse.
Vary orientation on purpose — rotate and mirror right angles off the upright — so 'right angle' is not tied to a standard L.
Connect the two facets: a quarter turn LEAVES a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker / folded-paper tester, and the small-square right-angle mark
The clock face and compass rose showing quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns
Body turns and a hinge / geo-strip opened exactly to a right angle
The four right-angled corners of squares and rectangles
commonMisconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start

learn.summary: Year 3 children learn the right angle as a reusable benchmark unit: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. They build and use a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) to test real corners, classify other angles as less open or more open than a right angle, and compose turns from right angles (two make a half turn, four a complete turn / 360°). Key goal: the right angle's identity is independent of orientation and arm length.

activities.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
feedback: If the checker sits flush, it is a right angle — stamp the small square; a rectangular window corner should fit exactly.
If the corner is more open than a right angle, the checker's arm cannot reach the corner's other side and leaves a gap between them.

If the corner is less open than a right angle, the checker's arm overhangs past the corner's side — a pizza slice tip is usually less open than a right angle when the pizza is cut into more than four equal slices, but test it to check.
For the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation: it still fits exactly, so it is still a right angle — being 'on its side' does not change it.
For the long-armed corner, place the checker on both the long-armed and a short-armed right angle: both fit, so arm length does not make a corner 'bigger'.
(Adult note: the more-open case is an obtuse angle and the less-open case an acute angle; keep the child's language to 'more open' / 'less open' at this stage.)
activities.rationale: A concrete, self-checking tester lets children test rather than eyeball corners, intended to counter the 'sharp-looking = right angle' habit. Seeding tilted and long-armed right angles aims at the orientation-dependence and arm-length misconceptions; framing angle as opening (fit of the checker) rather than side length addresses the whole-object/side-length misconception, which the cited source notes is countered by framing angle as turn/opening.
sourceClaims: Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.
Deliberately test corners that are tilted off-upright and corners drawn with very long arms, turning the checker to match each corner before reading the fit.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

activities.title: Build turns from right angles
feedback: If you predicted two turns to get home, notice that after two quarter turns in the same direction from your stated starting direction you are facing backwards — it takes four quarter turns in the same direction to return home.
After each quarter turn, confirm one right angle has been added; two make a half turn / straight line, four make 360°.
If you lose count, mark each quarter position on the floor or compass rose so the right angles stack visibly.
activities.rationale: Physically composing turns, with a prediction stated first against a named starting direction, surfaces the common miscount (that two right angles make a full turn, or that a half turn returns you to the start). Connecting the quarter turn to the static square corner joins the two facets of the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.
learnerActions: Stand facing a chosen landmark (e.g. the window). Predict: how many quarter turns will bring you back to facing exactly the way you started? Say why before turning.
Make the turns one quarter at a time, always turning the same way (e.g. all clockwise), counting one right angle each time and noticing which way you face after each.
Pause after two quarter turns: notice you are facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), not home.
Link to the four compass points and a clock face: a quarter turn is one right angle, two a half turn, three a three-quarter turn, four a full turn (360°).
With a hinge or two geo-strips, open exactly to a right angle and connect: a quarter turn leaves a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
activities.intendedInsight: Turns are composed of right angles: two right angles make a half turn (facing back), three make a three-quarter turn, and four make a complete turn (360°) back to the start.

activities.title: Sort and classify mixed angles
feedback: You should select the tilted and long-armed right angles as well as the upright one — all three fit the checker exactly.
Leave out the just-less and just-more angles: the checker will not sit flush on them.
Justify by fit / quarter turn / square corner, not by which way the angle points or how long its arms are.
If you missed the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation and re-test.
activities.rationale: A mixed set including a tilted and a long-armed right angle lets the task discriminate a child who tests against the benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. Asking for the reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Look at a set of about five angles laid out in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious upright right angle.
Point to every right angle you can find, testing each with your checker rather than judging by appearance.
Sort the remaining angles into 'less open than a right angle' and 'more open than a right angle'.
Pick one angle you called a right angle and explain how you know — 'it fits my checker / it's a quarter turn / it makes a square corner'.
Order a few angles from least open to most open.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying angles relative to the right-angle benchmark (less / equal / greater) establishes the less-than and greater-than idea informally, ahead of the words acute and obtuse, and relies on testing not appearance.

constraints: The right-angle concept is planar; turning in space or testing real 3D object corners can add interest but is not required to establish the benchmark idea.

Classification/counting questions (right / less / greater, order by openness, count right angles in a turn) can reliably assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the hands-on testing of fitting a checker or the physical composing of turns — pair any such assessment with hands-on testing and turning.

A static picture that reveals 'right angle / not' when corners are tapped can support recognition and the small-square notation, but does not let a child test corners or compose turns; treat it as a partial scaffold for one facet only.
Deliberately include rotated/mirrored and long-armed right angles in any task so the benchmark is not tied to a standard upright L or to arm length.
When children predict turns, have them state the result relative to a stated starting direction (e.g. 'facing the window') so the count of right angles is unambiguous.
Keep child-facing language to 'less open' / 'more open' than a right angle at this stage; introduce acute/obtuse only as later vocabulary, not within these Year 3 prompts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Removed the formal terms acute/obtuse from child-facing feedback to stay consistent with the stated goal of establishing less-open/more-open informally ahead of those words; retained them only as an adult note.

An optional on-screen version could use a draggable checker that glows green and stamps a small square on an exact fit (showing 'less open' / 'more open' otherwise) and a turn dial that adds quarter turns while a counter shows right angles (2 = facing back, 4 = home / 360°). These are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.

The source claimed 3D 'adds cost without deepening' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot deliver' the felt fit of a checker; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited evidence and have been softened to scoped notes about affordances.

The source framed a quiz as assessing but 'not building checker intuition' — retained only as an objective limit that recognition/selection tasks do not themselves elicit hands-on testing; a selected-response format can still be used during teaching.
Efficacy phrasing in activity rationales was kept as 'intended/aims to' because these are unvalidated proposals; only the side-length-as-opening framing is directly supported by sources[2].claim.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT how many right-angle (quarter) turns it takes to end up facing exactly the way they started, and to say WHY, before doing it. Then have them make the turns one quarter at a time, counting a right angle each time and noticing where they face after two. A child who predicts two must confront landing facing backwards after two turns; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This corner is tilted over on its side. Is it still a right angle? How could you check?
If you stand facing me and make two quarter turns, which way are you facing now, and how many right angles was that?
I drew this right angle with really long arms and this one with short arms. Is the long one a bigger angle? Why?
How is a right angle different from this one that's just a little bit more open than your checker?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects the true right angles regardless of orientation or arm length (including the tilted one and the long-armed one), leaves out the just-less and just-more ones, and justifies by 'it's a quarter turn / it fits my right-angle checker / it makes a square corner' rather than by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: A right angle must point up like an L; a tilted or mirrored one is not a right angle ('that one's on its side, so it's different')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the checker itself onto the tilted corner so it still fits exactly — show the right angle is preserved under rotation; have the child re-test each corner with the checker turned to match.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the tilted right angle and selects only upright ones

errorPatterns.pattern: The right angle with long arms is bigger / 'more than' a right angle ('its lines are longer so the corner is bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place the checker on the long-armed and the short-armed right angles in turn — both fit exactly; return to opening-not-length with the hinge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-armed right angle as too big, or ranks it as more open than the checker

errorPatterns.pattern: Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle ('that looks about square to me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the checker — place it and read 'more open' or 'less open'; build the habit of testing rather than eyeballing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Selects the just-less and just-more angles as right angles without testing them

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts right angles in a turn — two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn brings you back to the start
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically make the turns, one right angle per quarter, marking each: two land you facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), four bring you home.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to count right angles in a turn, says two make a full turn, or cannot say four make 360°

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only the upright L as a right angle, or labels corners as right angles by appearance without testing; miscounts right angles in a turn.
responseLevels.full: Uses the right angle as an orientation- and length-independent benchmark: tests any corner against it, classifies less/greater confidently, and explains a turn as built from right angles (two make a half turn, four a full turn / 360°), transferring to new corners and turns (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies upright right angles, uses the checker on standard cases, and can recall that four right angles make a full turn, but treats these as separate skills — fails on the tilted or long-armed right angle, or cannot connect the quarter turn to the static square corner (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out about five angles in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle drawn with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious right angle. Ask: 'Point to every right angle you can find.' Then: 'Pick one you chose and tell me how you know it's a right angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a tilted right angle and a long-armed right angle separates a child who tests against the quarter-turn/checker benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. The tier-2 reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding angles
topic.description: Recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn
evidence: Identify angles at the corners of 2-D shapes
Describe a turn (e.g. quarter turn, half turn) in terms of the angle made
Explain that an angle measures the amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to point to an angle on the corner of a book or door frame, can they find it — and explain that swinging a door open is also a kind of turn (angle)?

pedagogy.summary: At Y3 'angle' is a genuinely dual idea: it names both the static corner of a shape and the dynamic amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point. Research (Williams & Shuard) argues the dynamic turn/opening conception is the more fruitful one and should be developed first through embodied turning, then bound to the static corners children already see in shapes. The central conceptual hurdle is separating the SIZE of an angle (its opening/turn) from the lengths of the lines that form it — children default to judging by side length.
bestPractices: Begin dynamically: children physically turn (whole body, then arms) and describe quarter/half turns before any corner is named an angle, extending their Y2 turn vocabulary.
Use the 'opening' image — open a book, scissors or a fan and watch the angle grow while the sides stay the same length — so size is felt as opening, not length.
Deliberately vary arm length while holding the opening fixed (and vice versa) so children see the angle stay the same though the lines change, directly confronting the length misconception.
Bind the two meanings explicitly: walk the perimeter of a large floor shape, making a turn at each corner, so every vertex is felt as a turn and seen as a corner.
Consider a fresh, non-length word for the quantity being measured; a novel label helps children stop mapping 'angle' onto the whole figure (Xu et al.).
keyRepresentations: Two hinged arms / geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker — the canonical dynamic model: open and close with arms of fixed length
The opening book, pair of scissors, or fan (opening grows, sides constant)
The child's own body turning (embodied quarter/half turn), then one arm held fixed while the other sweeps
Corners of familiar 2-D shapes with the angle arc marked at the vertex
commonMisconceptions: An angle is bigger when its arms/sides are longer — size judged by line length rather than opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. length-inconsistent trials near 0%)
An angle is 'the distance between the ends of the lines' — a gap between the tips rather than the opening
The whole-object assumption: 'angle' refers to the entire figure, so the amount-of-turn dimension is never separated out (van Hiele holistic processing)
A corner and a turn are unrelated ideas — the child fails to see a shape's corner as a turn, or a turn as producing a corner

learn.summary: At Year 3, 'angle' is a dual idea: the static corner of a shape AND the dynamic amount of turn/opening between two lines meeting at a point. The central hurdle is separating the SIZE of an angle (its opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines forming it — children default to judging by side length. Guidance develops the dynamic turn/opening conception first through embodied turning and 'opening' objects, deliberately varies arm length against a fixed opening to confront the length misconception, then binds turn and corner together explicitly.

activities.title: Turn, then open: building angle as amount of turn
feedback: If a learner says the angle grew 'because the lines got longer' while opening scissors, point out the two blades are the same length throughout — only the opening between them changed.
When a learner opens a book or fan, ask them to track one edge: the edge stays the same length, yet the angle clearly grows, so the growth is in the opening.
Affirm descriptions that use turn/opening language ('I opened the arms further apart') over descriptions that reference the figure's overall size.
activities.rationale: Research cited here argues the dynamic turn/opening conception is the more fruitful one and should be developed first, extending children's earlier turn vocabulary. 'Opening' objects (book, scissors, fan) keep the sides a fixed length while the opening visibly grows, so size is felt as opening rather than length.
sourceClaims: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.
The Year 3 statutory statement is to 'recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn'.
learnerActions: Physically turn your whole body a quarter turn, then a half turn; then do the same with an arm held out, describing each turn aloud.
Open a book, a pair of scissors, or a fan slowly and watch the angle between the parts grow while the two parts themselves stay exactly the same length.
Hold two hinged strips (geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker) pinned at one point; swing one strip open from a small opening to a large one and describe what is changing.
State in your own words what you actually had to do to 'make the angle bigger' (open the lines further apart / turn more).
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is the amount of turn or opening between two lines meeting at a point — something you grow by opening the lines apart, not by making the lines longer.

activities.title: Change the arms, keep the opening: confronting the length rule
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the long one is bigger because its lines are longer', overlay the two equal-opening angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned — the second arms land on the same line, showing the openings are identical.
When arms are lengthened with the opening fixed, draw attention to the arc/turn at the vertex staying the same while the arm ends shoot outward.

If a learner judges by the gap between the line tips, draw arcs centred on the vertex at several distances along the arms: arcs further out are longer, just as the gap between the arms widens further out, yet every arc shows the same amount of turn. Lengthening the arms moves the tips further from the vertex, so the tip-gap grows, but the angle is the amount of turn at the vertex, not the distance between the ends.
activities.rationale: Children default to judging angle size by irrelevant properties such as side length, enclosed area, or distance between the tips; on length-inconsistent trials accuracy is very low. Deliberately varying arm length while holding the opening fixed (and vice versa), plus predicting before testing, directly targets this misconception. Overlaying equal-opening angles makes the invariance observable.
sourceClaims: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.

Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Set a hinged angle maker to a fixed opening. Predict aloud whether making both arms twice as long would make the angle bigger, and say why BEFORE testing.
Lengthen (or swap for longer strips) both arms while keeping the opening unchanged; check whether the opening/turn has changed.
Reverse it: hold the arm length fixed and only change the opening, describing which action actually changes the angle.

Compare two drawn angles with the SAME opening but very different arm lengths: predict which is bigger, then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the second arms fall exactly on top of each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the lines longer does not make the angle bigger; only changing the opening/turn changes the angle. Length of the arms and size of the angle are independent.

activities.title: Walking the shape: a corner is a turn
feedback: If a learner says 'a square has corners, it doesn't turn', have them physically walk the perimeter and notice their body turns at each corner before marking the arc there.
If a learner can describe quarter/half turns but cannot point to the angle at a corner, lay the hinge onto the corner so the two sides become the two arms of a turn.
Praise answers that name both the corner and the turn together (e.g. 'this corner is a quarter turn').
activities.rationale: The two conceptions — static corner and dynamic turn — must be bound together explicitly. Walking a square or rectangular perimeter, where each walking turn is a quarter turn matching the right-angled corner, together with laying a hinge along the two sides of any corner, lets corners be felt as turns and seen as corners. This matches the Year 3 aim to recognise angles as a property of shape OR a description of a turn. For non-right corners the walking turn is not the corner's size, so use the hinge for those.
sourceClaims: The Year 3 statutory statement is to 'recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn'.

The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.
learnerActions: Walk the perimeter of a large taped square or rectangle, making the turn at each corner and feeling that each turn is a quarter turn.
At each corner, stop and point to the corner where you turned, then mark the arc inside the corner between the two sides, noticing that this square corner and your turn are both a quarter turn.
Place a hinged angle maker onto the corner of a familiar 2-D shape so its arms lie along the two sides; describe the corner as an amount of turn.

Say how much turn a square corner is (a quarter turn), then use the hinge on a narrower (sharper) and a wider corner to say whether each corner is less or more than a quarter turn of one side onto the other.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's corner is an angle: it is the amount one side would turn about the corner point to lie along the other side, which a hinge laid on the corner can show. At a square or rectangle corner this is a quarter turn, the same as the quarter turn you make walking round it, which links the static and dynamic meanings of 'angle'.

activities.title: A fresh name for the opening (optional scaffold)
feedback: If a learner slips back to describing the whole figure's size, re-point to the opening using the agreed fresh name and vary everything else.
Treat the whole-object framing ('the big one just has more to it') as a normal starting point, not a mistake to confront — keep pointing to the opening over time.
activities.rationale: Children's whole-object assumption (holistic processing) means 'angle' is read as the entire figure. Framing angle as the measure of rotation/opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, is reported to help children separate the size dimension. This is a supportive scaffold layered onto the hands-on work, not a standalone method, and its benefit for an individual learner is not established here.
sourceClaims: Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Agree a fresh, non-length word for the quantity being measured (the 'opening' or 'turn amount') and use it instead of 'angle' for a while.
Each time you compare two angles, point to the opening/turn with the new name while varying arm length, tip distance, or figure size, checking only the opening decides.
Return to the word 'angle' once you can consistently point to the opening as the thing being compared.
activities.intendedInsight: Giving the measured quantity a fresh, non-length name may help stop 'angle' being mapped onto the whole figure, so the size dimension (the opening/turn) can be separated out.

activities.title: Check and discriminate: same opening, different arms
feedback: A judgement justified by the opening/turn is the target. If a learner reaches a correct choice by reasoning about line length instead — even a correct 'same' — re-ground it by overlaying the pair vertex-on-vertex: equal-opening pairs show the openings coinciding, while different-opening pairs show the openings genuinely differ regardless of arm length.
If a learner picks the long-armed angle as bigger when the openings are actually equal, return to the hinge and lengthen the arms with the opening held fixed to show the angle does not change.
Use the reason, not just the choice, to tell a secure understanding from a lucky guess — the mix of equal- and different-opening pairs prevents scoring by always answering 'same'.
activities.rationale: A discrimination task comparing angles with varied arm lengths, including both equal and genuinely different openings, is useful to CHECK whether the opening-versus-length separation has formed; requiring the stated reason distinguishes genuine from lucky correct answers. Recognition/discrimination tasks assess the idea rather than build the felt separation, so this follows the hands-on construction rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Judge several angle pairs with varied arm lengths — some pairs with EQUAL openings and some with GENUINELY DIFFERENT openings — choosing 'same', 'bigger', or 'smaller' for each, so that each choice is sometimes the correct answer.

For each judgement, state the REASON before confirming — e.g. 'same, because the lines have opened by the same amount', or 'that one is bigger because it has turned further open' — justifying by the opening/turn, not the arm length.
Explain whether two lines that meet but barely open apart make a big or a small angle, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: You can reliably decide whether an angle is the same, bigger or smaller by comparing openings/turns, ignoring arm length and tip distance, and you can say why.

constraints: Develop the dynamic turn/opening conception first, then bind it to the static corners children already see in shapes; the Year 3 aim is to recognise angles as a property of shape OR a description of a turn.

The key conceptual target is separating the SIZE of an angle (opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines that form it — activities must vary arm length against a fixed opening (and vice versa), not only present angles with equal arms.

A static reveal that merely labels corners as angles is a limited scaffold: it can name corners but does not let a child vary opening against length, which is where the concept forms. Pair any such display with manipulation.

Recognition or sorting tasks CHECK the discrimination but do not by themselves build the felt invariance of opening under changing arm length; use them after hands-on construction, require the learner's reason (not just the choice), and include both equal- and different-opening pairs so no response can be chosen by default.
Treat the whole-object framing ('angle' means the whole figure) as a normal developmental starting point to grow past over time, not a false belief to confront head-on.

A live hinge with a turn readout and a slider that stretches both arms while the arc/counter stay frozen is an optional interaction example that makes the opening-versus-length mechanism concrete; it is one way to realise the idea, not a required technology. Equivalent physical manipulatives (geo-strips, split-pin angle maker, scissors, book, fan) serve the same purpose.

Physical objects (scissors, books, fans, strips) approximate the mathematical idea: their arms are finite and have thickness, whereas a mathematical angle is the opening between two idealised lines; keep returning attention to the opening at the vertex rather than the ends.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy row rated a 3D rendering as adding 'little' and a dialogue/conversation as unable to produce the felt invariance. These are catalogue-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been reframed as scaffold limits rather than universal claims. An embodied whole-body turn (a spatial, physical action) is retained as valuable, and talking about turns can still support learning even if it does not by itself create the felt opening-versus-length separation.

The legacy claim that a static tap-to-reveal 'cannot deliver the concept' has been softened: a fixed display can still teach by labelling corners, but cannot be manipulated to vary opening against length — stated as a scaffold limit, not an absolute.

Note the physical approximations: scissors, books, fans and strips have real thickness and real ends, whereas a mathematical angle is the opening between two idealised lines of unbounded length; the 'gap between the tips' intuition arises precisely because the drawn/physical arms are finite. This approximation is also addressed directly in activity 2 feedback, not only here.

Quantitative figures in the sources (e.g. ~3% and ~25% correct on length-inconsistent trials) are reproduced verbatim from the source claim text and were not independently checked in this rewrite; the original row's looser 'near 0%' phrasing was not carried through in favour of the more precise sourced figures.

assess.poeTask: Draw two angles with the same opening but very different arm lengths on separate cards. Ask the child to PREDICT which is the bigger angle and to say WHY before you test anything. Then overlay the cards, vertex on vertex with one arm aligned, so the second arms lie exactly on top of each other. A child who predicted 'the long one, because its lines are longer' must confront the second arms falling on the same line — the openings are identical. The reason, stated before observing, is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: You said they're the same. What if I made the lines on this one three times as long — would that change the angle? How do you know?
Show me with your arms: make a small angle, now make it bigger. What did you actually have to do to make it bigger?
Here's a corner of this triangle — where's the turn? If you walked along this side and round the corner, how much would you turn?
If two lines meet but hardly open apart at all, is that a big angle or a small one, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are the same size, because an angle is how much the lines have turned or opened apart from each other, and both have opened by the same amount — the length of the lines does not change the angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle with the longer lines is bigger ('these lines are longer, so it's a bigger angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the openings coincide; show the arms differ in length but the opening is identical. Return to the hinge model, lengthening the arms with the opening held fixed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The one with the longer lines is bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the long-armed angle, or answers 'same' but justifies it by talking about the line lengths

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle is the distance between the ends of the two lines ('it's how far apart the tips are')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the arc at the vertex and slide it inward and outward along the arms, showing the opening is the same however far out you look; contrast this with the ever-widening gap between the tips.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges by the gap between the endpoints, so a long-armed same-opening angle looks bigger; points at the space between the tips when justifying

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Angle' means the whole corner figure, so its size includes the lines and the space inside ('the big one just has more to it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat this as a false belief to confront — the whole-object framing is a normal starting point (van Hiele holistic processing). Give the quantity a fresh non-length name and repeatedly point to the opening/turn while varying everything else, letting the dimension separate over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the overall size of the figure (arms plus enclosed area) rather than the opening; cannot isolate the turn as a single quantity being compared

errorPatterns.pattern: A corner of a shape and a turn are different, unrelated things ('a square has corners, it doesn't turn')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk the perimeter of a large floor shape making the turn at each corner, then mark the arc at that corner — bind the felt turn to the seen corner so the two conceptions are recognised as one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can find corners but denies the vertex is a turn, or can describe quarter/half turns but cannot point to the angle at a shape's corner

responseLevels.gap: Judges angle size by the length of the arms or the gap between the tips; picks the long-armed angle as bigger and cannot say what quantity is being compared, treating 'angle' as the whole figure.
responseLevels.full: Explains an angle as the amount of turn/opening between two lines meeting at a point, holds this fixed when arm length changes, and transfers it — recognises a shape's corner as a turn and a turn as an angle, applying the idea to a new figure (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies angles at corners and can echo quarter/half-turn language, but holds these as separate facts — names the corner OR describes a turn without connecting them — and is inconsistent when arm length is varied (multistructural: parts present, relation absent).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put in front of the child two angles with the SAME opening, one drawn with long lines and one with short lines. Ask: 'Which angle is bigger — the one with the long lines, the one with the short lines, or are they the same?' Then, whatever they answer: 'Now tell me how you know.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands angle-as-opening answers 'same' AND justifies it by the amount of turn/opening. A child relying on side length picks the long-armed angle and typically says 'because the lines are longer.' The tier-2 reason is decisive: it separates a genuine 'same' (justified by equal opening) from a lucky 'same', and it exposes the length rule even when a child guesses correctly — right and wrong reasoning give different justifications.

sources.claim: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.
sources.source: NCETM, Misconceptions with the Key Objectives (citing Askew & Wiliam 1995; Williams & Shuard 1994)

sources.claim: Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
sources.source: Xu, Chen, Ma, Zhao, Jiao & Xin (2020), Frontiers in Psychology 11:568388

sources.claim: The Year 3 statutory statement is to 'recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn'.
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (gov.uk)

Recognising angles as turns extends Y2 work on quarter/half/three-quarter turns
