topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the hands on a clock showing different times, can they tell you which angle between the hands is acute (sharper than a right angle) and which is obtuse (wider)?

pedagogy.summary: Y4 extends the right-angle benchmark into naming and ordering: an acute angle is less open than a right angle, an obtuse angle is more open (up to a straight line, i.e. two right angles). Children classify angles as acute / right / obtuse and order them by openness. The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering when arm lengths differ — the exact task where the arm-length misconception bites (Askew & Wiliam locate the most common error here). Naming should follow secure less-than / greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
bestPractices: Anchor both names to the right angle: acute = less open than a right angle, obtuse = more open (but less than a straight line); compare every angle to the checker before naming it.
Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared — this defeats the arm-length and area traps.
Use a dynamic opening (hinge or fan) to sweep from acute through right to obtuse, naming each zone as it is passed.
Hunt for and colour-sort the acute, right and obtuse angles inside real triangles and quadrilaterals.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition, which is the comparison to a right angle.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker as the dividing benchmark, and an 'openness' scale from nothing to a straight line with the right angle marked in the middle
A hinge / fan sweeping through acute → right → obtuse
Overlay (vertex-on-vertex) comparison for ordering by opening
Acute / right / obtuse angles picked out and colour-sorted within shapes
commonMisconceptions: Ordering angles by arm length or by the distance between the tips rather than by the opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. list side length, enclosed area and distance between the sides as the irrelevant properties children use)
Judging by the space or area enclosed between the arms rather than the opening
Naming by appearance rather than by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or the two names simply swapped
Naming before comparing: applying acute/obtuse labels without checking against the right angle

learn.summary: Year 4 learners identify acute and obtuse angles and compare/order angles up to two right angles by size. Both names are anchored to the right angle: acute is less open than a right angle, obtuse is more open (but less than a straight line, i.e. two right angles). The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering angles when the arm lengths differ — children tend to judge by arm length, enclosed area, or the distance between the tips rather than by the opening. The proposed core teaching move is vertex-on-vertex overlay comparison, with naming intended to follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison rather than preceding it.

activities.title: Order the baited angles, then overlay to check
feedback: If a learner orders by arm length and places the long-armed narrow angle as largest, overlay that trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; then re-sort by opening.
If a learner asks whether shortening the long arms would change its place, let them test it — shortening the arms does not change the opening, so the order stays the same.
Confirm correct orderings that are justified by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each angle to a right angle, rather than by line length.
activities.rationale: A common comparison error is treating an angle as the distance between the ends of its lines, judging the angle with longer lines as larger; this may be reinforced when taught examples mostly use equal-length arms. Deliberately anti-correlating arm length with opening and then providing an overlay comparison is proposed to target exactly this misconception. An optional overlay tool that snaps two angles vertex-on-vertex, and a seeded four-angle task where the smallest opening has the longest arms, are intended to make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.
learnerActions: Receive four angles to drag into order from smallest to largest, where the smallest opening is deliberately drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms.
State out loud, before moving anything, which angle you think is biggest and why.
Overlay any two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned, so only the openings are compared.

Overlay the longest-armed angle on the shortest-armed one and watch the long-armed 'big-looking' angle's opening fall INSIDE the short-armed angle's opening, then compare the other pairs the same way and re-sort all four by opening.
Re-state the rule you now use to decide the order.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle's size is its opening, not the length of its arms, the distance between the tips, or the area enclosed. Overlaying vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned isolates the opening, so an angle with longer arms but a narrower opening is seen to be the smaller angle.

activities.title: Sweep a hinge through acute, right and obtuse
feedback: If a learner names an angle in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, return to the checker: less open than a right angle is acute, more open (but less than a straight line) is obtuse — test before labelling.
Confirm that obtuse 'stops' at a straight line (two right angles); an angle that is exactly a straight line, or more open than one, is not obtuse.
Treat mnemonics such as 'a cute little angle' as a memory hook only, not the definition — the definition is the comparison to a right angle.
activities.rationale: A dynamic opening that sweeps continuously through the three named zones, with the right angle marked as the dividing benchmark, is intended to attach names to degrees of openness rather than to how a shape looks, supporting naming by comparison rather than by appearance. The live label and small-square snap-in are optional feedback examples that make the benchmark visible.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Open a hinge or fan slowly from nearly closed to a straight line.

Watch (or control) a label that ticks through acute → right → obtuse as the opening grows, with a small square snapping in at the right angle, and that changes to 'straight line (not obtuse)' when the opening reaches a straight line.
Pause the sweep and name the zone the opening is currently in.
Identify where obtuse stops — at a straight line, which equals two right angles.
activities.intendedInsight: The names acute, right and obtuse are zones of openness defined relative to the right-angle benchmark: acute is less open than a right angle, right is exactly a right angle, and obtuse is more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

activities.title: Hunt and colour-sort angles inside shapes
feedback: If a learner labels an angle by appearance (e.g. calls a long-armed acute angle obtuse because it 'looks big'), return the naming to the checker and have them test the angle against a right angle before labelling.
Confirm classifications that are justified by comparison to the right angle rather than by overall size or orientation of the figure.
activities.rationale: Hunting for and colour-sorting the acute, right and obtuse angles inside triangles and convex quadrilaterals applies classification in a relational context — finding all angles of a type in a new shape — which is a more demanding application than classifying isolated angles. It is also intended to guard against naming by appearance when orientation or arm length is misleading.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Examine a given triangle or convex quadrilateral (one with no inside angle more open than a straight line).
Find every angle and decide whether it is acute, right or obtuse by comparing each to a right angle.
Colour-sort the angles by type (e.g. one colour for acute, one for right, one for obtuse).
Explain, for a tricky angle, how you checked it against the right angle rather than guessing from its appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Acute, right and obtuse angles occur inside real shapes, and each is classified by comparison to a right angle — not by the orientation of the shape or the length of its sides.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: short wide angle vs long narrow angle
feedback: If a learner predicts the long-armed angle is bigger because of its line lengths, overlay the pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening folds inside the wide one, then relate each back to the right-angle benchmark.

If a learner judges by the gap between the tips or the enclosed space, mark an arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; then overlay to compare the opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
Confirm answers that order by opening and justify by overlaying or comparing to a right angle, not by line length.
activities.rationale: Asking for a prediction and a reason before any movement is intended to surface whether the learner is using the length rule or comparing openings; the overlay then provides the disconfirming evidence. Marking and sliding an arc at the vertex addresses the related area/tip-distance misconception by showing the opening is invariant to how far out along the arms you look.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Look at two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening.
Predict which is the bigger angle and say why, before anything is moved.
Overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's.
Reconcile your prediction with what the overlay shows, and restate the rule for comparing angles.
Answer the probe: if the long arms were made much shorter, would the angle's place in the order change? Why? And could a short-armed angle ever be bigger than a long-armed one — can you draw one?
activities.intendedInsight: The reason a learner gives first is the diagnostic part: a learner who predicts B is bigger 'because its lines are longer' is asked to reconcile that with the wider opening of A winning once the angles are overlaid.

constraints: Anchor both names to the right angle: compare every angle to a right-angle checker before naming it. Acute = less open than a right angle; obtuse = more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared. Because the overlay compares the openings alone, differences in arm length, enclosed area and tip distance cannot drive the comparison.
Naming should follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition.

A static picture that reveals labels when tapped supports recognition and classification of clear cases, but it cannot carry out the overlay comparison or the dynamic sweep; treat it as a scaffold for classification only, not a replacement for the overlay work.

Classification and ordering practice (classifying angles as acute/right/obtuse, ordering them by size, and finding all of a type in a shape) is useful for assessment and practice, but recognising and ordering angles does not by itself build the overlay intuition for the length trap; pair it with hands-on overlay work.

If learners manipulate physical paper/card angle cutouts, note that cutouts have slight real thickness and can be held and overlaid, whereas the on-screen or ideal figure is a zero-thickness model of the mathematical angle; the comparison is about the represented angle, not the physical card.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D and in-role dialogue formats as poor fits and asserted a static image cannot build overlay intuition. These are presented here as narrowly scoped affordance/limit observations (a static reveal cannot perform the dynamic overlay or live sweep), not as universal claims about what any medium can teach; the cited sources establish the misconception and curriculum content, not comparative efficacy between media.

Self-audit of the geometry: an angle's measure is its opening and is invariant to arm length and to how far out along the arms you look; the 'slide the arc in and out' demonstration is consistent with this. Obtuse angles are those strictly between a right angle and a straight line; a straight line (two right angles) is the upper bound for this Year 4 topic. No arithmetic or force/motion content was present to correct.

The legacy attribution of this four-angle ordering task as 'Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task' and the phrase that the overlay 'defeats' the trap have been softened to proposed/geometric wording; the sources support the misconception's prevalence and the curriculum objective but not comparative efficacy of this specific design.

The colour-sort method itself is not evidenced by the cited sources; its supporting claims cover the identify-acute/obtuse content and the appearance-naming misconception it addresses, not the recolouring technique's effectiveness.

assess.poeTask: Show two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening. Ask the child to PREDICT which is the bigger angle and WHY before anything is moved. Then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's. A child who predicted B 'because its lines are longer' must confront the wider opening winning; the reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: You put this one first as the smallest, and it has the longest lines. If I made its lines much shorter, would it change its place in the order? Why?
Show me how you'd check, without measuring, whether this angle is acute or obtuse.
Is it possible for an angle with short little lines to be bigger than an angle with long lines? Can you draw me one?
How open can an angle get and still be called obtuse — where does obtuse stop?
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the angles by their opening, ignoring arm length (so the long-armed narrow angle goes first and the short-armed wide angle last), and justifies by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each to a right angle — not by how long the lines are.

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle with the longest lines is the biggest ('longer arms mean a bigger angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; re-sort by opening and return to the right-angle benchmark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by arm length, placing the long-armed narrow-opening angle as the largest, and justifies by mentioning the line lengths

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the space or gap between the arms — the angle that encloses more area, or whose tips are further apart, is the bigger angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; overlay to compare opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks a short-armed wide angle below a long-armed narrow one because it 'takes up less space' or its tips are closer together

errorPatterns.pattern: Names by appearance, not by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or acute and obtuse swapped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return every naming to the checker — less open than a right angle is acute, more open is obtuse — and have the child test before labelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an angle acute or obtuse in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, especially when arm length or orientation is misleading

responseLevels.gap: Orders and names angles by arm length, tip-distance, or enclosed space; swaps acute and obtuse or names by appearance; cannot separate the opening from the overall figure.
responseLevels.full: Orders and classifies purely by opening — overlaying or comparing to a right angle regardless of arm length — explains acute as less and obtuse as more open than a right angle (up to a straight line / two right angles), and finds all the acute and obtuse angles in a new shape (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Classifies clear acute / right / obtuse cases and recalls the names, and orders angles correctly when the arms are the same length, but is misled when arm length is anti-correlated with opening, or names an angle without comparing it to a right angle (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child four angles to order from smallest to largest, with arm length deliberately anti-correlated with opening — the smallest opening is drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms. Say: 'Put these four angles in order, from the smallest angle to the biggest.' Then: 'Tell me how you decided the order.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Anti-correlating arm length with opening means a child using the length rule produces a specifically reversed order on the trapped pair, while a child comparing openings orders correctly; the tier-2 reason reveals which method was used. This is Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task for the misconception.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Types of angles (age 8+)
topic.description: Use and interpret standard geometric diagram conventions: mark right angles with a small square, equal lengths with single or double tick marks, and equal angles with arc marks; label angles in three-letter notation (∠ABC) and individual angles with a single letter or number; draw diagrams showing angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and angles inside polygons with these conventions; read diagrams with these marks to identify given information and find unknown values
evidence: Mark a right angle with a small square symbol in a diagram and explain what it means
Use tick marks to show equal lengths in a shape and double tick marks for a second pair of equal sides
Read and interpret angle notation (e.g. angle ABC) and identify the angle being referred to in a diagram
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s maths diagram shows a small square in one corner and matching arc marks on two other angles, can they tell you what each mark means — and use them to figure out a missing angle without re-measuring?

pedagogy.summary: This is the shared LANGUAGE of geometric diagrams: a small square means exactly 90°, single and double tick marks mean 'these lengths are equal to each other' (a second, independent equal pair uses double ticks), matching arc marks mean equal angles, arrows mean parallel, and three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter, B. Fluency is two-way — reading a marked diagram to extract the given information, and producing correct marks when drawing. Crucially the marks encode relationships that are NOT to be read from the picture's appearance: a geometric diagram is a carrier of stated facts, not a scale drawing.
bestPractices: Teach each mark as a statement of a relationship — a tick pair asserts equal lengths, an arc pair asserts equal angles, a square asserts 90° — true regardless of how the picture looks.
Drill the three-letter rule with the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC is the angle at B; point to B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC.
Practise both directions: read a marked diagram aloud ('these two sides are equal, this angle is a right angle') AND mark up a plain diagram to encode given facts.
Stress 'not to scale' — use diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so pupils learn to trust the marks over the drawing.
Use double ticks for a second, different pair of equal lengths so pupils see that single versus double distinguishes independent equalities.
keyRepresentations: The mark key: small square = 90°, single/double ticks = equal lengths, single/double arcs = equal angles, arrows = parallel
A triangle or quadrilateral fully marked up and read as a set of statements
∠ABC with B highlighted as the vertex and BA, BC as the arms
A deliberately 'not to scale' diagram whose marks override its look
commonMisconceptions: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at the first (or last) letter rather than the middle letter (the vertex)
Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value rather than 'equal to each other', or treats single and double ticks as equal to one another
Treats the marks as decoration and judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance (assumes it is drawn to scale)
Thinks the small square is just 'a corner' rather than exactly 90°, or misses that unmarked features are unknown

learn.summary: Teach the shared language of geometric diagram markings as statements of relationships, not pictures: a small square asserts exactly 90°, a matching pair of single tick marks asserts 'these two lengths are equal to each other', a second independent equal pair uses double ticks, matching arc marks assert equal angles, and arrows assert parallel lines. Three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter (B), with arms BA and BC. Fluency runs in two directions — reading a marked diagram to extract the given facts, and adding correct marks when drawing. Critically, a geometric diagram carries stated facts and is not a scale drawing: the marks override the picture's appearance.

activities.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
feedback: If the learner labels ∠ABC using an arm letter (A or C), rehearse the rule: the middle letter is always the vertex — point to B first, then trace arms BA and BC. An optional interactive can light up the wrong angle when the wrong letter is tapped, making the mismatch visible.

If the learner reads a ticked side as a measurement (e.g. '1 unit') or treats a single-ticked and double-ticked side as equal, restate each mark as a relationship within its own pair and show that double ticks mark a separate, independent equal pair.
If the learner calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, insist the marks are the authority on a not-to-scale diagram.

When producing a diagram, check that every stated fact carries its mark and that equal marks are never left on just one side — a stated right angle needs a square, and equal sides need matching ticks on EVERY side in the equal group (both sides of a pair, or all sides if more than two are equal).
activities.rationale: The topic requires fluency in both reading and producing marks, so an activity that has the learner construct marks on a plain four-sided figure and then interpret a not-to-scale marked figure is intended to exercise both directions. A quadrilateral is used for the marking step so the single-tick pair and the independent double-tick pair can both be shown. Using appearance-contradicting diagrams targets the documented error of judging a figure by its look rather than its marked givens. (Proposed design; not empirically validated here.)
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.

A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.

Students with an accurate conception of angle read the additivity of angle measure from a diagram and solve for unknown angles using the MARKED given information (right angles and benchmark angles are marked in diagrams), i.e. the marks are the authoritative carriers of the givens.
learnerActions: Starting from a plain quadrilateral (a four-sided figure gives room to show two independent equal-side pairs without overlap), add a small square to the corner stated to be right-angled.

Add a single pair of tick marks to one pair of sides stated to be equal, and a double pair of ticks to a different, independent pair of equal sides — a four-sided figure is needed so the two pairs do not share a side.
Label a stated angle in three-letter notation by identifying its vertex: point to the vertex B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC, so the middle letter B names the angle ∠ABC.
Switch to reading: on a deliberately not-to-scale marked diagram where one side LOOKS longer but carries the matching tick, state which sides are equal from the marks, not the picture.
State aloud what each mark means as a relationship (e.g. 'these two sides are equal to each other', 'this angle is exactly 90°').
activities.intendedInsight: The marks, not the drawing, tell you the truth about a diagram, and the middle letter of three-letter notation is always the vertex.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal the mark key (reading scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct readings; where the learner's prediction differs from the reveal, name the relationship the mark asserts.
Highlighting the equal sides together reinforces that ticks mean 'equal to each other', not a measurement value.
activities.rationale: Reading conventional markings correctly is an explicit curriculum requirement, and misreading them is a convention violation; a reveal-based tool is intended to build the interpretation half of the skill by linking each symbol to a highlighted feature. It is a scaffold: it supports reading marks but does not ask the learner to produce marks, so it must be paired with construction practice. Its instructional effect is proposed, not empirically validated here.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Tap the small square to reveal 'this angle is exactly 90°'.
Tap a tick pair and see the two equal sides highlight together.
Tap ∠ABC and see the vertex B with its arms BA and BC light up.
Say each meaning aloud before revealing it, then check against the reveal.
activities.intendedInsight: Each symbol in the mark key encodes a specific relationship that can be read off a diagram reliably.

activities.title: Match and select: check interpretation and light production
feedback: If the learner selects the angle at A for ∠ABC, re-state the middle-letter rule and have them trace arms BA and BC from B.
If a single-ticked and double-ticked side are matched as equal, clarify that double ticks denote a separate, independent equal pair.
Choosing 'the angle at point A' for ∠ABC reveals the middle-letter misread; redirect to the vertex B.
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks are intended to check interpretation and limited production, and the ∠ABC item specifically targets the middle-letter misconception that source 1 identifies as a convention violation. Recognition tasks are efficient checks but do not require the learner to construct a full marked diagram, so they complement rather than replace hands-on marking.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Answer 'Which angle is ∠ABC?' by selecting the angle at vertex B, not the angle at A or C.
Match each mark (square, single tick pair, double tick pair, arc pair, arrows) to its meaning.
Mark the equal sides on a figure by selecting/drawing the pair that carries matching ticks.
On a not-to-scale item, identify equal sides from the marks even when one side looks longer.
activities.intendedInsight: Both interpreting marks and identifying where marks belong can be checked explicitly, including the middle-letter vertex rule.

activities.title: Probe diagram authority and unmarked features
feedback: Reinforce that two equally-ticked sides are equal regardless of apparent length.
∠BCA has vertex C, so it is a different angle from ∠ABC (vertex B).
If the learner assumes an unmarked corner is a right angle because it looks square, point out that only a drawn square asserts 90°; unmarked features are unknown.
activities.rationale: These prompts target the specific misconceptions of trusting appearance, misplacing the vertex, confusing single/double ticks, and assuming unmarked features. Reasoning about what the diagram does and does not state is intended to deepen the 'marks over appearance' principle.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.
learnerActions: Answer: 'This side LOOKS longer than that one, but both carry a single tick — which is actually longer?' (Answer: they are equal.)
Show ∠BCA on the same diagram and decide whether it is the same as ∠ABC or a different angle.
Decide what mark to add for a second pair of equal sides so no one confuses it with the first pair (double ticks).
Answer: 'This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?' (You cannot assume it; unmarked features are unknown.)
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are authoritative, three-letter names with different middle letters (vertices) denote different angles (though reversing the outer letters, as in ∠ABC and ∠CBA, names the same angle), and an unmarked feature is not a stated fact.

constraints: Cover BOTH directions: reading marked diagrams AND producing marks when drawing. A reading-only reveal tool is a scaffold and does not assess production; pair it with construction tasks.

Recognition and matching tasks check interpretation and light production but do not require constructing a complete marked diagram, so include a production task where the learner draws the square and adds matching ticks in pairs.
Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so learners practise trusting the marks over the picture.

Always add equal marks to every member of an equal group, so at least two sides are marked and never just one (e.g. both sides of an equal pair, or all three sides of an equilateral triangle); a stated right angle must carry a drawn square; unmarked features must be treated as unknown.

Reserve double ticks for a second, independent equal pair, and make clear single- and double-ticked sides are NOT equal to each other. Demonstrating two independent equal-side pairs needs a figure with at least four sides (a quadrilateral), not a triangle.

This notation is a convention of 2-D diagrams; a 3-D environment is not required for this objective. Paper-and-pencil marking is an acceptable medium for the production half alongside any interactive tool.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy wording is intended/proposed only.

The original row's recommendation described marking two independent equal-side pairs on a TRIANGLE; a triangle has only three sides, so two disjoint equal pairs cannot both be marked. Corrected to a quadrilateral for the marking step so the single- and double-tick pairs are coherent. Logged as an original-row error.

The legacy row claimed a 3-D environment 'has nothing to add' and that open dialogue cannot deliver this skill. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; softened to narrowly scoped notes that 2-D marking (including on paper) suffices for this objective and that spoken discussion can support reasoning about marks even if it is not the primary production medium.

Self-audit: verified that ∠ABC has vertex B (middle letter) and ∠BCA has vertex C (a different angle) — consistent throughout. Verified that matching single ticks mean equal lengths and that single vs double ticks denote distinct independent pairs, with single- and double-ticked sides NOT equal to each other. No arithmetic claims present.

Source 1 is cited in the reading/matching activities only to support the convention-reading principle and the fact that misreading a convention is a violation; it is not evidence that any particular interaction format is effective.

If I add a second pair of equal sides, what mark should I use so no one confuses them with the first pair?
This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the small square as 'this angle is exactly 90°', the tick marks as 'these two sides are equal in length', and identifies ∠ABC as the angle at vertex B (the middle letter); and on the plain diagram draws a small square in a corner to denote 90° and adds a matching pair of tick marks to two sides to denote equal lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at A (or C) instead of the vertex B ('ABC, so it's at A')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the rule explicit and rehearse it — the middle letter is always the vertex; point to it first, then trace the two arms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the wrong vertex for ∠ABC, or names an angle using an arm letter rather than the vertex letter

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value, or treats single- and double-ticked sides as equal to each other, rather than 'equal within their own pair'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State each mark as a relationship ('these two are equal to each other') and use double ticks for a separate, independent equal pair.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a ticked side is '1 unit', or claims a single-ticked and a double-ticked side are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the marks and judges lengths, angles and right angles from how the diagram looks (assumes it is drawn to scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams where the marks contradict the appearance, and insist the marks are the authority.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a not-to-scale diagram, calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, or calls an unmarked corner a right angle because it looks square

errorPatterns.pattern: When drawing, omits or misplaces the marks — states a right angle but adds no square, or ticks only one side of an equal pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check that each stated fact carries its mark, and that equal marks are added in pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The produced diagram does not encode the stated facts (missing square, a single tick on only one side)

responseLevels.gap: Judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance; misreads the vertex in ∠ABC; treats marks as decoration or as measurements.
responseLevels.full: Reads a marked diagram as a coherent set of stated relationships (trusting the marks over appearance), identifies ∠ABC by its middle-letter vertex, and produces diagrams that correctly encode given facts with square, tick and arc marks, transferring to a new figure (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual marks correctly in isolation (a square = 90°, a tick pair = equal) but misplaces the vertex in three-letter notation, is swayed by appearance on a not-to-scale diagram, or omits marks when producing a diagram (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a triangle marked with a small square at one corner, single tick marks on two of its sides, and one angle named ∠ABC. First (read): 'What does the small square tell you? What do the tick marks tell you? Which angle is ∠ABC — point to it.' Then (produce): 'On this second plain diagram, mark a right angle with the correct symbol, and show that two of its sides are equal in length.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child both to READ the marks and to PRODUCE them catches the pupil who can recite a meaning but mislabels the vertex or marks equal lengths as measurements. The ∠ABC item specifically catches the middle-letter misread, and requiring production (draw one) is the interpret-translate discriminator — recognition alone hides the gap.
