topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Degrees and turns
topic.description: Know that angles are measured in degrees, where one degree is 1/360 of a full turn; understand that an angle turning through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees
evidence: Explain that a full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°
Describe what 'one degree' means in terms of a fraction of a circle
State that an angle of 45° has turned through 45 one-degree angles
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a full circle is 360 degrees, can they tell you how many degrees a quarter turn is — and explain roughly what one single degree looks like?

pedagogy.summary: A degree is introduced not as a mark on a protractor but as a UNIT ANGLE: one degree is the angle made by cutting a full turn (a whole circle of rotation) into 360 equal parts. An angle's measure is then how many one-degree angles it turns through — 90° means 90 one-degree angles (a right angle), 180° a half turn, 360° a full turn. This mirrors how length and area are measured by iterating a unit (CCSS Progressions), and it must precede protractor use, or the protractor becomes a meaningless ritual.
bestPractices: Build the degree as a fraction of a full turn: partition a circle of rotation into equal parts, name 1/360 the one-degree angle, and connect 90° = quarter turn, 180° = half turn, 360° = whole turn.
Treat measuring as counting unit angles (iteration and additivity): a 45° angle is 45 one-degree wedges; decompose and recompose angles to total their degrees.
Anchor benchmark degrees as mental images — 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, 360° — using pattern blocks (six 60° triangles round a point make 360°) before precise measuring.
Use circular (360°) protractors or a rotating ray first, so a degree reads as an amount of turn rather than a length on a ruler-like scale.
Keep the arms as rays — the number of degrees does not depend on how long they are drawn.
keyRepresentations: A circle of rotation partitioned into equal parts, with the one-degree wedge as the unit
The clock and compass: quarter (90°), half (180°), full (360°) turns
Pattern blocks meeting at a point (6 × 60° = 360°) for benchmark degrees
A circular 360° protractor or a rotating ray sweeping the circle
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a degree measures length, arc length, or the number of tick marks rather than an amount of turn
Sees 360 as arbitrary — no sense that it is the count of equal parts of a full turn — so 90°/180° aren't connected to quarter/half turns
Doesn't see a degree as itself a tiny angle that can be counted and added — treats the number as a label read off a tool
Believes the degree count changes if the arms are drawn longer (arm-length trap carried into measurement)

learn.summary: Degrees are taught as a unit angle: one degree is the angle made by cutting a full turn (a whole circle of rotation) into 360 equal parts, and an angle's measure is the number of one-degree angles it turns through (90° = 90 one-degree angles = a right angle, 180° = half turn, 360° = full turn). This mirrors measuring length and area by iterating a unit, and should precede protractor use so the protractor does not become a meaningless ritual. The activity most directly aimed at building the felt one-degree count has the child sweep a rotating ray and watch a one-degree count accumulate; benchmark images (pattern blocks, clock, compass) and static diagrams support the idea; written response formats (matching, selection, fill-in) can check it.

activities.title: Sweep a ray and count degrees of turn
feedback: When the count reaches 90 the rim snaps to a quarter turn: 'Ninety one-degree angles make a right angle.'
If the learner expects the count to rise when the ray is extended, show the number holding steady: 'Longer arms, same turn — the degree count stays the same.'
At 360 confirm: 'A full turn is 360 one-degree angles because we cut the whole circle into 360 equal parts.'
activities.rationale: CCSS defines an angle turning through 1/360 of a circle as a one-degree angle and an angle turning through n such angles as n degrees; sweeping a ray while counting is intended to make the unit-iteration meaning felt rather than read off a tool, and extending the ray is intended to surface the arm-length misconception by showing the count unchanged.
sourceClaims: An angle is measured with reference to a circle centred at the common endpoint of the rays, by the fraction of the circular arc between where the rays cross the circle; an angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is a 'one-degree angle', and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees.

As with length, area and volume, children need equal partitioning and unit iteration to understand angle and turn measure; degrees are the unit (a full rotation 360°; right 90°, straight 180°), and angle measure is additive — when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts the whole is the sum of the parts. Circular 360° protractors and pattern-block activities (six 60° triangles about a vertex sum to 360°) build benchmark degrees; many students confuse angle size with length/distance/area even in dynamic contexts.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — chiefly the length of the sides — a robust misconception rooted in a whole-object assumption; framing angle as the measure of turn/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Grab a ray at the centre of a circle and sweep it round, watching a counter tick up one degree at a time as a thin wedge fills in behind the moving ray.
Notice the rim glow and snap at a quarter turn (90°), half turn (180°), three-quarter turn (270°) and full turn (360°).
Carry out the task 'turn through 45 degrees' and watch 45 little one-degree wedges stack up into half of a right angle.
Make the ray longer and check that the degree count does not change.
activities.intendedInsight: A degree is a tiny angle you can count: 90° literally means ninety one-degree turns, and measuring an angle is counting how many one-degree turns it makes — just like measuring length with a tiny unit. Stretching the arms longer leaves the count unchanged.

activities.title: Partition a full turn and name the one-degree angle
feedback: If a learner cannot say what fraction 90° is, return to the partitioned circle and fold the turn into four equal parts.
Confirm: 'If we cut the circle into 100 equal parts instead, each part would be a different-sized unit and a right angle would be 25 of them, not 90.'
activities.rationale: Connecting benchmark degrees to fractions of a full turn addresses the misconception that 360 is an arbitrary label disconnected from quarter/half/whole turns; a static partitioned circle is well suited to explaining the idea even though it cannot let the child iterate the unit by hand.
sourceClaims: As with length, area and volume, children need equal partitioning and unit iteration to understand angle and turn measure; degrees are the unit (a full rotation 360°; right 90°, straight 180°), and angle measure is additive — when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts the whole is the sum of the parts. Circular 360° protractors and pattern-block activities (six 60° triangles about a vertex sum to 360°) build benchmark degrees; many students confuse angle size with length/distance/area even in dynamic contexts.

An angle is measured with reference to a circle centred at the common endpoint of the rays, by the fraction of the circular arc between where the rays cross the circle; an angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is a 'one-degree angle', and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees.
learnerActions: Look at a circle of rotation partitioned into equal parts and mark off a quarter, a half and the whole.
Name 1/360 of the full turn as the one-degree angle, and state 90° = quarter turn, 180° = half turn, 360° = whole turn.
Answer: 'What fraction of a full turn is 180°? And 45°?' and 'Why is a full turn 360° and not, say, 100° — what would change if we cut the circle into 100 equal parts instead?'
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing 360 parts is a convention (handy because 360 divides evenly by many numbers), but once chosen it fixes the unit: a degree is one of 360 equal parts of a full turn, so each benchmark degree is a definite fraction of a turn (90° = 1/4, 180° = 1/2, 45° = 1/8).

activities.title: Build and combine benchmark angles with pattern blocks
feedback: When six 60° blocks close the circle: 'Six sixties make three hundred and sixty — a full turn.'
For the 30° + 60° task confirm the total is 90° because the two turns combine: 'The parts add to the whole.'
If a learner only recalls 90°/180° as isolated facts, rebuild them from the blocks so each is seen as a count of unit turns.
activities.rationale: Pattern blocks meeting at a vertex make additivity and benchmark degrees concrete, and composing adjacent angles targets the misconception that a degree is 'just what the protractor says' rather than a countable, addable angle. Note that a physical pattern block has slight thickness and models the ideal flat angle; treat the represented angle as the mathematical object.
sourceClaims: As with length, area and volume, children need equal partitioning and unit iteration to understand angle and turn measure; degrees are the unit (a full rotation 360°; right 90°, straight 180°), and angle measure is additive — when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts the whole is the sum of the parts. Circular 360° protractors and pattern-block activities (six 60° triangles about a vertex sum to 360°) build benchmark degrees; many students confuse angle size with length/distance/area even in dynamic contexts.
learnerActions: Fit six 60° triangular pattern blocks around a single point and check they close up to a full turn (6 × 60° = 360°).
Use the blocks and a clock/compass image to fix mental pictures of 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180° and 360°.
Place a 30° angle and a 60° angle side by side at a point, sharing an arm without overlapping, and state how many degrees altogether, and explain how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle measure is additive: decomposed adjacent angles add to the whole (30° + 60° = 90°), and benchmark degrees can be held as mental images before any precise measuring.

activities.title: Check understanding with varied response formats
feedback: For the predict-then-check: both angles are 90° and equal because arm length does not change the amount of turn — the arms fall along the same two lines. The reason stated first is the important part.
If the learner selects 'longer arms, more degrees', rotate a ray to rebuild the angle and show the degree count is the amount of turn, independent of arm length.
Reinforce that one degree is one of 360 equal parts of a whole rotation, a tiny angle you count — so 90° is 90 of them.
activities.rationale: Matching, selection and fill-in formats efficiently check whether benchmarks and the definition are held, and the predict-then-check with its 'why' demand is diagnostic of the arm-length trap; stating the reason first distinguishes a child who understands turn from one reading a number off a tool. These response formats confirm the idea but do not by themselves build the felt unit-count, which the ray-sweep activity provides.
sourceClaims: Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — chiefly the length of the sides — a robust misconception rooted in a whole-object assumption; framing angle as the measure of turn/rotation helps separate the size dimension.

An angle is measured with reference to a circle centred at the common endpoint of the rays, by the fraction of the circular arc between where the rays cross the circle; an angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is a 'one-degree angle', and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees.
learnerActions: Match each benchmark to its turn: 90° to a quarter turn, 180° to a half turn, 360° to a whole turn.
Choose what one degree is: 1/360 of a full turn (not a length, not a number of tick marks).
Complete 'a 45° angle has turned through ___ one-degree angles' and explain the answer.

Predict-then-check: shown a right angle with short arms, predict how many degrees it becomes if both arms are extended much longer and say why, before the arms are extended or a long-armed right angle is overlaid vertex-aligned.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state and apply the definition independently: one degree is 1/360 of a full turn, 45° is 45 one-degree angles, and arm length does not change the amount of turn.

constraints: Build the degree as a fraction of a full turn and as a countable unit angle BEFORE introducing a protractor, or protractor use becomes a meaningless ritual.
Keep the arms as rays: the number of degrees does not depend on how long they are drawn — make this explicit, as arm length is a robust misconception.
Use circular (360°) protractors or a rotating ray before a straight ruler-like scale, so a degree reads as an amount of turn rather than a length.

A static diagram can explain the partitioned circle and label a one-degree wedge, but it cannot let a child iterate or rotate to feel the degree count accumulate; treat it as a support, not the main manipulation.
Matching/selection/fill-in response formats confirm recall and the definition but do not elicit the independent, felt construction of the unit count; use them to check, not to introduce, the idea.

Degree measure is a planar rotation, so a flat (2D) rotating model is sufficient for this objective; a spatial 3D treatment is not needed here (this is a scope statement for this objective, not a universal claim that 3D adds nothing).
A pattern-block or paper angle cutout has physical thickness and is an approximation of the ideal flat angle; treat the represented angle as the mathematical object.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic and geometry: 6 × 60° = 360° (correct, closes a full turn); 30° + 60° = 90° (correct, additive); 45° = 45 one-degree angles and 45° = 1/8 of a full turn (correct); 90° = 1/4, 180° = 1/2, 360° = whole turn (correct); cutting a circle into 100 parts makes a right angle 25 parts (correct). No learner-facing arithmetic errors found.

The source phrasing 'directly separates/defeats' the length misconception was softened throughout: framing angle as turn is presented as helping separate the size dimension (per source) and as intended to surface the misconception, not as a guaranteed cure.

The claim that a planar rotation means 3D 'adds nothing' was narrowed to a scoped statement that a flat rotating model is sufficient for this objective, rather than a universal claim about 3D; the 'open dialogue cannot teach this' claim was dropped as categorical.
The summary's 'written/spoken' wording was corrected to 'written response formats', since all implemented checks are matching/selection/fill-in and no spoken/dialogue activity is provided.

The predict-then-check overlay (extending arms / vertex-aligned long-armed angle) is drawn from the assessment design and is offered as an activity option; the diagnostic weight rests on the learner stating the reason first.

The summary's preference for the ray-sweep activity reflects the original design ranking (artefact fit 'ideal'/'recommended'), not a measured comparison of media; efficacy of specific interactions is untested.

assess.poeTask: Show a right angle drawn with short arms. Ask the child to predict how many degrees it becomes if you extend both arms much longer, and why, before extending. Then extend the arms (or overlay a long-armed right angle, vertex aligned). A child who predicts 'more degrees' sees the arms fall along the same two lines — still 90°. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I extend the arms of this 90° angle right across the room, how many degrees is it now? Why?
What fraction of a full turn is 180°? And 45°?
A 30° angle and a 60° angle are put together at a point sharing an arm — how many degrees altogether, and how do you know?
Why is a full turn 360° and not, say, 100°? What would change if we cut the circle into 100 equal parts instead?
assess.correctAnswer: Both are 90° and equal, because arm length does not change the amount of turn; and one degree is 1/360 of a full turn — one of 360 equal parts of a whole rotation, a tiny angle you count — so 90° is 90 of them.

errorPatterns.pattern: The long-armed angle is more degrees ('bigger lines, more degrees'), or a degree measures length / arc rather than turn
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate a ray to build the angle and show the degree count is the amount of turn, independent of arm length.
errorPatterns.distractor: The one with the longer arms is more degrees
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the long-armed right angle is more than 90°, or explains a degree as a length or a number of marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 360 as an arbitrary number — does not connect 90° to a quarter turn or a degree to a fraction of a circle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition a circle of turn into equal parts and link a quarter turn = 90°, a half = 180°, a whole = 360°.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say what fraction of a full turn 90° is, or why a full turn is 360°

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't see a degree as itself an angle that can be counted and added — it is 'just what the protractor says'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build angles by iterating unit wedges, and decompose/recompose angles to total their degrees (additivity).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot explain 45° as 45 one-degree angles, or that the degrees of decomposed adjacent angles add up

responseLevels.gap: Treats a degree as a length or a number read off a protractor; thinks the long-armed angle is more degrees; cannot link 90°/180°/360° to fractions of a turn.
responseLevels.full: Explains a degree as one of 360 equal parts of a full turn and an angle's measure as the count of one-degree angles it turns through (additive), holds this independent of arm length, and connects benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn, transferring to new angles (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 90°/180°/360° and that a full turn is 360° and reads benchmarks, but as isolated facts — cannot explain a degree as 1/360 of a turn or 45° as 45 unit angles, and is caught by the arm-length trap (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a right angle drawn with short arms and a right angle drawn with long arms. Ask: 'How many degrees is each — is one more than the other, or are they the same?' Then: 'Tell me what one degree actually means.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The long/short arm pair catches the length trap in tier one; the 'what does a degree mean' question separates a child who understands a degree as a countable fraction-of-a-turn unit from one who thinks it is a number read off a protractor or a length. Correct and incorrect reasoners give different answers to what a degree is.

sources.claim: An angle is measured with reference to a circle centred at the common endpoint of the rays, by the fraction of the circular arc between where the rays cross the circle; an angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is a 'one-degree angle', and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees.
sources.source: CCSS 4.MD.C.5.a and 4.MD.C.5.b

sources.claim: As with length, area and volume, children need equal partitioning and unit iteration to understand angle and turn measure; degrees are the unit (a full rotation 360°; right 90°, straight 180°), and angle measure is additive — when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts the whole is the sum of the parts. Circular 360° protractors and pattern-block activities (six 60° triangles about a vertex sum to 360°) build benchmark degrees; many students confuse angle size with length/distance/area even in dynamic contexts.
sources.source: Progressions for the CCSS in Mathematics (draft), K-5 Geometric Measurement (Illinois SBE mirror of the identical document)

sources.claim: Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — chiefly the length of the sides — a robust misconception rooted in a whole-object assumption; framing angle as the measure of turn/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
sources.source: Xu, Chen, Ma, Zhao, Jiao & Xin (2020), Frontiers in Psychology 11:568388

dependencies.reason: Degree measurement system requires understanding what an angle is

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Lines, Rays & Angles
topic.description: Draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines; identify these in two-dimensional figures
evidence: Draw a pair of perpendicular lines and a pair of parallel lines
Identify all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid
Mark a right angle, an acute angle, and an obtuse angle in a given figure
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a piece of paper and a ruler, can they draw a line segment, mark a point, and then draw another line through that point that runs perfectly parallel to the first?

pedagogy.summary: By age 9-10 children move from recognising angles and parallel/perpendicular lines to drawing and identifying them precisely inside figures (CCSS 4.G.A.1). The central teaching battle is dislodging two deep visual habits: judging an angle's size by how long its arms are drawn (or how far apart their endpoints sit), and recognising right angles / perpendicularity only when lines sit 'upright' in a horizontal-vertical prototype. Effective instruction separates the defining property from its incidental appearance — the angle is the amount of opening at the vertex regardless of arm length; parallel means constant distance / never meeting regardless of how long or short each line is drawn; perpendicular means a square corner at any orientation. Vocabulary (point, line, line segment, ray, right/acute/obtuse) is taught through drawing and marking, not memorised definitions.
bestPractices: Teach angle size as the OPENING at the vertex independent of arm length: overlay two angles vertex-on-vertex, extend one arm, and show the opening is unchanged; pair with a dynamic 'turn'/fan/wedge image so angle is felt as rotation not a static picture

Attack the horizontal-vertical prototype directly: present right angles, perpendicular pairs and parallel pairs in tilted and rotated orientations, and rotate the page to confirm a right angle stays a right angle
Use the corner-of-a-card (or set-square) as a portable right-angle tester that works at any orientation, so 'right angle' is verified by a physical square corner, not by looking upright
Make parallel mean 'always the same distance apart / never meet' using rails and roads drawn at different lengths, so unequal-length sides are still seen as parallel
Draw and mark to learn the vocabulary — have children draw a ray vs a line segment, mark right/acute/obtuse angles and every parallel pair in a given (tilted) polygon, rather than recite definitions
keyRepresentations: Dynamic angle-as-turn model (fan, windscreen wiper, or hinged arms about a fixed vertex)
Two angles overlaid vertex-on-vertex with adjustable arm lengths (to divorce size from arm length)
Parallel rails / road lines drawn at different lengths but constant separation
Corner-of-a-card or set-square as an orientation-free right-angle tester
A tilted trapezoid to mark parallel sides and right/acute/obtuse angles off-axis
commonMisconceptions: Angle size depends on arm length or the distance between the arms' endpoints — a wider-drawn angle with longer rays is judged 'bigger' (arm-length / whole-object bias)
'Angle is the distance between the ends of the lines' — treating the gap between endpoints as the measure
Parallel lines must be the same length, so a trapezoid's unequal parallel sides are rejected as not parallel
Right angles and perpendicular lines are only recognised in horizontal-vertical (upright) orientation and missed when the figure is tilted
A ray and a line segment are the same, or a 'line' stops at the drawn endpoints rather than extending

learn.summary: Children aged 9-10 learn to draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right/acute/obtuse) and parallel/perpendicular lines, and to find these inside two-dimensional figures (CCSS 4.G.A.1). The core teaching work is separating each defining property from its incidental appearance: an angle is the amount of opening at the vertex regardless of how long the arms are drawn; parallel means lines stay the same distance apart and never meet, and segments or sides are parallel when they lie on such lines, whatever their drawn lengths; perpendicular means a square corner at any orientation. Two deep visual habits must be dislodged — judging angle size by arm length or endpoint gap, and recognising right angles/perpendicularity only when lines sit 'upright'. Vocabulary is taught through drawing and marking, not memorised definitions.

activities.title: Stretch the arm, keep the angle
feedback: If the learner calls a short-armed obtuse angle 'acute', overlay it vertex-on-vertex with a known angle and stretch one arm live so they see the opening is unchanged.
Reground angle as an amount of turn using a fan, wedge or hinged arms about a fixed point before re-testing.
If they rank two equal angles as unequal because one is drawn longer, place them point-on-point so the arms coincide and the equal opening is visible.
activities.rationale: Research reports that children widely judge angle size by arm length rather than opening, with accuracy collapsing on length-inconsistent trials; letting the learner change arm length while the opening is held fixed (ideally with a live degree readout) targets exactly this holistic/whole-object bias. A degree readout that stays put as the endpoint is dragged, or hinged/fan arms about a fixed vertex, makes the invariant concrete; a static labelled figure can introduce the vocabulary but cannot show the opening staying the same as an arm stretches.
sourceClaims: Children widely judge angle size by the length of the arms/rays rather than the opening: on length-inconsistent trials mean accuracy fell to ~3% and 219/228 pupils lacked angle size as a separate dimension, reflecting a Van Hiele holistic/whole-object processing bias; the same error appears in US and Chinese samples.

Documented angle/line misconceptions: identical angles judged unequal because their arm lengths differ ('angle is the distance between the ends of the lines'); static-corner vs dynamic-turn conception; and vocabulary confusion including the belief that parallel lines must be the same length — remedied by prototype and 'nearly' examples in varied orientations (drawing on Askew & William 1995).
learnerActions: Swing one ray of a fixed-vertex angle open to roughly 130° and name it obtuse.

Grab the end of that arm as drawn (the ray itself goes on forever; only its drawn part changes) and drag it outward along the same direction so the drawn arm gets much longer, while watching the degree readout stay at 130°.
State what changed (arm length) and what did not change (the opening at the vertex), concluding the angle size is unchanged.
Overlay two angles vertex-on-vertex with arms coinciding, then extend or shorten one arm to confirm the opening is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is the amount of opening (or turn) at the vertex, not the length of its arms or the distance between their endpoints.

activities.title: Parallel at any length, perpendicular at any tilt
feedback: If the learner refuses to call unequal-length sides parallel, show rails drawn at different lengths with constant separation and redefine parallel as staying the same distance apart so that, however far they are extended, they never meet — independent of drawn length.
If they only accept right angles that look upright, rotate the page until the angle is upright, confirm it is still 90°, then rotate back; use the corner-of-a-card tester at several orientations.
If they draw a perpendicular pair only as one horizontal and one vertical line, challenge them to make a square corner tilted off-axis and test it with a card corner.
activities.rationale: Two load-bearing misconceptions — 'parallel lines must be the same length' and 'right angles exist only when upright' — are addressed by presenting parallel and perpendicular pairs at varied lengths and tilts, and by using a physical square corner (card or set-square) as an orientation-free right-angle tester. A rotate-the-scene control and a flag that lights when lines stay equidistant can make the property, not the orientation, salient. A physical card corner tests a right angle at any orientation; the represented lines are idealised (no thickness), while drawings and card edges are physical approximations.
sourceClaims: Documented angle/line misconceptions: identical angles judged unequal because their arm lengths differ ('angle is the distance between the ends of the lines'); static-corner vs dynamic-turn conception; and vocabulary confusion including the belief that parallel lines must be the same length — remedied by prototype and 'nearly' examples in varied orientations (drawing on Askew & William 1995).
4.G.A.1: 'Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.'
learnerActions: Draw (or drag) two line segments that stay the same distance apart (so they would never meet however far they were extended), deliberately making one shorter than the other, and label them parallel.
Draw rail or road-line segments of clearly different lengths but constant separation, and explain why they are still parallel (extended, they would never meet).

Draw two lines meeting at a square corner and label them perpendicular; verify the corner by fitting the corner of a card or a set-square into it, and repeat with perpendicular pairs drawn at several different tilts.
Rotate the whole figure so a right-angled corner tips off-axis, and confirm with the card corner that it is still a right angle; rotate back to check.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart; segments or sides are parallel when they lie on such lines, whatever their lengths; perpendicular means a square corner at any orientation, so rotating a figure does not change whether an angle is a right angle.

activities.title: Mark the tilted trapezoid
feedback: If the learner skips the off-axis right angle because it is not upright, have them test it with a card corner at the figure's actual tilt.
If they reject the trapezoid's unequal-length parallel sides, re-run the equidistant-rails check at different lengths.
If they treat a ray and a segment as the same, have them draw each and mark where it ends versus where it keeps going.
activities.rationale: A tilted, unequal-length figure forces the defining property to show itself because it cannot be marked correctly by prototype-matching, giving a discriminating performance task that also exercises the full vocabulary set required by the standard. Drawing and marking, rather than reciting definitions, builds the targeted procedural skill.
sourceClaims: 4.G.A.1: 'Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.'

UK Y5 statutory: pupils know angles are measured in degrees, draw given angles and measure them; non-statutory guidance expects accurate use of ruler and protractor and conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles — situating draw-and-identify of lines and angles at this stage.
learnerActions: On a right trapezoid (a trapezoid with right angles) drawn deliberately tilted off-axis, mark a right angle (90°), an acute angle (<90°) and an obtuse angle (between 90° and 180°).
Identify and mark every pair of parallel sides, including pairs where the two sides have different lengths.
Draw a ray and a line segment side by side and explain the difference (a ray extends without end in one direction; a segment stops at both endpoints; a line extends without end both ways).
Justify each mark by its defining property — square corner, never-meeting/equidistant, opening — rather than by how upright or how long the lines look.
activities.intendedInsight: The defining property, not the orientation or drawn length, decides whether an element is a right/acute/obtuse angle, parallel, or perpendicular; rays, segments and lines differ by where (or whether) they stop.

activities.title: Vocabulary reference and identification check-up
feedback: If a learner judges the longer-armed one of the equal-angle comparison pair to be the larger angle, return to the overlay-and-stretch demonstration before continuing.
For a mis-sorted angle, ask whether lengthening its arms would change the category, and why not.
Treat free-hand drawing accuracy leniently; focus feedback on whether the defining property was applied, not on neatness.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference figure and a sorting/identification check support vocabulary and verify recognition, and are well placed as a check-up after the manipulative work. Recognition-and-sorting responses confirm identification but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so they supplement rather than replace the drawing activities; include an equal-angle/unequal-arm comparison pair to surface the arm-length bias.
sourceClaims: 4.G.A.1: 'Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.'
learnerActions: Use a labelled figure — ray vs segment vs line, right/acute/obtuse angles, a parallel pair and a perpendicular pair — as a glossary, naming each element and its defining property.
Sort a set of angles in tilted figures into right, acute and obtuse, including a comparison pair of EQUAL angles drawn with clearly unequal arm lengths (which should be judged equal).
Separately, pick out all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid, including a pair whose two sides have different lengths.
After the hands-on work, re-state in your own words why arm length and orientation do not change an element's category.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct vocabulary and identification should rest on defining properties that transfer to tilted and unequal-length figures, not on upright prototypes.

constraints: Teach vocabulary (point, line, line segment, ray, right/acute/obtuse, parallel, perpendicular) through drawing and marking, not memorised definitions.
Present right angles, perpendicular pairs and parallel pairs in tilted and rotated orientations, not only horizontal-vertical, to attack the upright-prototype habit.
A static labelled figure is a useful glossary and reference but cannot show the opening staying fixed as an arm is stretched; use it alongside, not instead of, drawing or live manipulation.

A fixed multiple-choice or sorting check can verify identification but does not by itself elicit independent construction and cannot deliver live 'arm length doesn't change the angle' feedback; use it as a check-up after hands-on work.
Lines, rays and angles are planar; for this drawing-and-marking topic a 3D model offers no distinct affordance over 2D drawing and manipulation, so it is not recommended here.
Score free-hand drawing leniently — judge whether the defining property was applied, not fine accuracy.
Mathematical lines and angle arms are idealised with no thickness; card corners, drawn lines and set-squares are physical approximations used to test the property.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims on arm-length bias and length/orientation misconceptions describe documented learner errors; they support the targeted misconceptions but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium (draggable readout, rotate control, card tester). Phrasings implying a given interaction is the only way to teach have been softened.
The ~3% accuracy and 219/228 figures are quoted from the legacy source claim and were not independently re-verified in this rewrite.
Degree readouts, parallel/perpendicular flags, drag and rotate controls are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory requirements.

probeDeeper: You marked this one acute — if I make its two lines twice as long, is it still acute? Why?
Show me why these two sides are parallel even though one is longer than the other.
Turn the page any way you like — is that still a right angle? How do you know?
These two corners — which angle is bigger, and what exactly are you comparing to decide?
assess.correctAnswer: Draws two never-meeting, equidistant lines (any orientation) as parallel and two lines meeting at a square corner as perpendicular; on the tilted trapezoid marks a 90° angle as right, a <90° as acute and a >90° as obtuse, and identifies the pair(s) of parallel sides — judging by defining property (square corner / never-meeting / opening), orientation- and length-independent, not by how 'upright' or how long the lines look.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The angle with the longer arms (or wider-apart ends) is the bigger angle' — judges angle size by ray length or endpoint gap, not the opening at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-on-vertex so the arms coincide, then extend/shorten one arm live to show the opening is unchanged; reground angle as amount of turn using a fan/wedge before re-testing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls an obtuse angle 'acute' because its arms are drawn short, or ranks two equal angles as unequal because one is drawn with longer arms

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Parallel lines must be the same length' — rejects unequal-length sides as not parallel
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show rails/road lines drawn at different lengths but constant separation; redefine parallel as never meeting / always the same distance apart, independent of length
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to mark the trapezoid's two parallel sides because 'they're different lengths, so they can't be parallel'

errorPatterns.pattern: Right angles and perpendicularity are recognised only in an upright (horizontal-vertical) orientation and missed when the figure is tilted
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the page so the angle becomes upright, confirm it is still 90°, then rotate back; use the corner-of-a-card test at several orientations so 'right angle' is verified by a square corner not by looking upright
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the tilted trapezoid fails to mark the right angle because it is not 'upright', or draws a perpendicular pair only as one horizontal and one vertical line

responseLevels.gap: Draws and marks by appearance only — cannot reliably produce a parallel or perpendicular pair, judges angle size by arm length, and finds right angles only when the figure is upright.
responseLevels.full: Draws and marks all elements correctly regardless of orientation or arm length, justifying each by its defining property (never-meeting/equidistant; square corner; opening not length), and finds every pair of parallel sides on the tilted trapezoid.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly draws and labels parallel and perpendicular pairs and names right/acute/obtuse in a standard orientation, but slips on the tilted figure or on unequal-length parallel sides — names the terms without applying the defining property in the new position (lists the elements without transferring the rule).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a ruler and a printed figure in front of the child — a trapezoid drawn tilted off-axis, with two extra straight lines crossing nearby — plus a blank space. Say: 'Draw me one pair of parallel lines and one pair of perpendicular lines. Then on this shape, mark a right angle, an acute angle and an obtuse angle, and show me every pair of parallel sides.' Watch how they draw and mark — do not ask them to define the words.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept marks right angles and parallels correctly on the TILTED figure and treats unequal-length sides as parallel; a child relying on appearance misses the off-axis right angle, rejects unequal parallels, or ranks equal angles by arm length. The tilted, unequal-length figure forces the property to show itself — you cannot mark it correctly by prototype-matching.

Sort angles from a set of drawn shapes into acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex
Estimate whether an angle drawn between clock hands is less than or more than a straight angle

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding angles (age 9+)
topic.description: Use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles
evidence: Given one side of a rectangle is 8 cm and the perimeter is 28 cm, find the other side
Explain that all angles in a rectangle are 90°
Find a missing side of a rectangle given its area and one side length
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows one side of a rectangular garden is 7 m, can they tell you the length of the opposite side and all four corner angles — without measuring?

pedagogy.summary: This is deductive reasoning from a rectangle's defining properties: because a rectangle has four right angles and two pairs of equal opposite sides, a child can DEDUCE unknown facts — a missing angle must be 90°, an opposite side equals the given one, and a missing side follows from the perimeter (P = 2(l+w)) or the area (A = l×w). The work is reasoning, not measuring: the diagram is usually not drawn to scale, so lengths and angles must come from the stated properties and given numbers, not from the picture. The dominant obstacle is confusing area and perimeter (and their inverse operations); a second is reading unknown lengths off the not-to-scale drawing; a third is forgetting that opposite sides are equal, so a single given side already fixes its opposite.
bestPractices: Reason from the definition: all four angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal, so a given side determines its opposite — mark the equal sides and squared corners on the diagram before calculating
Keep perimeter and area distinct: perimeter is the distance round (P = 2(l+w), cm), area is the space inside (A = l×w, cm²); read which one the problem gives before choosing the inverse step
Work the inverse deliberately: from a perimeter, halve to get l+w then subtract the known side; from an area, divide by the known side — model each as 'undoing' the formula
Treat the diagram as NOT to scale — use the marked and given information, never a ruler on the picture (a side that looks longer may be the equal one)
Attach correct units throughout (cm for length, cm² for area) and sense-check the answer against the rectangle
keyRepresentations: The rectangle with opposite sides tick-marked equal and all four corners squared (90°), given values labelled and the unknown as a box
P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w overlaid on the shape, with 'undo' arrows for the inverse step
A bar / part-whole model for perimeter showing l+w as half the perimeter
Deliberately not-to-scale rectangles where the marks and numbers override the look
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter, or their formulae/units — e.g. divides by a side when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area (Machaba: taught together, learned instrumentally)
Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it
Reads unknown lengths or angles off the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing them from the properties and givens
Forgets that opposite sides are equal, so treats all four sides as unknown even after one is given, or doubts that the fourth angle is 90°

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9-10) learn to DEDUCE missing lengths and angles of a rectangle from its defining properties (four right angles; two pairs of equal opposite sides) and the given numbers, rather than measuring the diagram. Core work: find a missing side from a given side and the perimeter (P = 2(l+w): halve, then subtract) or from a given side and the area (A = l×w: divide); state that the fourth angle must be 90°; attach correct units (cm, cm²). The deliberately not-to-scale drawing forces reliance on numbers and properties. The dominant obstacle is confusing area with perimeter (and their inverse operations); others are reading lengths/angles off an inaccurate picture, short-cutting the perimeter inverse (subtracting from the whole perimeter instead of from half), and forgetting that one given side already fixes its opposite.

activities.title: Deduce the missing side: perimeter then area, from a not-to-scale rectangle
feedback: If the child types the missing perimeter side correctly, an optional boundary-trace can run a pen round all four sides and click shut at exactly 28, confirming the sides total the perimeter; for the area task, an optional interior-tiling can fill the inside exactly with a 6-by-8 region — these visual confirmations are supportive, not required to validate the reasoning.

If the child writes 28 - 8 = 20, point out that 28 is the whole way round (two lengths plus two widths); undo P = 2(l+w) by halving to 14 first, then subtract the known 8 — a bar or part-whole model showing l+w as half the perimeter makes the halving step visible.

If the child divides 28 by 8 (applying the area method to a perimeter), or halves 48 (applying the perimeter method to an area), ask which quantity the problem gave — distance round or space inside — before choosing the step.
If the child measures or eyeballs the picture, remind them the drawing is not to scale: a side that looks longer may be the equal one; trust the marked and given numbers.
If the child leaves two sides unknown, point back to the tick marks — one given side already fixes its opposite because opposite sides are equal.
If the child says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90°, press that it must be 90° because every rectangle angle is a right angle.
activities.rationale: Deducing missing lengths and angles from rectangle properties is the stated Year 5 objective, and the common error of measuring an inaccurate diagram is addressed by making the figure not-to-scale so facts, not the picture, must be used. Pairing perimeter and area tasks targets the well-documented area/perimeter confusion by forcing a deliberate choice of inverse operation.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures

A common error is trying to MEASURE a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'when the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure ... we need to use [the] facts to calculate' — i.e. deduce from given information rather than read lengths/angles off the picture
learnerActions: Work with a rectangle labelled '8 cm' on one side and 'perimeter = 28 cm', drawn deliberately almost square so measuring is useless; one side is a blank box.
Before calculating, mark the equal opposite sides (tick marks) and the four squared (90°) corners so the given 8 cm is seen on its opposite side too.
Reason the perimeter case aloud or in writing: two sides are 8; the four sides total 28; half the perimeter is 14; 14 - 8 = 6, so the missing side is 6 cm.
Switch to an area task: '48 cm², one side 8 cm' — divide 48 ÷ 8 = 6 to find the missing side, and note the inside is filled by a 6-by-8 region.
State the size of the fourth angle (90°) and justify it from the definition, not the picture.
Attach units throughout: cm for sides, cm² for area.
Transfer to a fresh rectangle with different numbers, choosing halve-then-subtract for perimeter and divide for area.
activities.intendedInsight: Missing facts about a rectangle are deduced from its properties and the given numbers, not read off the drawing; 'going round' (perimeter: halve, then subtract) and 'filling in' (area: divide) are different inverse operations that must be chosen by what the problem gives.

activities.title: Short-answer deductions with targeted wrong-answer options
feedback: For an answer of 28 - 8 = 20: the subtraction was from the whole perimeter; halve to 14 first, then subtract 8.

For an answer found by halving the area: halving 48 cm² only gives 24 cm², which is half the area, not a side. Halving is the first step for undoing a perimeter, not an area. To undo A = l×w, divide by the known side: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm.
If a length is labelled cm² (or an area cm), re-link the unit to the quantity: lengths are cm, areas cm².
If the child picks the misleading pictured proportion, restate that the figure is not to scale.
activities.rationale: Fixed items can score the deductions cleanly and present carefully chosen wrong-answer options (halved-area; subtract-from-whole-perimeter) that reveal the specific misconceptions. This format checks recognition and single-answer production but does not let the child watch the boundary close as the inverse lands, so it complements rather than replaces the constructive task.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures
learnerActions: Given one side and the perimeter, construct the other side (e.g. side 8 cm, perimeter 28 cm → fill in 6 cm) and show the halve-then-subtract working.
Given the area and one side, find the other side (e.g. 48 cm², one side 8 cm → 6 cm) and show the division.
Answer a units item: decide whether a given answer should be in cm or cm².
Face a not-to-scale figure whose proportions mislead, and justify the answer from the numbers rather than the look.
When choosing among options, reject the halved-area answer and the subtract-from-whole-perimeter answer (28 - 8 = 20) and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can reliably select and carry out the correct inverse operation and attach the correct unit, resisting the area/perimeter confusion and the not-to-scale picture.

activities.title: Rectangle properties reference card
feedback: If asked whether a rectangle can have only three right angles, reason that the angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°, so three right angles force the fourth to be 90° too — it cannot have exactly three.
When comparing a square and a rectangle, note both have four right angles and opposite sides equal; a square additionally has all four sides equal.
activities.rationale: A properties reference supports recall of the definitions that underpin the deduction and seeds NCETM reasoning discussion. It is a static reference: the child does not perform the deduction here, so it is a scaffold beside active practice, not the skill itself.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective on the properties of rectangles; suggested probes include 'tell me some facts about rectangles', 'is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?', and 'what is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?' — reasoning from properties (opposite sides equal, four right angles); the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle
learnerActions: Consult a labelled rectangle: each corner reveals '90°', each side reveals 'equals its opposite', and the formulae P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w reveal their undo steps.
Use it alongside practice to recall the defining properties before calculating.

Answer NCETM-style reasoning probes: 'Tell me some facts about rectangles'; 'Is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?'; 'What is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?'
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle's defining properties — two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles — are the authority for deduction, and holding them in mind prevents treating sides or the fourth angle as unknown.

constraints: The task is reasoning and calculation with feedback, not measuring: diagrams should be marked as not to scale so lengths and angles come from stated properties and given numbers.
Keep perimeter and area (and their inverse operations and units) explicitly distinct; present both side by side so the child must choose the correct step rather than apply one method by default.
The reference/tap-to-reveal card is a recall scaffold only — it does not require the child to perform a deduction, so it should sit alongside active practice, not replace it.

Fixed-item practice (single-answer construction and multiple-choice) checks recognition and single-answer production and can present diagnostic wrong-answer options, but it does not let the child construct and visually confirm the inverse step; use it to complement constructive practice.
Boundary-trace and interior-tiling animations are optional confirmations of a correct answer, not the mechanism the child must use to reason.

Keep the work planar: length, area and perimeter of a rectangle are two-dimensional; adding a third dimension risks drifting toward surface area and volume, which is a different objective at this stage.
The perimeter inverse is halve-then-subtract (28 → 14 → 14 - 8 = 6); do not subtract the known side from the whole perimeter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The National Curriculum source (Year 5 'use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles') is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

Legacy claims that open dialogue and 3D are 'poor' fits were framed as near-universal in the source. Retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes: open dialogue suits reasoning probes but not step-by-step compute-and-deduce practice with feedback, and a third dimension can mislead toward volume for a planar objective. No comparative efficacy is asserted.

Arithmetic self-audit: perimeter 28 cm with one side 8 cm → half is 14, 14 - 8 = 6 cm (correct); area 48 cm² ÷ 8 = 6 cm (correct); the value 28 - 8 = 20 is deliberately wrong and must appear only as a flagged misconception, never as a valid answer.

The NCETM claim also mentions 'the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle'; this is beyond the current missing-side objective and was not built into an activity to avoid scope creep.

probeDeeper: This problem gives the PERIMETER — why do you halve it before subtracting? What would 28 - 8 give you, and is that a side?
The picture looks almost square, but the numbers say one side is 8 cm and the perimeter 28 cm — which do you trust, and why?
You found one side is 6 cm — what are the other three sides, and how do you know without measuring?
The second rectangle gives an AREA — why do you divide here, but halve-and-subtract for the first one?
assess.correctAnswer: First rectangle: reasons that opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is 14 cm and the missing side = 14 - 8 = 6 cm; states that all angles, including the fourth, are 90°. Second rectangle: missing side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Uses the given numbers and rectangle properties (not the drawing), with correct units (cm and cm²).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area and perimeter, or their inverse operations — e.g. divides when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area to find a side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: perimeter is the distance round (halve to l+w, then subtract), area is the space inside (divide by the side); read which is given before choosing the step (Machaba: the two are taught together and confused when learned instrumentally).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the area method to the perimeter task or vice-versa (divides 28 by 8, or halves 48), or labels a length in cm²

errorPatterns.pattern: Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter (28 - 8 = 20) instead of from half of it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model P = 2(l+w) as two lengths plus two widths; undo by halving to get l+w, then subtract the known side — a bar model showing the half-perimeter helps.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 28 - 8 = 20 (or similar) rather than halving to 14 first

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing length or angle off the not-to-scale drawing instead of deducing it — measures or eyeballs the picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: State that the diagram is not to scale — the numbers and the rectangle's properties are the authority; use the marks, not the picture (Third Space: when a diagram is not drawn accurately you cannot measure, you must use the facts).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a length close to what the wrong-proportioned picture shows, or reaches for a ruler; says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90° rather than knowing it must be

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets opposite sides are equal — treats the given side as fixing only itself, so tries to solve with all sides unknown, or is unsure that the fourth angle is 90°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground the defining properties — a rectangle has two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles; mark the equal sides and squared corners before calculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not use '8 also appears on the opposite side'; leaves two sides unknown, or hesitates over the fourth angle

responseLevels.gap: Applies the wrong operation (divides the perimeter, halves the area, or subtracts from the whole perimeter), or reads the length off the not-to-scale picture; cannot reliably state that the fourth angle is 90°.
responseLevels.full: Deduces each missing side from the rectangle's properties and the given numbers — halving the perimeter then subtracting, and dividing for the area — states that the fourth angle is 90° from the definition, ignores the not-to-scale drawing, attaches correct units, and transfers to a new rectangle problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one type — say the area division — but slips on the perimeter inverse (subtracts from 28 rather than 14), or gets the numbers but muddles the units, or needs prompting to use opposite-sides-equal; manages the routine case but not both reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle drawn deliberately NOT to scale (make it look almost square), with one side labelled 8 cm, the perimeter labelled 28 cm, and one side left blank — plus a second rectangle with area 48 cm² and one side 8 cm. Say: 'Find the missing side of each, and tell me the size of the fourth angle. Show your working.' Say nothing about method; watch how they get the missing sides and whether they measure the picture or reason from the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The perimeter and area problems sit side by side so the child must pick the right inverse, and the not-to-scale drawing means measuring the picture gives a wrong answer — exposing the child who reads lengths off the diagram. A child reasoning from properties halves the perimeter before subtracting and divides for the area; a child confusing the two divides the perimeter or subtracts from the whole 28; a child trusting the picture reports the wrong measured length. Watching the working — not asking 'what is the difference between area and perimeter?' — shows which.
