topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: What Is an Angle?
topic.description: Understand that an angle is a geometric shape formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex); recognise angles in real-life contexts and 2-D shapes
evidence: Identify the vertex and arms of an angle in a diagram
Find examples of angles in the classroom (e.g. open door, clock hands)
Explain why two rays meeting at a point form an angle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you draw two lines starting from the same point on paper, can {{name}} tell you that the space between them is an angle — and point to the vertex where they meet?

pedagogy.summary: Here the informal angle — a corner, a turn, an opening — is formalised as a geometric object: two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint, the vertex, with size given by the amount of rotation between the arms. The central challenge (CCSS Progressions; Mitchelmore & White) is that children hold SEPARATE angle concepts for different physical situations — the turn of a door, the corner of a shape, the opening of scissors, the slope of a ramp, a bend in a road — and must abstract the common structure (two rays and a vertex) across all of them, including cases where one arm is only implicit (the horizontal in a slope).
bestPractices: Collect angles from many situations — open door, clock hands, scissors, a ramp, a bent straw, shape corners — and draw out what they share: two arms meeting at a point (varied situations → abstraction).
Name the parts explicitly and consistently: the vertex (the meeting point) and the arms/rays, marking the angle with an arc at the vertex.
Make the arms genuine rays — stress they can be extended without changing the angle — to pre-empt the arm-length trap.
Surface implicit arms: in a slope, or a 'how high is the tree' sighting, one ray is the horizontal — draw it in.
Contrast a static corner with the turn that opens it, so both the figure and rotation conceptions attach to the same object.
keyRepresentations: Two rays hinged at a vertex, with vertex and arms labelled and an arc marking the angle
A gallery of real situations (door, clock, scissors, ramp, road bend) each reduced to vertex + two arms
The clock face — hands as two rays from the centre — as a canonical everyday angle
A dynamic hinge showing the arms as extendable rays
commonMisconceptions: Holds separate, unconnected angle ideas for different contexts — a 'turn' and a 'corner' are treated as different things, with no single general concept
Judges or defines angle size by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends rather than the opening (persists even for doors and hinges)
Thinks the arms must be a fixed length, or that lengthening a ray changes the angle (arms are unbounded rays)
Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses angles that are rotated or have an implicit arm (a slope)

learn.summary: Learners formalise the everyday idea of an angle (a corner, a turn, an opening) as a geometric object: two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint (the vertex), with size given by the amount of rotation or opening between the arms. The central challenge is that children hold SEPARATE angle ideas for different physical situations — the turn of a door, the corner of a shape, the opening of scissors, the slope of a ramp, a bend in a road — and must abstract the shared structure (two rays and a vertex) across all of them, including cases where one arm is only implicit (the horizontal in a slope or a sighting line). Suitable for roughly ages 9–10.

activities.title: From many situations to one skeleton
feedback: If a learner says 'that's a corner, not an angle' or 'a door opening isn't an angle', lay the different situations side by side and strip each to a vertex and two arms, naming the shared structure they all have.
If a learner only accepts an angle drawn upright, rotate the examples off the upright and confirm the vertex and arms are still there.
If a learner cannot find the ramp's angle, point out that only the slope line is drawn and draw in the horizontal arm with them so both arms are visible.
Praise locating the vertex correctly and reducing a real object to the two-ray diagram, not just naming the object.
activities.rationale: Exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including implicit-arm cases, is the recommended route to help children abstract 'angle' as two rays and a vertex rather than hold separate context-bound ideas. A tap-to-reveal interactive scene where each object highlights its vertex and arms and then drills down to the identical two-ray-and-arc diagram can make the abstraction moment concrete, but the same work can be done with physical objects and drawn diagrams.
sourceClaims: Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.

Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
learnerActions: Gather or look at pictures of angles in many different situations: an open door, clock hands, open scissors, a propped ramp, a bent straw, a bend in a road, and the corner of a shape.
For each one, mark where the two arms are and put a dot on the vertex (the meeting point), drawing an arc at the vertex to show the angle.
Strip each situation down to the SAME bare diagram — two rays meeting at a point with an arc — and lay these stripped diagrams side by side.
Say in your own words what the door, the clock and the scissors all share.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit second arm (the horizontal ground line) so the angle has both arms.
activities.intendedInsight: A door, a clock and a pair of scissors are all the same underlying thing — two arms meeting at a point — so an angle is that shared skeleton, not any one particular picture. Some situations (slopes, sightings) have one arm that must be drawn in.

activities.title: The arms are rays: lengthening does not change the angle
feedback: If a learner predicts 'it gets bigger' when arms are lengthened, show the extended arms lying along the same two lines — it is the same angle — and return to the opening as the measure of size. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
If a learner cites arm length or the distance between arm-ends when comparing, extend a ray to show the angle is unchanged, and redirect attention to the opening/turn.
Affirm reasoning that refers to the opening or turn between the arms rather than to arm length.
activities.rationale: Children commonly judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length and think lengthening a ray changes the angle. A predict–then–test task targets this directly, and a live hinge with extendable arms and a fixed arc can make the ray-invariance visible. The prediction and the reason given first are the diagnostic parts; the hands-on resolution follows.
sourceClaims: An angle has two conceptions — static (a corner / two adjoining lines) and dynamic (an amount of turn) — which must be brought together; children judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length.

Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
learnerActions: Draw an angle, then predict (before doing anything) what will happen to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and say why.
Now extend both arms — or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, with the vertices aligned — and compare.
Describe what you notice: the longer arms lie along the same two lines, so the opening is unchanged.
Compare two angles that have the same opening but different arm lengths and decide whether they are equal, giving your reason.
activities.intendedInsight: The arms of an angle are rays that can be extended without changing the angle; the size is the opening (the turn) between the arms, not how long the arms are or how far apart the arm-ends sit.

activities.title: Connecting the corner and the turn
feedback: If a learner treats the corner and the turn as unrelated, slow down the opening of the hinge so they can see the same two arms both at rest and sweeping.
If a learner struggles to find the vertex on the clock, point to the centre where both hands begin and confirm the hands are the two arms.
Encourage describing the clock angle as the turn between the hands, linking it back to the corner view.
activities.rationale: Both the figure (static) and rotation (dynamic) conceptions need to attach to the same object; contrasting a static corner with the turn that opens it supports this. The clock face is a canonical everyday angle with the vertex at the centre and hands as rays. A live hinge can show both views on one object, but physical objects such as doors and scissors also serve.
sourceClaims: An angle has two conceptions — static (a corner / two adjoining lines) and dynamic (an amount of turn) — which must be brought together; children judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length.
Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.
learnerActions: Take one object, such as an open door or a pair of scissors, and look at it as a static corner: two lines meeting at a point.
Now open and close it, watching the arms sweep through a turn, and notice the amount of turn is the size of the angle.
Explain how the still corner and the turning action describe the same angle on the same object.
Use a clock face: point to the vertex (the centre) and name the two hands as the two arms, then describe the angle as the turn between them.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle has two connected conceptions — a static corner (two arms at a vertex) and a dynamic turn (an amount of rotation) — and these describe the same geometric object.

activities.title: Is it an angle? Including rotated and implicit-arm cases
feedback: If a learner misses the rotated angle, rotate it back to upright, confirm it is an angle, then rotate it again so they see the angle is unchanged by orientation.
If a learner denies the ramp has an angle because only one line is drawn, draw in the horizontal arm with them.
If a learner claims the parallel lines make an angle, trace both lines and show they never meet, so there is no vertex.
Confirm a full explanation that names two rays, a shared vertex, and the opening/turn between them.
activities.rationale: Including a rotated angle, a ramp with an implicit arm, and a non-angle separates a child who has abstracted the general two-ray concept from one who only recognises a prototypical drawn angle. Surfacing implicit arms and rejecting non-angles are key to the full understanding. This task also doubles as a diagnostic: the reason given reveals whether 'angle' means the structure or just a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.
learnerActions: Look at a set of pictures: a clearly drawn angle, an angle rotated off the upright, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and two parallel lines that never meet.
For each picture, decide whether there is an angle and, if so, mark the vertex.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit horizontal arm and decide whether there is an angle there.
Say why the parallel lines do NOT form an angle (they never meet, so there is no vertex).
Explain in your own words what makes something an angle.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is two rays meeting at a vertex, recognisable even when rotated or when one arm is implicit; two lines that never meet do not form an angle because there is no shared vertex.

constraints: Name the parts explicitly and consistently: the vertex (the meeting point) and the arms/rays, marking the angle with an arc at the vertex.
Stress that the arms are genuine rays that can be extended without changing the angle, to pre-empt the arm-length trap.
Always surface implicit arms: in a slope or a sighting ('how high is the tree'), one ray is the horizontal — draw it in.
Use at least one rotated angle and at least one non-angle (two lines that never meet) so recognition is not limited to the prototypical upright drawing.

Matching or multiple-choice tasks (e.g. identifying the vertex, matching situations to angle diagrams) can check recognition, but a recognition-only response does not by itself elicit the cross-context abstraction or the learner's spoken/written reason; include at least one task where the learner states why.
Paper cut-outs or physical hinges have slight thickness and are approximations; treat them as models of the ideal two-ray figure and keep attention on the vertex and opening rather than the material.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row, without fresh source verification; the sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support the underlying teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

The original row rated a 3D interactive scene 'possible' with the remark that '3D adds realism without conceptual depth'; this comparative claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted. A spatial scene could still help learners spot angles in their environment.

The original rated in-role dialogue 'poor', asserting it 'cannot deliver the see-the-shared-skeleton moment'. This universal claim is not established by the sources; it is reframed here as the narrower observable point that the core work is visual/constructive and that talk alone does not by itself require the learner to mark vertices and arms.

The predict-then-test prediction 'it gets bigger' is the expected misconception, not a correct answer; it is used as a diagnostic to be confronted, and the feedback corrects it. No arithmetic, fraction, or force/motion claims were present to audit.

Activity 2 re-uses the varied-situations abstraction claim; it is retained only because that claim explicitly names the arm-length/endpoint-distance misconception the activity targets, not for its abstraction content.

assess.poeTask: Draw an angle, then ask the child to predict what happens to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and why, before doing it. Then extend them (or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, vertex aligned). A child who predicts 'it gets bigger' confronts the arms lying along the same two lines — the same angle. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This ramp only has the slope drawn. Where is the other arm of the angle — is there still an angle here?
If I make the arms of this angle twice as long, is it still the same angle? Why?
Here are two lines that never meet. Is there an angle? Why not?
The clock hands make an angle — point to the vertex. What are the two arms?
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies angles including the rotated one and the ramp (recognising the implicit horizontal as the second arm), marks the vertex where the two rays meet, rejects the parallel-lines non-angle, and justifies that an angle is two rays/arms meeting at a point (a vertex) with its size the turn or opening between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a turn, a corner and an opening as different things rather than one general angle ('that's a corner, not an angle', or 'a door opening isn't an angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the different situations side by side and strip each to a vertex and two arms, naming the shared structure they all have.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the plainly drawn angle but denies the ramp or the door/turn is 'an angle'

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the angle by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends, or thinks extending a ray changes the angle ('the longer one is more of an angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend a ray and show the angle is unchanged — the arms are rays (unbounded); return to opening/turn as the size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When comparing or describing, cites arm length; claims a longer-armed angle is bigger, or that lengthening an arm changes it

errorPatterns.pattern: Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses rotated angles or those with an implicit arm (a slope)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate examples off the upright and draw in the implicit horizontal arm on slopes and sightings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the rotated angle or denies the ramp has an angle because only one line is drawn

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only a prototypical drawn angle; treats turns, corners and openings as different things; cannot locate the vertex reliably, and misses rotated or implicit-arm cases.
responseLevels.full: Defines an angle as two rays sharing a vertex with size given by the rotation between them, and recognises that structure across new situations — including where an arm is implicit or the figure is rotated — while rejecting non-angles (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the vertex and arms in standard drawn angles and names several real examples, but as separate cases — does not articulate the common two-rays-at-a-vertex structure, and stumbles on the ramp (implicit arm) or a rotated figure (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out several pictures: a clearly drawn angle, a rotated angle, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and a non-angle (two parallel lines that never meet). Say: 'Point to the angle in each picture and mark its vertex — and for the ramp, tell me if there's an angle there at all.' Then: 'Explain what makes something an angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a rotated angle, a ramp with an implicit arm, and a non-angle separates a child who has abstracted the general two-ray concept from one who only recognises a prototypical drawn angle. The tier-2 reason reveals whether 'angle' means the two-rays-at-a-vertex structure or just a familiar picture.

Order four angles from smallest to largest by estimation before measuring
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} three different angles drawn on paper, can they estimate which is biggest, label each as acute, obtuse, or reflex — and then check with a protractor?

pedagogy.summary: Estimating angles is the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool, by comparing it against internalised benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The pedagogical goal is a stable mental image of a right angle and a half/three-quarter turn, so that any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends the acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), which children meet here for the first time and which the semicircular protractor cannot directly read. Estimation is what makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.
bestPractices: Anchor a small set of benchmark angles as physical/mental images first — the right angle (corner, quarter turn), the straight angle (180°), 45° as half a right angle, 270° as three right angles — then estimate everything by comparison to the nearest benchmark.
Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck placement, not to discard the estimate.
Introduce reflex angles explicitly as 'more than a straight line, less than a full turn' and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller angle, since a semicircular protractor reads only to 180°.
Order/compare several angles by eye before any measuring, so relative judgement (which is bigger) is trained alongside absolute estimation (how many degrees).
Use bodily and everyday referents — clock hands, opening doors, ramps, turns — to build the benchmark images.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark angles as mental anchors: 45°, 90° (right angle), 180° (straight), 270°, 360°
The right angle as the master reference ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner')
Reflex angle as 360° minus its companion angle (turn imagery)
Clock hands / opening door as dynamic referents for angle size
commonMisconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.

learn.summary: Teach angle estimation as the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool by comparing it to internalised benchmarks (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The goal is a stable mental image of a right angle, a straight angle and a three-quarter turn, so any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), met here for the first time and not directly readable on a semicircular protractor. Estimation makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.

activities.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
feedback: Reward closeness within a tolerance band rather than exactness, so an estimate stays a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.

When a child guesses '90-ish' for a clearly reflex angle, reveal the turn swinging past the straight line and show its true size as 360° minus the companion angle (for example about 270° when the companion is about 90°), so reflex stops being invisible.

When a child under-estimates wide-but-short-armed angles, let the error score flag the pattern, then overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so their openings compare directly regardless of arm length, and extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
Treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck both the protractor reading (placement and scale) and the estimate, not simply to discard the estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a perceptual-numerical skill proposed to be built by repeated visual trials with feedback: a predict-then-reveal loop over many varied angles commits the child to an estimate, then feeds back the error, intended to calibrate the benchmark sense. Varying ray length independently of opening directly targets the documented arm-length misconception; including reflex angles forces the '360 minus companion' reasoning that a semicircular protractor cannot read directly.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.

activities.title: Scored estimation and classification practice
feedback: Score the slider estimate against a tolerance band so a near miss counts as success.
Flag an arm-length error when ordering tracks ray length rather than opening, and prompt direct comparison of the openings.
If the child mis-classifies the reflex angle as acute or right, show that it opens past the straight line.
activities.rationale: Estimation maps cleanly onto scored response formats (slider estimate, ordering, classification choice), giving varied practice and checking. A response-format task may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop, so it is proposed as a complement rather than a replacement. Including a short-ray wide-angle item targets the arm-length misconception.
sourceClaims: Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: Use a slider to estimate a shown angle's degrees, aiming to land within a tolerance band.
Order four angles smallest-to-largest by eye as an ordering task before any measure is shown.
Classify shown angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and pick out the reflex angle in a diagram.
Tackle at least one deliberately short-armed, wide-opening item designed to catch the arm-length habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Relative judgement (which is bigger), absolute estimation (how many degrees) and classification (acute/obtuse/reflex) are distinct skills that can each be practised and checked.

activities.title: Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
feedback: Confirm the benchmark image and name when revealed, and connect it to its everyday referent.
When the child decides 'more or less than a right angle', show the angle against the corner image to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal gallery can seed estimation by anchoring the benchmark set as stable mental images with everyday referents. It is a scaffold: it may establish the anchors but does not itself run the estimate-check loop that calibrates estimation, so it is intended to precede, not replace, repeated estimation practice.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Tap or reveal each benchmark in turn — 45° (half a right angle), 90° (right angle/corner/quarter turn), 180° (straight), 270° (three right angles), 360° (full turn) — and link it to a reference image.
Connect each benchmark to a bodily or everyday referent: clock hands, an opening door, a ramp, a turn.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'more or less than a right angle?' layer to decide, for a shown angle, whether it is above or below the corner benchmark.
activities.intendedInsight: A small set of benchmark angles, anchored as physical and mental images, is the master reference set against which every other angle is judged ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner').

activities.title: Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution
feedback: If estimates snap only to 90° or 180°, point out the gap and introduce an intermediate anchor the angle sits near.
Accept a reasoned range stated against two anchors rather than demanding one exact number.
activities.rationale: When benchmark resolution is too coarse, estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines; this is a sparse-anchor-deployment issue, not a concept failure, so the fix is to bring in and practise intermediate anchors rather than reteach the concept of angle.
sourceClaims: The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: For a learner whose estimates snap only to 90° and 180°, bring in the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a right angle plus a third of a right angle' (120°) as working anchors alongside the secure 90° and 180° images.
Estimate angles that deliberately sit BETWEEN benchmarks, such as 60°, 110° or 130°, naming the two anchors each one falls between.
Justify at least one estimate aloud with benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°').
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring only to 90° and 180° makes estimates cluster there with poor resolution in between; deploying intermediate anchors gives the mental ruler finer gradations.

constraints: Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; a large estimate-vs-measure gap signals that both should be rechecked (protractor placement and which scale was read, and the estimate itself), not that the estimate was worthless.
Reward closeness within a tolerance band, not exactness: an estimate is a reasoned approximate range, not a failed exact answer. An estimate of 120° when the protractor reads 128° is a good estimate.
A semicircular protractor reads only to 180°, so reflex angles must be reasoned as 360° minus the smaller companion angle; do not treat the smaller companion as the answer.

The benchmark gallery is a scaffold that anchors reference images; it may seed estimation but does not build the skill on its own, which requires repeated estimate-then-check trials. It is a useful precursor, not a universal requirement.

Classification and ordering response items check relative and absolute angle sense but, used alone, may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop; combine formats rather than claiming any one medium is required.
Vary ray length independently of opening deliberately: wide-but-short-armed angles are the key trap for the arm-length misconception and should be included on purpose.

45° is part of the target benchmark set; the resolution-sharpening activity only re-deploys it for learners who have anchored to 90°/180° alone, and does not imply 45° is an optional extra for everyone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ±15° tolerance band and the specific benchmark set (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) come from the legacy assessment and pedagogy fields; they are reasonable for ages 9–10 but are design choices, not values established by the cited sources.

The original pedagogy summary additionally lists 30° and 60° as benchmark angles, which its own keyRepresentations omits. This rewrite follows keyRepresentations: 30° is not carried through, and 60° appears only as an intermediate anchor in the resolution-sharpening activity. The inconsistency is inherited from the source and is not resolved by the cited references.

Legacy catalog rationales claiming a 3D environment 'adds spatial overhead without improving' estimation, that a character 'cannot show hundreds of angles', and that a static image 'cannot run the estimate-check loop' were medium-comparison statements; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not asserted as universal pedagogical laws. A fixed image can still teach the benchmark set.

The sources support benchmark-degree reasoning and the arm-length misconception; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive medium or the stated tolerance band. Efficacy-flavoured comparisons are stated with proposed/may wording only.

probeDeeper: Point to the short-armed wide angle and a long-armed narrow one: 'You said this one is smaller — what if I made its lines just as long as the other's? Would it still be smaller?' (counterexample: arm length is irrelevant.)
'How did you decide this one was about 130° — what did you compare it to?' — listen for a benchmark (right angle) rather than a guess.
'This reflex angle — how could you use the smaller angle next to it to work out its size?' (probes 360°-minus-companion reasoning.)
'Your estimate was 120° and the protractor says 128° — is your estimate wrong?' — checks the child understands an estimate is a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the four correctly by opening (not by arm length), estimates each within roughly ±15° of its true size, classifies the ~270° one as reflex (over a straight line, under a full turn) rather than reading its 90° companion, and uses benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle') to justify at least one estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by arm length not opening — puts the short-armed wide angle earlier (smaller) than a long-armed narrow one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so the openings compare directly regardless of arm length; extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ordering tracks ray length rather than degrees; the child may point to the longer lines as the reason it's 'bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: No reflex concept — estimates the ~270° reflex angle as its ~90° companion, or as 'about 90°', reading the wrong side of the opening.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the turn dynamically past the straight line; estimate reflex as 360° minus the companion; explicitly name 'reflex: more than 180°, less than 360°'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the reflex angle acute/right or gives a sub-180° number; treats the reflex mark as if it were the smaller angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark resolution too coarse — snaps every estimate to 90° or 180°, so a 130° angle is called '90' or '180' with nothing in between.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a bit past a right angle' (~120°) as extra anchors; practise estimating angles that sit between benchmarks. No reteaching of concept — the anchor set is just sparse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Estimates cluster only at right angles and straight lines; no use of 45°/60°/120° as intermediate anchors.

responseLevels.gap: Estimates bear little relation to actual size and ordering follows arm length or orientation; no benchmark reasoning and no reflex concept (reads reflex as its companion).
responseLevels.full: Orders all four by opening regardless of arm length, estimates each within about ±15° using benchmark comparisons including intermediate anchors, correctly identifies and estimates the reflex angle via 360°-minus-companion, and treats the estimate as a reasoned range confirmed (not replaced) by measuring.
responseLevels.partial: Estimates acute and obtuse angles reasonably against 90°/180° and orders standard angles correctly, but is caught by at least one of: the short-arm wide angle (orders by length), the reflex angle (no over-180° concept), or coarse resolution (snaps to 90/180). Can name benchmarks but not deploy intermediate ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out four angles the child can see but not measure — include one clearly acute (~40°), one obtuse (~130°), one drawn with short arms but a wide opening, and one reflex (~270°), with ray lengths deliberately uneven. Say: 'Without measuring, put these in order from smallest to largest, and tell me roughly how many degrees each one is.' Then let them measure to check. Watch the ordering and the estimates — do not coach.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The uneven ray lengths separate opening-based judgement from arm-length judgement; the short-arm wide angle is the trap. The reflex angle separates a child who has extended their concept past 180° from one who collapses it back to the acute companion. Ordering plus numeric estimate together expose both relative and absolute angle sense in one two-minute task.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Measuring angles
topic.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor; draw given angles and sketch angles of specified measure
evidence: Measure an angle with a protractor and read 47°
Draw an angle of 135° using a protractor
Identify which scale on the protractor to use for an obtuse angle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a protractor and an angle drawn on paper, can they measure it accurately and then draw a new angle of a size you specify?

pedagogy.summary: By Y5 children already know angle is an amount of turn measured in degrees (1/360 of a full turn). The protractor turns that idea into a tool skill: superimpose a fixed 'fan' of 180 one-degree angles onto the angle so its vertex sits at the centre and one ray runs along the zero line, then read where the second ray crosses the scale. The single hardest part is not the reading but the SET-UP (vertex on centre-cross, baseline on a ray) and CHOOSING WHICH of the two scales to read. Teach estimation-first: decide acute or obtuse before touching the protractor, so the read is checked against sense rather than trusted blindly. The Progressions recommend meeting a full-circle (360°) protractor before the standard two-scale semicircular one, so the connection to 'fraction of a turn' stays visible.
bestPractices: Estimate first: have the child say 'acute / right / obtuse' (and roughly how many degrees) BEFORE measuring, then use that to decide which scale to read — a 47° angle read as 133° is caught immediately because 133° is obviously not acute.
Teach placement as a two-part check every time: vertex exactly on the centre cross, AND one ray exactly along the 0-line; only then read the OTHER ray.
Rotate the angle into non-standard orientations from the start (ray pointing up, down, diagonal) so the child does not learn 'protractor only works when a ray is horizontal'.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale, extend the ray with a ruler first — reinforce that an angle's size does not depend on ray length.
Introduce a full-circle 360° protractor before the two-scale semicircle so degrees stay tied to fraction-of-a-turn; use a two-scale semicircular protractor once scale-choice is secure.
For drawing (e.g. 135°): mark the vertex and baseline, count up the correct scale to the target, mark a dot, then join — draw then check by re-measuring.
keyRepresentations: Protractor as a fixed fan of 180 one-degree unit angles laid over the angle (links directly to 'n one-degree angles = n degrees')
Full-circle 360° protractor (fraction-of-a-turn made visible) before the standard two-scale semicircular protractor
Benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) used as an estimation check on the read
The acute-vs-obtuse decision as the rule for choosing the inner vs outer scale
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale — lands on the mirror value (e.g. 133° instead of 47°) because the child reads whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
Believes the protractor only works when a ray is horizontal ('standard position') and cannot measure a rotated angle.
Measures the length of the rays or the gap between their ends rather than the rotation between them (arm-length carryover).
Does not extend rays that fall short of the scale arc, then reads a smaller/ambiguous value or gives up.

learn.summary: Teach protractor use as a placement-and-read procedure for measuring and drawing angles in whole-number degrees (Y5, ages 9–10). Learners already know an angle is an amount of turn measured in degrees (a full turn = 360°, so n one-degree turns = n degrees). The hard parts are the SET-UP (vertex exactly on the centre cross, one ray exactly along the 0-line) and CHOOSING which of the two scales to read. Lead with estimation: decide acute/right/obtuse (and roughly how many degrees) before measuring, then use that judgement to pick the scale and sanity-check the read. Meeting a full-circle 360° protractor before the standard two-scale semicircular one keeps the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible. Target errors: reading the mirror value (133° for 47°), believing the tool only works when a ray is horizontal, judging size by ray length, and not extending short rays.

activities.title: Estimate-first measuring across orientations
feedback: If a reported number contradicts the angle's obvious type (an acute angle called 133°, or an obtuse one called 60°), pause: re-commit to acute/obtuse, compare against the 90° benchmark, then re-read the matching scale.

If the child turns the page or lines the baseline along the paper edge instead of along a ray, show the same angle rotated several ways and confirm it reads the same measure every time — placement follows the ray, not the page edge.

If readings are consistently a few degrees out in the same direction, check both parts of the placement: the baseline may be slightly rotated off the ray (a common cause of a steady offset), or the vertex may have slipped off the centre cross. Redo the two-part placement check.
On the short-ray angle, if the child reads a small/ambiguous value or says it is 'smaller because the lines are shorter', extend the rays with a ruler and re-measure to show the value is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Grade-level standards require measuring angles in whole-number degrees with a protractor and relating degrees to a fraction of a 360° circle. Documented difficulties — reading the wrong scale, failing on non-standard positions, and not extending rays — are directly rehearsed here, and estimate-first gives an independent check on the read.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).

Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.
Children commonly judge angle size by the length of the arms/rays rather than the amount of opening (turn), a persistent measurement misconception.
learnerActions: Before touching the protractor, say aloud whether each angle is acute, right, or obtuse, and give a rough degree estimate against benchmarks (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°).
Place the protractor so the vertex sits exactly on the centre cross AND one ray lies exactly along the 0-line — check both before reading anything.

Read the OTHER ray on the scale that starts at 0 on the ray you lined up, and check that the number matches your acute/obtuse estimate, then state the measure (e.g. report a rotated angle as 47°, not its mirror value 133°).
Repeat with angles drawn in non-standard orientations: a ray pointing up, down, and diagonally — do not rotate the paper to force a ray horizontal.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale arc, extend a ray with a ruler first, then measure; confirm the measure is the same before and after extending.
activities.intendedInsight: The measure is the amount of opening between the rays, read once the tool is correctly placed; it does not depend on ray length or on any ray being horizontal. The correct scale is the one that starts at 0 on the aligned ray; the acute/obtuse estimate (checked against the 90° benchmark) is a quick check that the right scale was read. For angles very close to 90° both scales read about the same, so careful placement decides the read.

activities.title: Full-circle before two-scale semicircle
feedback: If the child cannot say why one scale is chosen over the other, return to the full-circle tool and re-anchor the reading to the fraction of the turn.
If scale choice is still guessed, have them mark the 90° line first and decide acute/obtuse relative to it before reading.
activities.rationale: The progressions recommend meeting a full-circle protractor before the two-scale semicircular one so the fraction-of-a-turn meaning stays visible and scale choice becomes principled rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.

Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Measure several angles first on a full-circle (360°) protractor, reading the degrees as a fraction of a whole turn.
Then switch to the standard two-scale semicircular protractor and, for each angle, state whether you will read the inner or outer scale and why, before reading it.
Verbalise the link: '90° is a quarter turn; this angle is a bit less than a quarter so it is under 90°.'
activities.intendedInsight: Degrees are a fraction of a whole turn; the two scales on a semicircular protractor run in opposite directions, and the acute/obtuse judgement (checked against the 90° benchmark) is the main guide to which one applies — except for angles close to 90°, where both scales read near 90° and careful placement, not the acute/obtuse call, settles the read.

activities.title: Draw then check
feedback: If the drawn angle re-measures as 45° instead of 135°, the wrong scale was counted (45° and 135° are mirror values, 45+135=180) — re-identify acute/obtuse for the target and choose the scale deliberately.
If the vertex or baseline was not locked before marking, the dot will be placed off the true scale; redo the two-part placement check first.
activities.rationale: The standard requires sketching angles of specified measure, not only reading them; drawing then re-measuring closes the loop and reuses the same scale-choice and placement checks.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: To draw a 135° angle: mark the vertex, draw a baseline, place the protractor (vertex on centre, baseline on 0-line).
Count UP the correct scale to 135°, mark a dot, and join the dot to the vertex.
Re-measure the angle you drew and confirm it reads about 135° (within ±2°); redraw if it is off.
Try drawing in a non-horizontal orientation too, so drawing is not tied to a baseline along the bottom of the page.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing an angle is the inverse of measuring one: the same placement and scale-choice skills apply, and re-measuring your own drawing is a built-in check.

activities.title: Reasoning probes and reflex-angle stretch
feedback: If the child says 'that's the number the line hit' when asked why a scale was chosen, reteach estimate-first scale selection against the 90° benchmark.
If they treat the longer-armed angle as bigger, extend both pairs of rays to equal length and re-measure to show the measures are unchanged.

For 210°, acknowledge the semicircular scale physically stops at 180° so no single direct reading is possible; guide them to measure the smaller non-reflex angle of 150° and subtract from a full turn (360−150=210), or to use a full-circle 360° protractor.
activities.rationale: These prompts separate a real procedure from a brittle 'ray-along-the-bottom' ritual by surfacing the standard-position, ray-length, and wrong-scale misconceptions, and extend reasoning toward reflex angles beyond the semicircular scale.
sourceClaims: Children commonly judge angle size by the length of the arms/rays rather than the amount of opening (turn), a persistent measurement misconception.

Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.
learnerActions: Compare a rotated angle and a horizontal one and answer 'Which is bigger? How could you be sure without being told?' — justify by measuring, not by orientation.
Answer: 'If these two lines were made twice as long but opened the same, what would the protractor say?' and explain why the measure is unchanged.
Explain why you read one scale and not the other for a given angle.
Attempt to start drawing a 210° angle and explain what happens when the semicircular scale only runs to 180° (reasoning about reflex angles).
activities.intendedInsight: A secure measurer justifies readings by the amount of opening and by acute/obtuse scale choice, recognises ray length is irrelevant, and notices the semicircular scale's 180° limit when facing a reflex angle.

constraints: Learners must perform the placement themselves (physical protractor and paper, or a draggable/rotatable on-screen tool): reading a value off a pre-placed protractor, choosing inner-vs-outer scale, or identifying a measure in multiple-choice form practises sub-skills but does not assess the placement performance that is the core objective.
A static labelled diagram can name the parts of a protractor but cannot let the child place it, choose a scale, or recompute a reading; use it only as a reference, not as the main practice.
Include non-standard orientations from the start; do not let rotating the paper become a crutch that masks whether the child can align the baseline to any ray.
Include at least one short-ray angle so extending rays (and the ray-length-is-irrelevant idea) is explicitly rehearsed.

Interactive examples (snap/glow feedback when vertex-on-centre and baseline-on-ray are both met, a scale that lights based on the acute/obtuse choice, a draw-mode that re-measures the drawn angle) make the mechanism concrete but are optional implementations, not required.
Accuracy expectation is reading/drawing to within about ±2°.

The semicircular scale only runs to 180°; reflex angles (e.g. 210°) cannot be read directly from it and need separate reasoning (measure the 150° non-reflex angle and subtract from 360°, or use a full-circle protractor).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that only a 2D interactive tool teaches this skill and that a static image, a 3D environment, or a dialogue add nothing. These are catalog-preference claims, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened: a physical protractor on paper is a fully valid medium, a static diagram can serve as a reference scaffold, and spoken reasoning can support (though not replace) hands-on placement practice.
The claim that measuring a planar angle in 3D 'adds no conceptual gain' is a design preference, not a verified finding; retained only as a scoped note that the task is inherently 2D.

The acute/obtuse-chooses-the-scale rule is faithful to the original keyRepresentations but is a heuristic; it is least reliable for angles close to 90°, where both scales read near 90° and placement accuracy, not the acute/obtuse call, settles the read. This caveat is now stated consistently in both the measuring and full-circle activities.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: the 47°/133° and 45°/135° mirror pairs each sum to 180° (consistent with the two opposite-running scales), 360−150=210 for the reflex stretch, and the benchmark angles are internally consistent; no numeric errors found to correct.

probeDeeper: Point to the rotated angle and the horizontal one and ask: 'Which is bigger? How could you be sure without me telling you?' — listen for measuring rather than judging by orientation.
'You read 47°. If I made these two lines twice as long but kept them opened the same, what would the protractor say now?' (counterexample: ray length is irrelevant.)
'Why did you read this scale and not the other one?' — a secure child cites acute/obtuse; a brittle one says 'that's the number the line hit'.
'Show me how you'd start drawing a 210° angle' — surfaces whether they see the semicircular scale only goes to 180° and reason about reflex angles.
assess.correctAnswer: For each angle: vertex placed on the centre-cross, one ray on the 0-line, reads the scale that matches whether the angle is acute or obtuse (e.g. reports the rotated angle correctly rather than its mirror value), extends the short rays before reading, and reads to within ±2°. For the drawing: marks the vertex and baseline, counts up the correct scale, and draws an angle that re-measures to about 135°.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale — reports the mirror value ('it's 133' for a clearly acute 47° angle) because they read whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate estimate-first: before every read, commit to acute or obtuse, then use that to pick the scale; check the read against a 90° benchmark. Reteach the degree-size sense if the acute/obtuse judgement itself is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The reported number contradicts the angle's obvious type (calls an acute angle 133°, or an obtuse one 60°); often reads the inner scale for one angle and outer for the next with no rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Can only measure when a ray is horizontal — rotates the paper or gives up on the angle drawn in non-standard orientation, believing the protractor 'only works' along the bottom.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise placing the baseline on a ray regardless of orientation; show the same angle rotated several times reads the same measure. Do NOT let the child rotate the paper as a crutch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Succeeds on the horizontal angle but turns the page, or places the baseline along the page edge instead of along a ray, for the rotated one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures ray length or the gap between the ray ends rather than the rotation — thrown by the short-ray angle, reads where the drawn ray stops or reports the longer-armed angle as bigger.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the rays with a ruler and re-measure to show the value is unchanged; reconnect to angle as amount of turn, independent of ray length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the short-rays angle they read a small/ambiguous value, or comment that it is 'smaller' because the lines are shorter, instead of extending the rays to the scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vertex off the centre-cross — lines the tool up on the 0-line but leaves the vertex short of or past the centre, so every reading is skewed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-part placement check (vertex-on-cross THEN ray-on-zero) as a habit; no reteaching of concept needed — the idea is held, the hand slips.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Placement looks roughly right but readings are consistently a few degrees out in the same direction; the vertex visibly does not sit on the centre point.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably place the protractor: vertex and baseline are not both aligned, readings are essentially random or copied from wherever a line crosses, and the drawn angle bears no relation to 135°.
responseLevels.full: Places vertex-on-centre and baseline-on-ray in any orientation, chooses the correct scale by first judging acute/obtuse, extends short rays, reads within ±2°, and draws a 135° angle that re-measures correctly — the procedure is robust across the varied set, not tied to a standard position.
responseLevels.partial: Measures correctly when a ray is already horizontal and reads a single scale, but is derailed by at least one of: a rotated angle (rotates the paper or misaligns), short rays (reads without extending), or scale choice (gives the mirror value). Can state the steps but cannot transfer them to the varied cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three angles in front of the child, each drawn in a DIFFERENT orientation (one with a horizontal ray, one rotated so no ray is horizontal, one with rays drawn too short to reach the protractor's scale). Hand them a protractor and say: 'Measure each of these. Tell me the degrees.' Then give a blank and say: 'Now draw me an angle of exactly 135°.' Watch how they place the tool and choose the scale — do not explain the procedure.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three deliberately-varied orientations separate a child who has a real procedure from one who has memorised a single 'ray-along-the-bottom' ritual: the rotated angle exposes the standard-position misconception, the short-rays angle exposes arm-length/ray-extension, and the acute-vs-obtuse spread exposes wrong-scale reading. A child measuring correctly for the right reasons handles all three; a child with a brittle routine succeeds only on the horizontal one.

sources.claim: Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).
