topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Measuring angles (age 9+)
topic.description: Recognise angle measure as additive; find unknown angles by adding or subtracting on a diagram using equations with a symbol for the unknown
evidence: Two angles on a straight line are 65° and x°; find x = 115°
An angle is decomposed into 35° and 40°; state the whole angle is 75°
Solve: angles at a point are 120°, 90°, and x°; find x = 150°
topic.assessmentPrompt: If two angles sit next to each other on a straight line and one is 65°, can {{name}} work out the other angle — knowing that angles on a straight line always add up to 180°?

pedagogy.summary: This is the PROCEDURAL partner to the Angle Sum Rules concept: the child treats angle measure as ADDITIVE (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turns an angle diagram into an EQUATION with a symbol for the unknown, then solves it. The move that matters is representing 'the parts share a fixed whole' as arithmetic — 65° + x° = 180° on a straight line, or 120° + 90° + x° = 360° at a point — and solving by subtraction. Taught well it is not a new fact but a disciplined routine: read the configuration to fix the whole (180° or 360°), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram is a source of GIVEN facts, not something to remeasure.
bestPractices: Make the equation explicit every time: write 65 + x = 180 (or 120 + 90 + x = 360), name the whole first, then solve — so the reasoning is visible and checkable rather than a mental leap to an answer.
Anchor the whole to the configuration before any arithmetic: straight line → 180°, point → 360°; decide which BEFORE computing, so a point problem is never solved with 180°.
Use a bar/part-whole model of the fixed whole with the unknown as a labelled segment, connecting the algebraic symbol to the shared-whole picture.
Insist the diagram gives facts, not measurements: the answer comes from the marked angles and the rule, NOT from putting a protractor on the printed (often not-to-scale) figure.
Separate a reasoning error (wrong whole, non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180) when marking — they need different help.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (two parts making a named whole).
keyRepresentations: Equation with a symbol for the unknown: 65 + x = 180, 120 + 90 + x = 360
Bar / part-whole model of the fixed whole (180° or 360°) with the unknown as a labelled segment
The straight line (180°) and the full point (360°) as the two 'wholes' to subtract from
Decomposition diagram: a large angle split into marked parts that sum to it
commonMisconceptions: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° at a point or 360° on a straight line because the configuration was not identified first.
Treats angle measure as non-additive — tries to measure the unknown on the diagram instead of computing it from the others.
Reads the diagram as if it were to scale — assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal (e.g. an isosceles-looking triangle), or measures the printed unknown, rather than using the marked values.
Arithmetic slip when subtracting from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 gives 45 instead of 35) — the angle reasoning is sound but the subtraction fails.

learn.summary: Learners treat angle measure as additive (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turn an angle diagram into an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve by subtraction. The disciplined routine is: read the configuration to fix the whole (straight line = 180°, point = 360°, or a decomposition whole that is either named or found by adding the parts), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram supplies given facts from its marked values; it is not to be remeasured with a protractor, and it may be drawn not to scale.

activities.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
feedback: If the equation uses the wrong whole (e.g. 120 + 90 + x = 180 for angles at a point, or 360 on a straight line), this is a reasoning error: go back and re-name the whole from the configuration. Sort several diagrams by which whole applies before computing again.

If the equation is correct but the final number is off (e.g. writing 180 − 145 = 45 when the correct result is 35), this is an arithmetic slip, not an angle error: redo the subtraction carefully with a number line or column method; the geometry is already sound.
If no equation appears and a protractor is reached for, point back to the marked values: the other angles plus the rule fix the answer, so cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone.
activities.rationale: Making the equation and the chosen whole explicit every time keeps the reasoning visible and checkable, and lets a reasoning error be separated from an arithmetic slip — which need different help. Anchoring the whole to the configuration before computing prevents solving a point problem with 180°.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).

In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Look at each diagram and first decide and state the whole before any arithmetic: a straight line split by a ray is a half turn (180°); angles meeting at a point make a whole turn (360°); for a decomposed angle, either the whole is named and you find a missing part, or the parts are marked and you add them to find the whole.
For a straight line with one angle marked 65° and the other marked x, write the equation 65 + x = 180, then solve to get x = 115°.
For angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x, write 120 + 90 + x = 360, then solve to get x = 150°.
For a large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, write 35 + 40 = w with a symbol for the whole, then solve to get w = 75°.
After solving, check the answer back against the fixed whole (do all the parts add to 180° or 360°, or to the stated decomposition whole?).
activities.intendedInsight: An unknown angle is determined by the marked angles and the fixed whole, so it can be computed with an equation rather than measured. Choosing the correct whole (180° vs 360° vs a decomposition whole) is the first decision, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Part-whole bar model linking the symbol to the shared whole
feedback: If the segments overflow or underfill the bar, the parts do not sum to the chosen whole — recheck either the whole or the arithmetic.
If a learner can fill the bar but not write the matching equation, pair each step: 'the gap' becomes '180 − 65', and 'parts fill the whole' becomes '65 + x = 180'.
activities.rationale: A part-whole/bar model connects the algebraic unknown to the shared-whole picture, supporting learners who treat angle measure as non-additive by showing parts recombining to the whole and a missing part found by subtraction.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Draw or use a bar representing the fixed whole (e.g. a bar labelled 180° for a straight line, or 360° for a point).
Fill the bar with the known angles as labelled segments, leaving a gap for the unknown.
Label the remaining gap as x, and read off that x is what is left when the known parts are taken from the whole.
Connect this to the equation: the gap in the bar is 180 − 65, which is the same as solving 65 + x = 180.
Optionally, use a live model where solving the subtraction makes the x segment snap to exactly fill the bar, so the 'parts complete the whole' idea is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: The algebraic symbol x corresponds to a concrete missing segment of a fixed shared whole; subtraction finds the gap that completes the whole.

activities.title: Decompose and recombine a concrete angle
feedback: If a learner still reaches for a protractor on the missing part, revisit the recombination: since the parts provably sum to the whole, the missing part is fixed by subtraction and does not need measuring.
If the two parts don't sum to the stated whole, check which part is mismarked rather than assuming the rule failed.
activities.rationale: Decomposing and recombining a concrete angle makes additivity tangible before it is used in reverse to find a missing part — the development route described in the K–5 Progressions.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.
learnerActions: Take a concrete angle (e.g. a cut paper wedge, or an angle built from two strips) and split it into two marked parts.
Add the two parts to confirm they equal the whole angle (e.g. 35° + 40° = 75°).
Reverse the process: cover one part and find it by subtracting the known part from the whole.
State in words that non-overlapping parts that exactly fill the angle always sum to the whole, so a missing part can be computed rather than measured.
Note that the paper wedge or strips are physical approximations with slight thickness; the mathematical angle being reasoned about is the idealised figure they represent.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle measure is additive: parts sum to the whole, and reversing this gives a missing part by subtraction. This directly addresses the belief that an unknown angle must be measured.

activities.title: Not-to-scale diagram: reason from marked values, not appearance
feedback: If the answer is close to the printed size rather than 115°, the learner measured or trusted appearance — redo it from the marked values with the figure covered.
If an answer is justified by 'they look the same', point out that only marked or equal-labelled angles can be assumed equal.
activities.rationale: Diagnostic data shows learners who read diagrams as to-scale (e.g. assuming an isosceles-looking triangle) make reasoning errors; 'not drawn to scale' framing and solving from marked values counter this.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Work a diagram labelled 'not drawn to scale' where the printed unknown angle looks smaller than the given 65° angle (for example, drawn acute) but must still equal 115° by the rule.
Cover the figure and solve from the marked numbers and the fixed whole alone (65 + x = 180, x = 115°).
Only then reveal the drawing and notice the picture was misleading.
Discuss a case where two angles 'look equal' but are not marked equal, and explain why you cannot assume equality from appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: A diagram carries stated facts, not scale: answers come from the marked values and the rule, not from measuring the printed figure or assuming look-alike angles are equal.

activities.title: Mixed practice: choose the whole each time
feedback: If one whole is applied to every diagram regardless of configuration, sort the diagrams by which whole applies before solving.
If an impossible answer slips through (e.g. parts exceeding the whole), use the sanity-check step to catch it.
Writing the relationship two ways (65 + x = 180 vs x = 180 − 65) shows flexible understanding; if only one form is possible, revisit the part-whole model.
activities.rationale: Varied configurations force the learner to select the whole and expose a wrong-whole error; requiring a written equation reveals whether the additive structure is understood and distinguishes arithmetic slips from reasoning errors. This volume of varied, feedback-rich practice is how the routine is mastered.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Work a mixed set that includes a straight-line single-unknown case, a point case with several angles and one unknown, and a decomposition case (adding two marked parts to find the whole, e.g. 35 + 40 = 75°, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
For each item, write the equation first, labelling the whole, before giving a number.
Try writing the same relationship two ways for one diagram, e.g. 65 + x = 180 and x = 180 − 65, to show they describe the same additive structure.

Sanity-check each result: plug the answer back and confirm the parts add to the stated whole (e.g. for two 100° angles and x at a point, 100 + 100 + 160 = 360); ask whether the answer is even possible (e.g. a result of 180° or more for one of two angles on a straight line, or a zero or negative result, means the whole or a value was misread).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means choosing the correct whole for each configuration rather than applying one habitual routine, and verifying the answer against the fixed whole.

constraints: This is a procedural skill: learners must actually set up and solve their own equations across varied diagrams, not just watch a labelled worked example. A reveal-the-answer picture can illustrate a worked example but does not let the learner construct and solve, so it is only a scaffold toward independent solving.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. completing 65 + x = ___, or choosing whether to subtract from 180 or 360) give useful scorable practice and can be used during teaching, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves show independent equation setup; pair them with tasks where the learner writes the whole equation.

Always distinguish a reasoning error (wrong whole, treating measure as non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180 or 360) when giving feedback — they require different remediation.
Insist that the diagram supplies stated facts, not measurements; include at least one deliberately not-to-scale diagram so measuring or assuming look-alike angles are equal is caught.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (adding parts to find the whole, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
Physical angle cut-outs and strips are approximations with real thickness; use them to demonstrate additivity, but the represented angle is the idealised figure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in the source: 65 + x = 180 → x = 115° ✓; 120 + 90 + x = 360 → x = 150° ✓; 35 + 40 = 75° ✓; 100 + 100 + x = 360 → x = 160° ✓. The illustrative slip 180 − 145 has correct result 35; the value 45 is the deliberately-wrong slip used in feedback to model an arithmetic error, never offered as a learner answer. No errors were propagated into learner-facing correct answers.

The original material asserted that a 3D environment 'gains nothing' and that dialogue cannot deliver this skill; these catalog-style necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been reframed as scoped observations about affordances (procedural fluency needs learner-constructed solving and feedback-rich practice) rather than universal laws.

Activity 5's decomposition wording was corrected to match the worked example (whole found by adding) and activity 1's two sub-cases, resolving a minor internal inconsistency carried from the original 'named whole' progression phrasing.

probeDeeper: 'You wrote 65 + x = 180. Why 180 and not 360 here?' — listen for 'it's a straight line, a half turn' versus a memorised default.
Counterexample: 'This diagram is not drawn accurately. If I told you nothing looks the right size, could you still find x? How?' — checks reliance on the rule over appearance.
'If the two given angles at the point were both 100° instead, what would x be — and is that even possible?' (100+100+x=360 → 160; probes whether they sanity-check against the fixed whole).
'Show me a different equation for the same diagram' — e.g. x = 180 − 65 vs 65 + x = 180 — tests flexible understanding of the additive relationship.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) writes 65 + x = 180 and solves x = 115°; (2) writes 120 + 90 + x = 360 and solves x = 150°; (3) writes 35 + 40 = 75°. Uses the marked values and the correct whole for each configuration, and does NOT try to measure the printed (not-to-scale) angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° for the angles-at-a-point diagram (or 360° on the straight line) because the configuration wasn't identified first.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish 'name the whole first': straight line = half turn 180°, point = whole turn 360°; sort diagrams by which whole applies before any arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120 + 90 + x = 180, or gives a point answer that's 180° short; may apply one whole to every diagram regardless of shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the diagram as to-scale — measures the printed unknown with a protractor, or assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal, instead of computing from the marked values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that diagrams carry stated facts, not scale; cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone, then reveal that the drawing was misleading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the not-to-scale diagram gives a value close to the printed size rather than 115°; or justifies an answer with 'they look the same'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats angle measure as non-additive — doesn't believe the unknown is determined, so reaches for a protractor rather than writing an equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine a concrete angle to show parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find a missing part by subtraction; frame the whole as fixed and shared.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot start without measuring; produces no equation even though the other angles are given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Arithmetic slip — sets up the correct equation but mis-subtracts from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 = 45 rather than 35).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the subtraction (number line / column method); no angle reteaching needed — the geometry is held, the arithmetic slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equation is correct and the method sound, but the final number is off by a computation error, often consistent across items.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot set up or solve: no equation, wrong whole, or measures the diagram; answers bear no reliable relation to the marked angles.
responseLevels.full: Writes and solves the correct equation for line, point and decomposition, choosing the right whole each time, ignores misleading scale by using marked values, sanity-checks the result against the fixed whole, and any error is a clean arithmetic slip rather than a reasoning failure.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the standard single-unknown-on-a-line case and can state 'they add to 180', but is derailed by the point configuration (wrong whole), the not-to-scale diagram (measures/assumes equal), or produces an answer without an equation — applies one routine rather than choosing the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three diagrams in front of the child. (1) A straight line split by one ray, one angle marked 65°, the other x. (2) Angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x. (3) A large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, asking for the whole. Say: 'Find each unknown, and write down the equation you used to get it.' Make diagram (1) deliberately NOT to scale so the printed x looks bigger than 65°. Watch how they set up and solve — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three configurations force the child to choose the whole (180° vs 360°) rather than apply one habit, so a wrong-whole error is exposed. The not-to-scale diagram separates a child who reasons from the rule from one who measures or trusts appearance. Requiring the written equation shows whether the additive structure is understood or the answer was guessed, and it distinguishes an arithmetic slip (equation right, number wrong) from a genuine reasoning error.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Angle Sum Rules
topic.description: Know that angles at a point sum to 360° (one whole turn), angles on a straight line sum to 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal; use these facts to find missing angles
evidence: State that two angles on a straight line add to 180°
Explain that four right angles at a point make 360°
Identify 270° as three right angles
topic.assessmentPrompt: If three angles meet at a point and two of them are 120° and 95°, can {{name}} work out the third angle — knowing all the angles at a point add up to 360°?

pedagogy.summary: Angle sum rules are the first place children use angle facts to REASON rather than measure: because a full turn is 360° and a straight line is a half turn (180°), the angles that fill a point must total 360° and the angles on a straight line must total 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal. The load-bearing idea underneath is ADDITIVITY — an angle decomposed into parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts (CCSS 4.MD.7). Taught well, the child sees a straight line or a point as a fixed 'whole' (180° / 360°) that the parts share out, so a missing part can be found by subtraction without a protractor. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained'.
bestPractices: Ground the two totals in turn: a straight line is a half turn (180°), a full point is a whole turn (360°) — connect directly to the degrees-as-fraction-of-a-turn idea rather than presenting 180/360 as arbitrary.
Build additivity concretely: decompose an angle into two parts, measure each and the whole, and show the parts sum to the whole; then reverse it to FIND a missing part by subtraction.
Use the fixed-whole framing explicitly — 'these angles share out 180° (or 360°); if one takes 110° the rest must be 70°' — so children reason instead of reaching for the protractor.
Contrast the two rules deliberately (line = 180° vs point = 360°) so they are not confused; anchor 270° as three right angles and 360° as four.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from the straight-line rule (both share the same partner angle to make 180°), rather than asserting it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Straight line as a half turn = 180°; full point as a whole turn = 360°
The fixed 'whole' shared out among parts (bar-like partition of 180° or 360°)
Right angle as the 90° quarter unit: two make a straight line, four make a point, three make 270°
Decompose-and-recombine diagram showing angle measure is additive
Vertically opposite pair derived from two straight-line sums
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two totals — uses 360° for angles on a straight line or 180° for angles at a point.
Angle measure treated as non-additive / not conserved — insists on measuring every angle separately and does not believe a missing angle is determined by the others.
Does not recognise a straight line as an angle of 180° (a straight/half-turn angle 'doesn't look like an angle'), so cannot apply the rule.
Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°) rather than equal, confusing them with the adjacent straight-line pair.
Assumes the parts must be equal (splits 180° as 90° + 90° by default) regardless of the given angle.

learn.summary: Teach children that a straight line is a half turn (180°) and a full point is a whole turn (360°), so the angles filling each are parts that share out a fixed whole. The load-bearing idea is additivity: an angle split into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts. Once the whole is seen as fixed, a missing part is found by subtraction without a protractor, and vertically opposite angles can be derived as equal rather than memorised. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained.'

activities.title: The shared-whole angle bench
feedback: If a learner expects the total to change as they drag, pause and point to the banner: the parts trade size but their sum stays locked — that is exactly why one part fixes the other.
When a learner first says 'the other one must be 70° without measuring', confirm this is the key move: 70° is simply 180° − 110°.

In the crossing-lines view, if a learner expects the opposite angles to add to 180°, show the two measures staying equal as the lines turn — the pair that always adds to 180° is the adjacent pair on the straight line; the opposite pair adds to 180° only when the lines are perpendicular (90° each).
activities.rationale: Letting one angle grow as the other shrinks while the sum stays visibly locked makes the invariant-sum relationship concrete and lets the child predict a hidden part rather than be told the rule. A live, draggable model makes the constrained sum observable; a static picture can state the totals but cannot show them staying constant as the parts change.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Watch a ray that pivots on a straight line, with two angle wedges filling it; each wedge shows its degrees and a banner reads the running total, e.g. '110° + 70° = 180°'.
Drag the pivoting ray and notice that one wedge swells while the other yields, but the total never moves off 180°.
Say aloud the moment you realise you no longer need to measure the second angle: it is whatever is left of 180°.
Switch to a point version where three or four wedges share 360°, and drag to see the total stay locked at 360°.
Open a crossing-lines view: drag the lines and watch the vertically opposite pair stay equal as everything turns.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole (180° on a line, 360° at a point) is fixed, so the parts are constrained; a missing part is whatever is left of the whole, and vertically opposite angles are equal because each pair shares the same partner angle to make 180°.

activities.title: Hide and predict the missing angle
feedback: If a learner says 'you can't tell without measuring', decompose and recombine first: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find the missing part by subtraction.
If a learner answers 90° by assuming an equal split, show the ray redrawn so the angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180° — the equal case is just one of many.
If a learner subtracts from 360° on a straight-line diagram, place a line diagram and a point diagram side by side and re-derive from turn: a line is a half turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°).
activities.rationale: Predicting before revealing forces reasoning from the fixed whole rather than measurement, and directly confronts the non-additive, equal-split, and wrong-whole errors by making the correct subtraction explicit.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).
UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.
learnerActions: On a straight-line diagram with one angle given (e.g. 110°), state the other angle before any reveal and say why it must be that size.
Explain the reason in words: 'the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70.'
Repeat for a point where three or four angles share 360°, finding the missing one by subtracting the others from 360°.
Try a case where the ray is clearly not up the middle, so the two parts are visibly unequal yet still total 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing angle is determined by the others through subtraction from the fixed whole; the parts need not be equal.

activities.title: Contrast the line and the point, anchor on right angles
feedback: If a learner confuses the two totals, re-anchor on turn: a straight line is half of a full turn, so 180° is half of 360°.
If a learner marks vertically opposite angles as adding to 180°, revisit the crossing-lines model: the pair sharing a straight line adds to 180°, the opposite pair is equal.
Praise correctly identifying 270° as three right angles and connect it to 360° as four right angles.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting line and point prevents the two rules being muddled, and anchoring on the right-angle unit grounds 180°, 270°, and 360° in a shared quarter-turn benchmark rather than arbitrary numbers. Recognition and sorting tasks give scorable practice; they consolidate application but do not by themselves build the fixed-whole intuition that the live, draggable model provides.
sourceClaims: UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Sort a set of diagrams by which whole applies: 180° for angles on a straight line, 360° for angles at a point.
Tap a straight-line diagram to reveal '180° = half turn' and a point to reveal '360° = whole turn'.
Build the benchmarks: two right angles make a straight line (180°), four make a point (360°), and three make 270°.
Answer practice items that find a missing angle on a line and at a point, including an item that checks whether vertically opposite angles are equal (not that they add to 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: The two totals come from half-turn versus whole-turn; 270° is three right angles; vertically opposite angles are always equal, but they add to 180° only in the special case where the lines are perpendicular (both 90°), whereas adjacent angles on a straight line always add to 180°.

constraints: Ground both totals in turn (straight line = half turn = 180°, point = whole turn = 360°) rather than presenting the numbers as arbitrary facts to memorise.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from two straight-line sums sharing a partner angle, rather than asserting it as a separate memorised fact.

Recognition, sorting, and fill-in items consolidate applying the rules but do not elicit the independent reasoning that predicting a hidden part before revealing it requires; use them as practice, not as the sole check of understanding.
A static diagram can reveal and label the totals but cannot show the sum staying constant as the parts change, so the reasoning move stays told rather than discovered with it alone.
Always include cases where the two parts are unequal, so children do not infer that angles on a line must be 90° each.
Angles at a point and on a line are planar; a three-dimensional setting is not needed and can distract from the fixed-whole idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited standards and curriculum documents support angle additivity, benchmark turns, and the Year 5 angle facts; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive design, so claims of one medium being uniquely able to teach this have been softened to scoped affordances.

The core subtraction (180 − 110 = 70) and benchmark facts (two right angles = 180°, three = 270°, four = 360°) were checked and are correct. The original row's wrong-whole distractor printed '290°' while labelling it 360 − 110; this is an original error, since 360 − 110 = 250°. Neither the inconsistent 290° nor the corrected 250° is reproduced in any learner-facing item here; the wrong-whole pattern is taught abstractly as 'subtracting from 360° instead of 180°.'

assess.poeTask: Draw a straight line with a point on it and one ray up, making two angles; mark one as 110°. Ask the child to PREDICT the other angle and — before any measuring — say WHY it must be that size. Then measure both and add them. The reason given before measuring is the diagnostic part: a child who predicts 70° 'because it looks about right' but cannot say the two must total 180° (a straight line = half turn) reveals the additive straight-line rule is not yet there, even if the number happens to be close.
probeDeeper: 'If I'd told you the first angle was 30° instead of 110°, what's the other one? How did you get it so quickly?' — a rule-holder answers instantly by subtraction; a measurer stalls.
'Now there are THREE angles sitting on the straight line, not two. What do all three add up to?' — tests that additivity generalises beyond two parts.
Counterexample: 'A friend says these two angles must be equal, 90° each. Is that always true? Show me a case where it isn't.' — confronts the equal-split assumption.
'Angles at a point make 360° but on a straight line only 180° — why the difference?' — surfaces the half-turn vs whole-turn reasoning.
assess.correctAnswer: 70°, because the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they must make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70. (The reason — a straight line is 180° and the parts share it — is the part that matters.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — subtracts from 360° instead of 180° because the two rules (line = 180°, point = 360°) are confused.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two configurations side by side and re-derive from turn: a straight line is a HALF turn (180°), a full point a WHOLE turn (360°); sort diagrams by which whole applies.
errorPatterns.distractor: 290°, because the angles around the point add up to 360°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 290°, or explains 'angles round a point make 360°' for a straight-line diagram; may give 180° for angles at a point on other items.

errorPatterns.pattern: Angle measure treated as non-additive — does not believe the second angle is determined by the first, so insists it must be measured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse to FIND a missing part by subtraction; frame the straight line as a fixed 180° shared out.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't tell — you'd have to measure the other angle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for a protractor, or says 'you can't know without measuring'; cannot compute the missing angle even though 110° is given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes an equal split — halves the whole regardless of the given angle, answering 90°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the ray is not up the middle; drag/redraw it so the two angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180°; the equal case is just one of many.
errorPatterns.distractor: 90°, because the line is split into two equal angles
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 90° and justifies with 'they're the same' or 'it's split in the middle', ignoring the 110°.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the missing angle without measuring, or uses the wrong whole; treats each angle as independent and gives no valid reason.
responseLevels.full: Gets 70° and justifies it by the straight line being a half turn (180°) whose parts are additive; distinguishes it cleanly from the 360° point rule, transfers to three-part sums and angles at a point, and derives vertically opposite angles as equal rather than supplementary.
responseLevels.partial: States and uses the fact ('they add to 180°') to get 70°, but cannot explain WHY 180° (does not connect it to a straight line being a half turn) and does not transfer to a point, to three-angle sums, or to vertically opposite equality — lists the rules without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a straight line with a point on it and one ray going up, making two angles. Mark one angle as 110° and leave the other blank. Ask: 'What is the other angle?' — and then, whatever they say: 'How do you know it has to be that, without measuring it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only pattern-matched a number can sometimes land on 70°, but the second tier forces the reason: only a child who holds the straight-line-is-180°-and-additive idea can say WHY. A child using the wrong whole says 290° (360−110); a child who doesn't believe the sum is fixed says 'you can't tell without measuring'; a child assuming equal split says 90°. Each wrong route reveals a distinct, documented misunderstanding, and a right answer for the wrong reason is caught by the second tier.
