topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Angles in triangles (age 10+)
topic.description: Find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons using angle sum properties
evidence: Find a missing angle in a triangle given two angles (using angle sum = 180°)
Calculate a missing angle in a quadrilateral (angle sum = 360°)
Calculate the interior angle of a regular hexagon from the angle sum formula
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that angles in a triangle always add up to 180°, and two angles in a triangle are 55° and 70°, can they work out the third angle without measuring it?

pedagogy.summary: Here the fixed-whole idea generalises from lines and points to CLOSED SHAPES: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, of a quadrilateral to 360°, and of any polygon to (n−2)×180° — because every polygon can be cut into (n−2) triangles. The child uses these sums to find a missing angle by subtraction, and for a REGULAR polygon divides the sum equally among the vertices (regular hexagon: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°). The central pedagogical danger is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated fact to memorise; taught well, the triangle sum is DERIVED (torn corners laid on a straight line, or a triangle's angles rearranged to 180°) and the quadrilateral/polygon sums are built by partitioning into triangles — so the whole family hangs together and, crucially, the sum is seen to be INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size.
bestPractices: Derive the triangle sum, don't just state it: tear off the three corners and fit them onto a straight line (180°), or fold them to a point on the base — so 180° is a thing the child has seen happen, not a number to recall.

Build the quadrilateral (360°) and polygon sums by PARTITIONING into triangles — a quadrilateral is two triangles, an n-gon is (n−2) triangles — connecting every polygon back to the triangle rather than memorising separate facts.

Confront size-dependence directly: show that stretching a triangle bigger, or drawing it with longer sides, leaves the angle sum at 180° — many children (and adults) intuitively expect the angles to grow with the triangle.
Use 'not drawn to scale' problems and non-isosceles-looking triangles so children compute from given angles rather than assuming equal angles from appearance.
For regular polygons, separate the two steps clearly: find the total angle sum, THEN divide by the number of (equal) vertices — don't conflate the sum with a single interior angle.
Treat finding a missing angle as subtraction from the known sum, writing the calculation, and sanity-checking (a triangle angle can't exceed 180°).
keyRepresentations: Torn-corners demonstration: three triangle corners rearranged onto a straight line = 180°
Polygon partitioned into triangles: quadrilateral = 2 triangles (360°), n-gon = (n−2) triangles
Angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°
Regular polygon: total sum ÷ number of vertices = one interior angle (hexagon 720° ÷ 6 = 120°)
A stretchable triangle whose angle sum stays 180° as its size changes
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° rather than 180° (documented in diagnostic data), so subtracts from the wrong total.

Believes the angle sum (or a missing angle) depends on the triangle's SIZE — expects a bigger/longer triangle to have larger angles; contradicts the constant 180° sum (documented in children and adults).
Assumes a triangle is isosceles or equilateral because it looks that way on a not-to-scale diagram, so wrongly takes two angles as equal.
Knows '180° in a triangle' only as a disconnected fact and cannot extend it to a quadrilateral or polygon (does not partition into triangles).
For a regular polygon, reports the total angle sum as if it were a single interior angle (forgets to divide by the number of vertices).

learn.summary: Learners find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons using angle-sum properties — but with the triangle's 180° DERIVED (not merely recalled), the quadrilateral/polygon sums BUILT by partitioning into (n−2) triangles, and the crucial fact that the angle sum is INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size made visible rather than asserted. Activities span a hands-on/manipulable derivation of 180° and size-invariance, a partition-to-build-larger-sums task, scorable missing-angle practice (including 'not drawn to scale' and 360°-distractor items), and a two-step regular-polygon calculation (total sum ÷ vertices). The central danger addressed throughout is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated memorised fact.

activities.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
feedback: If the corners fill the line with no gap or overlap, the angles make a straight angle, 180°. Paper shows this up to small imperfections, and the exact value is the ideal geometric result.
Tearing and folding should give the same result: both arrange the three angles along a straight line.
Try a very differently-shaped triangle: if its corners still fill a straight line, the 180° result is not specific to one triangle.
A paper cutout has slight thickness and torn edges, so expect tiny imperfections; the screen model shows the idealised exact fit for the ideal (zero-thickness) plane figure.
activities.rationale: Deriving the triangle sum by physically rearranging corners onto a straight line — whether by tearing or by folding to a point on the base — connects it to 'angles on a straight line = 180°' and makes 180° an observed outcome rather than a disconnected fact, the pedagogy's central correction. Both paper and an optional drag-and-snap screen model make the mechanism concrete; efficacy relative to simply stating the rule is proposed, not tested.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Cut or tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them side by side so their vertices meet at a single point — observe that together they fill a straight line (180°), with no visible gap or overlap apart from small paper imperfections.

Alternatively derive the same result by using the longest side as the base: fold the top corner down so it touches the base at the foot of the height, then fold the other two corners in to meet it at that point — they again fill a straight line along the base.
Repeat either method with a differently-shaped triangle (e.g. a long thin one and a squat one) and confirm the three corners again fill a straight line.
On a drag-and-drop screen model, drag the three corner-wedges onto a straight line so they snap to fill 180°, with a banner reading the running sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The three interior angles of ANY triangle rearrange to lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180° — this is something you can see happen (by tearing or by folding the corners), not a number to recall.

activities.title: Does the sum change when the triangle changes size?
feedback: If you predicted the sum would grow but it stayed 180°, that is exactly the intuition this task is designed to surface and correct.

Stretching or squashing changes side lengths and individual angles, and simply enlarging the same shape keeps every angle the same. Either way the three angles total 180° (paper measurements may be off by a degree or two).
Making a triangle bigger does NOT make its angles bigger — an enlarged copy of a triangle has exactly the same angles. Work from the given angles, not from how big the triangle looks.
activities.rationale: Both children and educated adults intuitively expect a triangle's angles to scale with its size; confronting this prediction directly, then showing the sum hold constant under reshaping, targets a documented and persistent misconception. An optional live vertex-drag with a sum readout calculated from the current angles (an idealised model) makes the invariance experienceable; its advantage over simply asserting the rule is proposed, not demonstrated.
sourceClaims: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
learnerActions: Predict, before testing: 'If I make this triangle much bigger or stretch it long and thin, will the angle sum get bigger?' Write down your prediction.
Make the triangle larger, then longer and thinner, then squat and wide — on a screen model drag a vertex to reshape it; on paper draw each new triangle.

Each time, re-check the angle sum: read the live sum readout on the screen model, or (on paper) tear or fold the corners of each new triangle, or measure its three marked angles, and record the total.
Compare your prediction with what actually happened to the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum stays 180° no matter how big, small, long or stretched the triangle is — side length does not change the angle sum, even though many people expect bigger triangles to have bigger angles.

activities.title: Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles
feedback: Check: your number of triangles should always be two fewer than the number of sides.
If the quadrilateral gives 360° as two triangles of 180°, you have connected it to the triangle rather than memorised a separate fact.
If you can state WHY a quadrilateral is 360° ('it is two triangles'), you understand the partition, not just the number.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into triangles turns a set of separate memorised sums into one connected system and directly addresses the misconception of knowing '180°' only as an isolated fact that cannot be extended. A tap-to-partition screen mode can make the triangle count visible.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Draw a diagonal inside a quadrilateral to split it into two triangles (in a dented, non-convex quadrilateral, use the diagonal that stays inside); conclude its angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
Partition a convex pentagon (3 triangles) and a convex hexagon (4 triangles) from one vertex, counting the triangles each time.
Record results in an angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°.
State the pattern in words and as a rule: an n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles, so its angle sum is (n−2) × 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: Every simple polygon's (one with no crossing sides) angle sum is built from triangles: an n-sided polygon divides into (n−2) triangles, so its interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180° — the whole family connects back to the triangle.

activities.title: Missing-angle practice, including 'not drawn to scale'
feedback: If you subtracted from 360° for a triangle and got 230°, that exceeds 180° — a sign the wrong total was used; a triangle is 180°.
If a figure looks isosceles but the marked angles differ, trust the numbers: 'not drawn to scale' means both appearance AND measuring the drawing are unreliable — only the marked angles are correct.
Writing the subtraction and checking it is reasonable guards against both the wrong-total error and arithmetic slips.
activities.rationale: Scorable number-entry and multiple-choice practice efficiently rehearses the procedure and catches two documented errors — subtracting from 360° and assuming isosceles from appearance. On a not-to-scale figure, measuring the drawing returns the misleading drawn angles, so only the marked values work. Diagnostic data also notes that the most common wrong answer can be an arithmetic slip by students who DO know the rule, so writing and checking the calculation matters. This practice can check and rehearse the procedure but cannot itself stage the size-invariance discovery, which the manipulable tasks above provide.
sourceClaims: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
learnerActions: Find a triangle's third angle given two angles by subtracting from 180° (e.g. 180 − (70 + 60) = 50°); write the calculation.
Find a quadrilateral's missing angle by subtracting the three known angles from 360°.
Answer an item deliberately drawn roughly isosceles though it is NOT to scale: compute only from the marked angles, not from how the figure looks and not by measuring the drawing with a protractor.
Sanity-check each answer (each triangle angle must be more than 0° and less than 180°; the three sum to exactly 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: Missing angles are found by subtracting known angles from the correct total (180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral), using the MARKED values rather than the picture's appearance or a protractor reading of a not-to-scale drawing.

activities.title: Regular polygons: find the sum, THEN share it out
feedback: If you stopped at 720°, that is the TOTAL of all six angles, not one angle — you still need to divide by 6.
Labelling 'total sum' versus 'one angle' keeps the two steps from collapsing together.
Check scale: one interior angle of a hexagon (120°) should be far smaller than the full 720° total.
activities.rationale: A documented error is reporting the total polygon sum as if it were a single interior angle; explicitly separating the sum step from the divide-equally step addresses this without needing to reteach the sum. An optional regular-polygon panel showing sum ÷ vertices makes the share-equally step concrete.
learnerActions: For a regular hexagon, first find the total interior-angle sum (4 triangles × 180° = 720°).
Then, because all six interior angles of a regular hexagon are equal, divide: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for one interior angle.
Write the two steps separately and label which number is the TOTAL sum and which is ONE angle.
Repeat for another regular polygon (e.g. regular pentagon: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°).
activities.intendedInsight: For a regular polygon there are two distinct steps: find the total angle sum, then divide equally among the (equal) vertices to get one interior angle — the total sum is not itself a single angle.

constraints: '180° in a triangle' must be derived (e.g. torn corners on a straight line, or corners folded to the foot of the height on the longest side) and connected to the other polygon sums by partitioning into triangles — not taught as an isolated fact to memorise.
Scorable multiple-choice/number-entry practice rehearses and catches distractors but cannot by itself stage the size-invariance discovery; pair it with a manipulable or hands-on reshaping task.
Paper/card triangle cutouts have slight thickness and torn edges; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness plane figure. Label any screen model as an idealisation.

A static picture or table can seed the 180° fact and the angle-sum table but cannot let the learner reshape a triangle to experience the sum staying constant; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for manipulation.

'Not drawn to scale' problems require computing from marked angles only; do not infer equal angles from an isosceles-looking figure, and do not measure the drawing with a protractor to get the angles.
Separate genuine reasoning errors (wrong total, size-dependence, isosceles assumption) from mere arithmetic slips when interpreting a wrong answer.
Interior-angle sums here concern plane polygons; a 3D setting is not required and could be confused with solid angles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a 3D or conversation artefact as adding 'no conceptual gain' or being unable to teach the discovery; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements in constraints rather than universal laws.
sourceClaims are limited to claims that directly support each principle; the regular-polygon two-step activity has no directly supporting source claim and is marked [].
Arithmetic self-checked: 180−(70+60)=50; wrong-total 360−130=230; quadrilateral 2×180=360; pentagon 3×180=540, 540÷5=108; hexagon 4×180=720, 720÷6=120 — all consistent with the source row.

Edits in this independent review: clarified the size-invariance check method in activity 2 (read the screen sum readout, or tear/fold/measure each fresh paper triangle) because re-tearing the corners of an already-drawn or on-screen triangle is not coherent; retained the earlier restorations of the fold-to-a-point derivation (activity 1) and the 'measuring a not-to-scale drawing misleads' point (activity 4).

probeDeeper: 'You said the missing angle is 50°. If I stretched this triangle to twice as wide but kept these two angles the same, what would the third angle be now?' — counterexample targeting size-dependence (it stays 50°).
'How could you use triangles to work out the angle sum of this hexagon?' — probes whether the polygon sum is derived by partition or just recalled.
'This quadrilateral — why 360° and the triangle only 180°? What's the connection?' — listens for 'a quadrilateral is two triangles'.
'The drawing makes these two angles look equal. Are they? How can you be sure without measuring?' — tests reliance on marked values over appearance.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) third angle = 180 − (70+60) = 50°, using the triangle sum 180°; (2) missing = 360 − (sum of the three), using the quadrilateral sum 360°; (3) one interior angle = 720° ÷ 6 = 120°, having found the hexagon's angle sum (4 triangles × 180°). Computes from the marked/derived sums, not from appearance, and divides the sum for the regular polygon.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the two known angles from 360 instead of 180.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive 180° by tearing the corners onto a straight line; contrast triangle (180°) with quadrilateral (360°) and show the quadrilateral is TWO triangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the triangle's third angle as 360 − (70+60) = 230°, or explains 'a triangle is 360°'; often the rest of the working is correct.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the triangle's size — expects a bigger or longer-sided triangle to have a larger third angle / larger sum.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same angles on triangles of very different sizes, and reshape one triangle while the 180° sum holds; make explicit that side length does not change the angle sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges the missing angle by how big or stretched the triangle looks rather than computing 180 − known; says a wider triangle 'must have a bigger angle there'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the triangle is isosceles/equilateral from its appearance — takes two angles as equal because the not-to-scale drawing looks that way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce 'not drawn to scale': compute only from marked angles; show a case where the equal-looking angles are provably unequal from the numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Splits the remaining angle equally, or asserts two angles are equal, with no marking to justify it; relies on how the figure looks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the polygon's total angle sum as a single interior angle — for the regular hexagon gives 720° (the sum) instead of dividing by 6.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-step structure: total sum, THEN ÷ number of equal vertices; no reteaching of the sum needed — the final division was dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Finds 720° correctly but stops there, or writes 720° as 'the angle'; the sum step is right, the share-equally step is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find missing angles reliably: uses the wrong total, judges by appearance or size, or cannot get beyond the triangle; no method for the quadrilateral or hexagon.
responseLevels.full: Computes missing angles in triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon; derives the polygon sums by partitioning into triangles and divides for a regular polygon; recognises the sum is independent of size; and uses marked values rather than appearance — the 180° rule is a connected tool, not an isolated fact.
responseLevels.partial: Finds a triangle's missing angle using 180° in the standard case, but treats the sums as separate memorised facts — defeated by the regular hexagon (can't partition or forgets to divide), misled by the not-to-scale/isosceles-looking triangle, or shows size-dependence when the shape is stretched. Lists the sums without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures with angles marked (not to scale). (1) A triangle with two angles 70° and 60°, third unknown — draw it looking roughly isosceles though it isn't. (2) A quadrilateral with three angles marked, one unknown. (3) A regular hexagon, asking for one interior angle. Say: 'Work out each missing angle, and tell me how you got it.' Watch the method — which total they use, whether they partition, whether they trust the picture — without prompting the rules.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spanning triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon separates a child who holds a connected system (all sums built from triangles) from one who has a single memorised fact and no way to reach the hexagon. The not-to-scale, isosceles-looking triangle catches trust-the-picture reasoning. Asking 'how did you get it' exposes the 360°-for-a-triangle error and the size-dependence intuition, and separates a genuine reasoning error from a mere arithmetic slip.

sources.claim: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
sources.source: Oak National Academy, 'Angles in triangles' (KS2/Year 5)

sources.claim: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
sources.source: Craig Barton / Eedi, 'Angles in a Triangle: Guess the Misconception'

sources.claim: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
sources.source: Hart, Dillon, Marantan, Cardenas, Spelke & Mahadevan (2018), 'The statistical shape of geometric reasoning', Scientific Reports 8:12906

dependencies.reason: Finding unknown angles in polygons requires reading diagrams where known angles are marked with arcs and tick marks
Finding angles in polygons requires knowing shape properties
Finding unknown angles builds on Y5 angle sum facts (180°, 360°)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding angles (age 10+)
topic.description: Recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite; find missing angles using these properties
evidence: Find a missing angle at a point given the other angles (total 360°)
Use the straight-line property (angles sum to 180°) to find an unknown angle
Identify vertically opposite angles and use the property that they are equal to find unknowns
topic.assessmentPrompt: If two straight lines cross each other, can {{name}} tell you which pairs of angles are equal (vertically opposite) — and find a missing angle if you give them one of the others?

pedagogy.summary: This Y6 topic consolidates three configurations of angle facts at their sharpest: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and — the new element — vertically opposite angles (EQUAL). The pedagogical crux is getting children to hold TWO relationships apart on the same intersecting-lines diagram: the OPPOSITE pair is equal, while each ADJACENT pair (on a straight line) is supplementary (sums to 180°). Confusing which pair does which is the characteristic error. The NCETM's recommended route is a dynamic one — two hinged sticks crossing at a point — so children SEE that as one angle grows its vertically opposite partner grows with it and stays equal, while the neighbour shrinks to keep the straight line at 180°. The signature task is 'given one angle, what else do you know?', reasoning out and JUSTIFYING every other angle from the two rules.
bestPractices: Surface both relationships side by side on one crossing-lines diagram: 'opposite = equal' AND 'adjacent (on a straight line) = supplementary', so children see they are different claims, not the same one (NCETM).

Use a hinged two-sticks / dynamic-geometry model: as one angle opens, its vertically opposite partner opens equally and the adjacent angle closes — the equality is seen to be invariant, not memorised.
Teach with 'given one angle, find and justify the others': mark one angle (e.g. 43°) at an intersection and have the child deduce and NAME the rule for each remaining angle.
Insist on reasoned language — 'this angle is 130° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' / '…because angles on a straight line sum to 180°' — not shape mnemonics.
Vary orientation: present tilted intersections (neither line horizontal) so 'vertically opposite' is understood as sharing the vertex, not as up-and-down.
Derive vertically-opposite-equal from the straight-line rule (both angles are 180° minus the shared neighbour) rather than adding it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Two straight lines crossing at a point, forming two pairs of equal opposite angles and two straight lines of supplementary angles
Hinged two-sticks / dynamic model where opposite angles stay equal as the crossing angle changes
'Given one angle, find the rest' diagram (e.g. 43° marked, three unknowns)
Angles-at-a-point (360°) and angles-on-a-line (180°) diagrams as the two 'wholes'
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line 180° rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180° minus the known angle instead of equal to it.
Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' to conclude all four angles at the intersection are equal, ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
Attaches 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation, so fails to recognise the opposite pair when the lines are tilted, or mislabels which angles are opposite.
Carries over the wrong whole — uses 180° for angles at a point (or 360° on a straight line).

learn.summary: Year 6 geometry consolidating three angle configurations: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and the new element — vertically opposite angles (equal). The pedagogical crux is holding TWO relationships apart on one intersecting-lines diagram: the opposite pair is EQUAL, while each adjacent pair (on a straight line) is SUPPLEMENTARY (sums to 180°). The signature task is 'given one angle, find and justify every other angle', naming the rule used each time. Deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule (both angles equal 180° minus the shared neighbour) is preferred to memorising it as a separate fact. Orientation should be varied — tilted intersections — so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not as up-and-down.

activities.title: Crossing-lines reasoner: watch the opposite pair stay equal
feedback: If a learner expected the angle opposite 130° to be '180 − 130 = 50°', highlight that this value belongs to the ADJACENT angle (on the straight line); the OPPOSITE angle tracks at 130°. Show both on the diagram at once.
If a learner thinks all four angles are equal, draw attention to one straight line and its two angles summing to 180°: a = a and b = b, but a ≠ b unless the lines are perpendicular.

If a learner loses the opposite pair once the figure is tilted, clarify that 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (vertex, not up-and-down), with no arm in common, and rotate the same intersection through several orientations while tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: NCETM recommends a hinged two-sticks / dynamic model so children SEE that as one angle increases its vertically opposite partner increases equally while the neighbour closes to hold the straight line at 180°; manipulating the crossing angle makes the invariance observable rather than asserted. OPTIONAL interactive features that make this concrete: draggable crossing lines, all four angles labelled with live-updating values, the opposite pair highlighted as it stays equal, and each straight line showing its two angles summing to 180°.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Work with two straight lines crossing at a point, with all four angles labelled.

Rotate one line and observe how all four angle values change together: each pair of vertically opposite angles grows and shrinks TOGETHER and stays equal, while each adjacent angle changes so that the two angles on each straight line always sum to 180°.
Set the crossing angle to several values and each time read off the opposite pair, confirming it matches the given angle exactly (not 180° minus it).

Deliberately predict what the angle opposite a 130° angle will be; set the crossing angle to 130° and check the opposite angle reads exactly 130° rather than 50°, then rotate and check the opposite angle keeps matching the changing angle.

Repeat with the whole figure tilted so neither line is horizontal or vertical, confirming the opposite pair is still identified as the two angles opposite each other across the vertex, sharing no arm.
activities.intendedInsight: As an intersection turns, vertically opposite angles stay equal while each adjacent pair stays supplementary — these are two different claims about the same diagram, and 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not pointing up-and-down.

activities.title: Given one angle, find and justify the rest
feedback: If a learner gives the angle opposite 130° as 50° or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line', the rules have been swapped: the opposite pair is equal; only the adjacent pair is supplementary.
If a learner subtracts from 180° at a point, re-anchor the whole: a full turn around a point is 360°. Check: 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, not 180 − (150 + 90).
If values are given without justification, ask 'which rule tells you that?' before accepting the answer — a correct number reasoned from the rule is the goal, not a lucky guess.
activities.rationale: NCETM's signature task 'given one angle, find and justify the others' forces deployment of BOTH relationships and makes any confusion immediately visible. Requiring the named rule for each angle distinguishes reasoning from guessing. Common Core notes angle measure is additive: unknown angles at a point and on a straight line are found by adding/subtracting known angles. Tilting the figure prevents up-and-down intuition standing in for reasoning.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
Angle measure is additive; unknown angles at a point (360°) and on a straight line (180°) are found by adding/subtracting the known angles (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: On a tilted intersection with one angle marked (e.g. 43°), work out each of the other three angles.

For EACH angle, state both the value AND the rule that justifies it — e.g. 'this angle is 43° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' or 'this angle is 137° BECAUSE angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Repeat with a different given angle (e.g. 130°, giving an opposite angle of 130° and adjacent angles of 50° each).
Switch to an angles-at-a-point diagram: given two angles (e.g. 150° and 90°) find the unknown as 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, naming the 360° whole.
Write down every equation you can for an intersection diagram, surfacing both the equal pairs and the two 180° straight lines.
activities.intendedInsight: Every unknown angle at an intersection or point can be deduced and JUSTIFIED from a named rule, and the correct 'whole' must be chosen — 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs: equal or supplementary
feedback: A choice of '180 − known' for a vertically opposite angle reveals the straight-line rule wrongly applied to the opposite pair; mark it and show the opposite pair is equal.
If the derivation is unclear, walk through it: angle A and its opposite each sit with the same neighbour B on a straight line, so A = 180 − B and the opposite = 180 − B, hence they are equal.
Errors on tilted items signal orientation-dependence; return to rotating a single intersection and tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: Classification and fill-in practice with a deliberate '180 − known' distractor targets the characteristic error directly and checks the two relationships are held apart. This supports and assesses the reasoning but, on its own, presents fixed diagrams the learner cannot manipulate, so pair it with a dynamic model to let the equality be observed changing. Deriving the equality rather than memorising it is an NCETM best practice.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Look at a crossing-lines diagram with the four angles labelled and sort each pair of angles into 'vertically opposite — equal' or 'adjacent (straight line) — supplementary'.
Answer which rule applies to a specifically named pair, choosing between 'equal' and 'sums to 180°'.
Fill in the value of each unknown angle, resisting the tempting '180 − known' value when the angle is actually the opposite (equal) one.
Try a tilted-intersection item where orientation cannot be used to guess, and a point-diagram item that uses the 360° whole.
Explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal: both equal 180° minus their shared straight-line neighbour, so they equal each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying each pair by its relationship — and deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule — cements that the two claims are distinct and reasoned, not interchangeable.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal angle relationships (vocabulary scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct naming; where a learner swaps the rules, re-show the straight-line pair and the opposite pair side by side.
Encourage stating the rule before revealing, so the reveal confirms reasoning rather than supplying it.
activities.rationale: A static reveal can introduce the vocabulary and the paired structure and can be used during teaching, but it shows fixed values and cannot let the learner watch the opposite pair stay equal as the angle changes, so the invariance is told rather than observed. Use it to seed language, then move to a manipulable model and to reasoning tasks.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, tap an angle to reveal its vertically opposite partner (equal) and its two straight-line (adjacent) partners (each supplementary to it).
Use a 'given 130°, what are the other three?' reveal: predict each value and its rule, then lift the flap to check (opposite 130°, adjacent 50° each).
Name each revealed pair aloud with its rule before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeds the vocabulary — 'vertically opposite' vs 'adjacent/straight-line' — and the paired structure of an intersection.

constraints: Learners must JUSTIFY each angle with its named rule, not just state values; a correct number without reasoning does not demonstrate understanding.
Both relationships must appear on the SAME intersecting-lines diagram so children see they are different claims: opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary.
Vary orientation with tilted intersections so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not up-and-down.
Keep the two 'wholes' distinct: 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.
Prefer deriving 'vertically opposite angles are equal' from the straight-line rule over memorising it as a separate fact.
The static tap-to-reveal image is a vocabulary scaffold only: it shows fixed values and cannot display the equality holding as the angle changes.

Fill-in and sorting practice can score reasoning and target the characteristic error, but on their own present non-manipulable diagrams; pair them with a dynamic model so the invariance can be observed.

Vertically opposite angles are always equal; an adjacent angle equals the given one only in the special perpendicular (90°) case, where all four angles become 90° — do not let learners generalise all four angles to be equal otherwise.
OPTIONAL interactive features (draggable lines, live angle readouts, highlighting, tilt) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a 3D environment 'adds no conceptual value' and that a character/dialogue 'cannot' teach the distinction. These are categorical catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than propagated; a conversation could still support reasoning talk, and a 2D dynamic model is proposed on its stated affordance (manipulable, live-updating) without claiming other media are incapable.

The legacy recommendation's strong framing ('it must be manipulated to be felt', opposite pair 'locked equal') was softened: manipulation makes the invariance observable but is one effective route, not the only possible one.

Self-audit arithmetic checks all passed: angle opposite 130° = 130°; adjacent = 180 − 130 = 50°; at a point 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°; opposite 43° = 43°, adjacent = 137°. The error value '50°' for the opposite angle is retained only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a correct answer.

Confirmed the special-case caveat: the two adjacent angles equal the given one only when the lines are perpendicular (all four become 90°); the diagnostic counterexample about 90° crossings was preserved in substance within constraints and feedback.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims because it is a general topic/necessity requirement and does not support that activity's specific dynamic-model teaching principle; it remains part of the source record but is not cited as supporting a teaching principle in any activity.

Activity 4's NCETM sourceClaim is retained because the activity's learning target is distinguishing the equal pair from the supplementary pair, which the claim directly supports; the static-medium limitation is stated as an affordance observation, not as a source-backed efficacy claim.

probeDeeper: 'You said this angle is 130° — which rule tells you that, and which rule tells you the one next to it?' — checks the two relationships are held apart, not blurred.

Counterexample: 'If I told you these lines crossed at exactly 90°, would the opposite angle still equal the given one? Would the neighbours?' — probes that equal-opposite always holds while supplementary-opposite is only the perpendicular special case.
'I've turned the whole diagram on its side. Which angles are vertically opposite now?' — tests that opposite-ness survives rotation (not orientation-bound).
'Write down every equation you can for this diagram' — surfaces whether the child sees both the equal pairs and the 180° straight lines (NCETM 'what else do you know?').
assess.correctAnswer: At the intersection: the angle vertically opposite the 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles are equal); the two adjacent angles are each 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, 180−130). At the point: unknown = 360 − (150+90) = 120°. Justifies each with the correct named rule and is not misled by the tilt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180 − 130 = 50° instead of 130°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both relationships on the same diagram with the hinged model: show the opposite pair staying EQUAL as it turns while each straight line holds at 180°; name which pair is which explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the angle opposite 130° as 50°, or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line' when the two angles are actually the opposite pair; may get the genuinely adjacent angle right, showing the rules are swapped.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' — declares all four angles at the intersection equal (all 130°), ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw attention to each straight line and its two angles summing to 180°; show that a=a and b=b but a≠b unless the lines are perpendicular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels every angle 130°; no angle is given as 50°; cannot say why the neighbours differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ties 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation — on the tilted diagram fails to identify the opposite pair, or insists the term needs a vertical line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'vertical' means sharing the vertex, not up–down; rotate the same intersection through several orientations so the opposite pair is tracked as the figure turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot pick out the vertically opposite pair once the figure is tilted, or points to an adjacent pair as 'opposite'; comments about the lines not being upright.

errorPatterns.pattern: Carries over the wrong whole at a point — subtracts the known angles from 180° instead of 360°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the whole to the configuration — a full point is a whole turn 360° — before computing; no reteaching of vertically-opposite needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the point diagram gives 180 − (150+90) or an answer 180° short of 120°; the intersection work may be correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the other angles reliably: guesses, uses no named rule, or cannot identify the opposite pair; wrong whole at a point.
responseLevels.full: Finds all angles at an intersection using BOTH relationships correctly, justifies each with the named rule, is unfazed by tilt, keeps the point (360°) and line (180°) wholes distinct, and can explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal (via the shared straight-line neighbour).
responseLevels.partial: Finds the vertically opposite angle equal in a simple upright cross and can state 'they add to 180°' for a straight line, but blurs the two on a tilted diagram (opposite comes out as 180−given, or all four equal), or gives values without justifying them — lists angles without relating the equal and supplementary structures.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Draw two straight lines crossing at a point, TILTED so neither line is horizontal or vertical, and mark just one of the four angles as 130°. Say: 'Find the other three angles, and tell me how you know each one.' Then show a second diagram — angles round a point marked 150°, 90° and an unknown — and ask for the unknown. Watch which rule they use for each angle and whether tilt throws them; do not prompt.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: One given angle forces the child to deploy BOTH relationships — equal for the opposite, supplementary for the adjacent — so confusing them is immediately visible (the opposite comes out as 50°, or all four as 130°). The deliberate tilt separates a child who understands 'vertically opposite = shares the vertex' from one who relies on up–down orientation. The second diagram checks the point (360°) rule is not swapped with 180°. Requiring the justification distinguishes a correct answer reasoned from the rule from a lucky guess.

sources.claim: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
topic.description: Derive and use the angle sum in a triangle (180°), use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon ((n−2) × 180°), and calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
evidence: Calculate a missing angle in a triangle by subtracting the known angles from 180°
Find the sum of interior angles in a hexagon by dividing it into triangles
Calculate each interior and exterior angle of a regular polygon given the number of sides
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°, can they work out the third? And can they figure out the angles inside a regular pentagon?

pedagogy.summary: This topic builds from the triangle angle sum (180°) to the general interior-angle sum of any polygon, (n−2)×180°, DERIVED by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles, and to the interior/exterior angle relationship (they sum to 180° at each vertex; all exterior angles sum to 360° for any polygon). Best taught by deriving the formulas from structure — partitioning into triangles, walking the perimeter to feel the 360° of turning — rather than memorising them, and by carefully separating the two 'totals' pupils confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. For regular polygons each angle is the sum divided by n, but this division applies ONLY when the polygon is regular.
bestPractices: Derive (n−2)×180° by splitting the polygon into triangles from one vertex (a hexagon → 4 triangles → 720°); don't present the formula as a rule to memorise
Distinguish demonstration from proof: tearing off a triangle's corners to form a straight line DEMONSTRATES 180° but is not a proof — pupils should also meet the deductive argument
Keep the two exterior-angle totals apart: interior + exterior = 180° at a single vertex; the sum of ALL exterior angles is 360° for any polygon, however many sides

Attach the word 'regular' to every ÷n formula: each interior angle = sum ÷ n and each exterior = 360 ÷ n hold ONLY for regular polygons; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting known angles from the sum
Use the 'walking the perimeter' turning model to make the 360° total of exterior angles concrete
Stress that the angle sum depends on the NUMBER OF SIDES, not on the size of the polygon
keyRepresentations: Polygon partitioned into triangles from one vertex (n sides → n−2 triangles)
Torn-off triangle corners arranged on a straight line (demonstration of 180°)
A marker 'walking the perimeter', turning through 360° in total (exterior angles)
Interior and exterior angle pair at a vertex sitting on a straight line (sum 180°)
A regular polygon with equal angles beside an irregular one with the same sum but unequal angles
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a triangle's angles sum to 360°
Confusing interior and exterior angles
Dividing 360° (or the interior sum) by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assuming all its angles are equal
Believing a bigger polygon has a bigger angle sum (angle scales with size)
Reporting the interior-angle SUM as though it were one interior angle (forgetting to divide by n)

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 11–14) derive the interior-angle sum of a polygon by splitting it into n−2 triangles from one vertex ((n−2)×180°), feel the exterior-angle total of 360° by walking the perimeter, and carefully separate the two 'totals' they confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. Dividing by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. This is true of every regular polygon (the KS3 focus), and also of equal-angled shapes such as a non-square rectangle. The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not the polygon's size. The strongest route is proposed to be a construction the child performs (triangulate, walk the perimeter, toggle regular/irregular); fixed diagrams and scored questions are useful support with stated limits.

activities.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum
feedback: If a learner says the sum should be bigger for a physically larger polygon, enlarge the same shape with its angles unchanged and ask whether any angle changed — the sum depends only on the number of sides.

If a learner counts n triangles instead of n−2, ask them to look at the two sides meeting at the chosen vertex and check whether every side became the base of its own triangle; the two sides at the chosen vertex do not, which is why the count is n−2.
An optional running tally showing '(n−2)×180' as diagonals are drawn makes the link between triangle count and total concrete; this is a support, not a requirement.
activities.rationale: Deriving the formula from triangulation rather than memorising it targets the topic's core structure and the documented size-independence misconception. Learner-performed partitioning with immediate confirmation is proposed as the strongest route; fixed diagrams can show one split but cannot let the child vary n.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Children (and educated adults) tend to judge a triangle's missing angle as scaling with the triangle's size, contradicting the size-independent angle sum — they reason by mental simulation rather than by the rule
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Start with a polygon whose number of sides you can change. Before calculating, predict: what do all its interior angles add to?
Split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one corner. Count the triangles: a pentagon gives 3, a hexagon gives 4.
Record the running total as (number of triangles)×180°: pentagon 3×180 = 540°, hexagon 4×180 = 720°.
State the general pattern in your own words: splitting from one corner, a convex n-sided polygon always makes n−2 triangles, so the interior sum is (n−2)×180°.
Add two more sides and confirm the sum GROWS with the number of sides — not with the polygon's size.
activities.intendedInsight: The interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° is a consequence of how many triangles the polygon decomposes into, and it depends on the number of sides, not the size.

activities.title: Walk the perimeter: exterior angles total 360°
feedback: If a learner says more sides should give a bigger exterior total, have them walk two different polygons and compare: both complete exactly one full turn (360°).
If a learner reports 360° at a single vertex, point to the straight line at that corner: the interior and its exterior together make 180° there.
An optional mode that accumulates each turn as the marker strides round makes 'one full turn = 360°' concrete; keep it as an illustration, not the only way to reach the result.
activities.rationale: The perimeter-walk turning model makes the 360° exterior total tangible and directly separates the two totals pupils confuse. The exterior sum of 360° regardless of sides is supported by sources (convex KS3 case); the single-vertex 180° pairing is a distinct relationship.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Imagine (or move a marker) walking around the outside of the polygon, turning at each corner to follow the next side.
Add up all the turns you make to get back to your starting direction.
Repeat for convex polygons with different numbers of sides and confirm the turns always total exactly 360°, however many sides there are.
At a single chosen corner, mark the interior angle and the exterior angle sitting together on a straight line, and check they sum to 180°.
Say aloud the difference between the two totals: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
activities.intendedInsight: Walking the perimeter of a convex polygon means turning through one full 360° in total, so the exterior angles sum to 360°, regardless of the number of sides — a separate fact from the 180° interior/exterior pair at a single vertex.

activities.title: Regular or irregular: when may you divide by n?
feedback: If a learner divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, point to two visibly different angles in the figure and ask whether they could both equal the quotient; contrast directly with the regular hexagon of the same 720° sum where every angle really is 120°.

If a learner reports 540° as a single interior angle of the pentagon, ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?' and prompt the final ÷5 — the method is sound, only the last step was dropped.
An optional regular/irregular toggle where the '÷n' button is available only in regular mode makes the boundary visible; the greying-out illustrates the condition, it does not prove it.
activities.rationale: The equal-angles condition, which every regular polygon meets, is the distinction the topic hinges on. Holding the sum fixed (same-sided regular vs irregular hexagon) and keeping the subtract-from-sum method alongside the ÷n method prevents over-generalising ÷n and separately addresses the forget-to-divide lapse.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Take a regular pentagon: find the interior sum by triangulation (3×180 = 540°), then find EACH interior angle by dividing by n (540÷5 = 108°).
Find each exterior angle two ways and check they agree: 180 − 108 = 72° and 360÷5 = 72°.

Compare two hexagons that have the SAME interior sum of 720°: a regular hexagon, where ÷6 gives each angle = 720÷6 = 120°, and an irregular hexagon, where the angles are visibly unequal so no single quotient describes them all.

For the irregular hexagon, divide 720 by 6 to get 120°, then compare with the figure: its angles are not all equal, so 120° cannot be each angle — ÷n does not give each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal (even if one angle happened to equal the quotient).
Instead, find ONE missing angle of the irregular hexagon by subtracting the five known angles from 720°.

Write the rule: you may divide the sum by n to get each angle ONLY when every angle is equal, as in every regular polygon (a rectangle shows that equal angles are enough, even if the sides differ); the sum itself is the same for any hexagon.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing the interior sum by n (or using 360÷n for exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal, as in a regular polygon. Two polygons with the same number of sides share the same interior sum, but for one with unequal angles a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles rather than by dividing.

activities.title: Triangle angle sum: 180°, not 360°
feedback: If a learner gives 360 − 70 − 60 = 230°, they are treating the triangle's angles as going 'all the way round' to 360° — re-derive 180° from the torn corners on a straight edge and contrast with a full turn.

Note for the teacher: tearing corners DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum but is not a proof; pupils should also meet the deductive argument (e.g. draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles).
activities.rationale: The 'triangle sums to 360°' error is documented, and this activity both corrects it and distinguishes demonstration from proof as the pedagogy requires. The torn-corner task is concrete physical evidence; its status as demonstration (not proof) is stated.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception on a triangle missing-angle item is that the angles sum to 360° (subtracting the known angles from 360)

The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof
learnerActions: Find the third angle of a triangle whose other two angles are 70° and 60° by subtracting from 180°: 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them against a straight edge; observe they fit along a straight line (180°).
Contrast this straight-line 180° with a full turn of 360° so the two 'wholes' are kept apart.
Explain why you subtracted from 180° and not 360°.
activities.intendedInsight: A triangle's interior angles sum to 180° (a straight line), which is a different whole from the 360° of a full turn; a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles from 180°.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with mixed questions
feedback: If a learner picks the option that divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, revisit the regular/irregular distinction: ÷n needs equal angles.
If a learner selects an exterior angle when asked for an interior one, return to the straight-line pair at a vertex (they sum to 180°).

Scored questions confirm whether the facts and distinctions are secure, but on their own they do not show the learner deriving the sum by triangulation or reasoning openly about interior/exterior — pair them with the construction activities.
activities.rationale: Structured questions check fluency and surface the exact distractors (irregular ÷n, interior/exterior swap) the topic targets. They are proposed as a complement to, not a replacement for, the derivation work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Give the interior-angle sum of a named polygon (e.g. octagon → (8−2)×180 = 1080°).
For a regular polygon, give BOTH an interior angle and its matching exterior angle, and state how they relate (sum to 180° at a vertex).
Answer a question that contrasts interior versus exterior angles, and identify why a tempting wrong option (dividing the sum by n for an irregular polygon whose angles are unequal) is invalid.
Order several polygons by their interior-angle sum and explain what the ordering depends on (number of sides).
activities.intendedInsight: Named-polygon sums, interior/exterior relationships and the regular-only condition can be recalled and applied fluently and distinguished from common distractors.

constraints: Division by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. Every regular polygon has equal angles, and regular polygons are the KS3 focus, but some irregular shapes do too: a non-square rectangle has four 90° angles (360÷4). For polygons with unequal angles, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum. Never present ÷n as giving each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal.

Two polygons with the same number of sides have the same interior-angle sum. Whether all the angles are equal (as in any regular polygon) affects only whether each angle equals sum÷n, not the sum itself.
Keep the two totals distinct: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
Tearing off triangle corners onto a straight line DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum; it is not a proof. Pupils should also meet the deductive argument.
The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not on the polygon's size; an enlarged copy of the same shape has the same angles.

When a convex polygon is split from one vertex, an n-sided polygon yields n−2 triangles (not n); diagonals are drawn only from the single chosen vertex, and the two sides meeting at that vertex do not each form a separate triangle base.
The perimeter-walk 'one full turn = 360°' model applies to convex (non-reflex) polygons, the intended KS3 case; the interior-sum (n−2)×180° and subtract-from-sum methods hold for any simple polygon.

Fixed diagrams (tap-to-reveal) can show one triangle split and label interior/exterior at a vertex but cannot let the child vary n or test the regular/irregular boundary; treat them as support, not as inferior in every respect.
Scored/recognition questions assess facts and distinctions but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own triangulation or open interior/exterior reasoning; pair them with construction work.
Polygon angle sums are planar; polyhedron angle defect is a different, later topic and is not needed here.

Optional interactive features (running sum as diagonals are drawn, perimeter-walk accumulator, regular/irregular toggle with ÷n button enabled only in regular mode) are illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tools and not evidence that the rules hold.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the KS3 national curriculum citation as verified:false; its claim is used only to describe curriculum expectations, not to assert efficacy.

Self-audit (arithmetic/geometry) checks passed and were retained: triangle 180−70−60=50°; pentagon 3×180=540°, 540÷5=108°, exterior 180−108=72°=360÷5; hexagon 4×180=720°, regular hexagon 720÷6=120°; octagon (8−2)×180=1080°; exterior-sum identity 180n−(n−2)×180=360.

Corrected an overstated claim in the regular/irregular activity: dividing an irregular hexagon's 720° by 6 need not differ from EVERY angle (one angle could coincidentally be 120°); the valid point is that a single quotient cannot describe unequal angles, so ÷n does not apply.

The perimeter-walk one-full-turn model assumes convex polygons; learner examples here are convex, which is the standard KS3 case. The (n−2)×180° interior-sum derivation and the subtract-from-sum method remain valid for any simple polygon.

Original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue 'neither performs the triangulation nor checks the arithmetic' as fit rationales; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established comparative claims, and have been softened to narrowly scoped limits in constraints rather than propagated as universal laws.
The Hart et al. (2018) source concerns triangle size-independence specifically; it is extended here to polygon size-independence, which the source does not directly establish for all polygons.

Retained the original key representation of a regular polygon beside an irregular one with the SAME sum but unequal angles (regular vs irregular hexagon at 720°); no mathematical error was found in that content.

probeDeeper: 'If I made this pentagon twice as big, would each angle change? Why or why not?' — a counterexample targeting size-dependence
'You split the hexagon into 4 triangles — why 4 and not 6?' — pushing the (n−2) structure into a reason
'This hexagon is irregular — can you still divide 720 by 6 to get each angle? Why not?' — a counterexample on the regular-only division
'At this corner, how are the interior and exterior angles related, and how do you know?' — pressing the 180°-at-a-vertex link
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°. (b) The hexagon splits into 4 triangles from one vertex, so the interior sum is 4×180 = 720°; a missing angle is 720 minus the other five. (c) Regular pentagon interior sum = 3×180 = 540°, so each interior angle = 540÷5 = 108°; each exterior angle = 180 − 108 = 72° (equivalently 360÷5 = 72°). The child derives the sum by triangulation and divides by n only because the pentagon is stated to be regular.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the known angles from 360 ('shapes go all the way round to 360')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive triangle = 180° from the straight line (tear the three corners onto a straight edge); contrast with the 360° of a full turn so the two wholes are kept apart
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a) gives 360−70−60 = 230°, or any answer built on a 360° whole for the triangle

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses interior and exterior angles — gives the exterior when asked for the interior (or vice versa), or treats them as unrelated rather than summing to 180° at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the interior and exterior angle at one vertex sitting on a straight line so they must sum to 180°; label both on the same diagram before calculating
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) reports 72° as 'the interior angle' or 108° as 'the exterior', or cannot connect the two at a vertex

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assumes all its angles are equal — applies 360÷n or sum÷n without checking regularity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress that ÷n gives each angle ONLY when the polygon is regular; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) divides 720 by 6 to 'find each angle' of the irregular hexagon, though its angles differ

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the polygon's SIZE — a bigger triangle/polygon has bigger angles ('the longer side makes a wider angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same-shape polygon enlarged with its angles unchanged; make explicit that the sum depends only on the number of sides, not the size
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges or adjusts an angle according to side length or overall size rather than using the fixed sum

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the interior-angle SUM as if it were a single interior angle — forgets to divide by n for the regular polygon
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?'; prompt the final ÷5 — the method is right, only the last step was dropped, so scaffold rather than reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) gives 540° as 'each interior angle' of the pentagon instead of 540÷5 = 108°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the angles reliably — sums a triangle to 360°, cannot derive a polygon's angle sum, or divides an irregular polygon's sum by n; interior and exterior are confused
responseLevels.full: Derives the interior-angle sum by splitting into n−2 triangles, calculates interior and exterior angles keeping the two distinct, divides by n only for regular polygons, and explains that the sum depends on the number of sides not the size — transferring the method to a polygon with a new number of sides
responseLevels.partial: Uses 180° for the triangle and can recall or apply (n−2)×180° for the sum, but cannot derive it by triangulation, forgets to divide by n (or divides when the polygon is irregular), or confuses interior with exterior — has the formulas as isolated rules, not a connected structure, and cannot transfer to a new polygon or justify why

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures and a pencil: (a) a triangle with two angles marked 70° and 60°; (b) an IRREGULAR hexagon; (c) a regular pentagon. Set them to: (a) find the third angle; (b) find the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon, showing how — invite them to split it up — then find one missing angle given the other five; (c) find EACH interior angle and EACH exterior angle of the regular pentagon. Watch whether they subtract from 180 (not 360) for the triangle, whether they split the hexagon into triangles to get (n−2)×180, whether they divide by n only because the pentagon is regular, and whether they keep interior and exterior angles distinct.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands subtracts the triangle's angles from 180 and derives the hexagon sum by triangulating; a child with the classic error subtracts from 360 (a visibly different answer) or divides the irregular hexagon's sum by 6. Asking for EACH angle of the regular pentagon and its exterior angle exposes interior/exterior confusion and the forget-to-÷n lapse; the irregular hexagon exposes those who apply ÷n indiscriminately.
