topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
topic.description: Derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles using appropriate language, including interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, and relationships between side lengths
evidence: List and verify properties of a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel/equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other)
Explain why a square is a special case of both a rectangle and a rhombus
Derive the relationship between the radius, diameter, and circumference of a circle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} why the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal in length, can they explain it using the properties of the shape — rather than just measuring to check?

pedagogy.summary: At age 11-13 pupils move from recognising shapes to DERIVING and justifying their properties — the interior angles, diagonals, symmetry and side relationships of triangles, quadrilaterals and circles — and to reasoning about how the shapes relate. The signature idea is hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it possesses all their defining properties and more. The dominant obstacle, robustly documented, is the prototype phenomenon and partition thinking: pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, so they deny that 'a square is a rectangle' (rectangles are 'long'/slanted parallelograms look a certain way), and even when they accept one direction they miss the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational and multiplicative — diameter = 2 × radius, circumference = π × diameter — with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, works from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic shapes so pupils see one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties.
bestPractices: Derive properties rather than assert them: have pupils construct, fold, measure and mark to establish (e.g.) that a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other, distinguishing this from a rectangle's equal diagonals
Teach hierarchical (inclusion) definitions explicitly and contrast them with partition definitions (de Villiers): a square counts as a rectangle because it meets every rectangle property
Use dynamic shapes to defeat prototype/partition thinking: drag a rectangle until all sides are equal and note that 'square' switches on while 'rectangle' never switches off
Target the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly (every square is a rhombus AND a parallelogram; not every rectangle is a square) with always/sometimes/never tasks
For circles, establish diameter = 2r and circumference = πd by measuring several circles, so π emerges as a constant ratio independent of size
keyRepresentations: Dynamic quadrilateral with live name-tags (parallelogram/rectangle/rhombus/square) that light up as properties are met
Quadrilateral hierarchy Venn diagram / family tree
Fold-and-measure derivations of diagonal and symmetry properties
Circle with labelled radius, diameter and circumference and a circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14 readout
Property tables comparing triangles/quadrilaterals for always/sometimes/never reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Partition/prototype classification: denying that a square is a rectangle (or a rhombus) because the shapes 'look different' or a rectangle 'must have two long and two short sides'
One-directional / non-transitive inclusion: accepting square ⊆ rhombus but not square ⊆ parallelogram, or thinking a rectangle cannot share square properties
Judging properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
Confusing radius and diameter, or believing π (circumference ÷ diameter) depends on the size of the circle
Treating each named shape as an isolated category with no overlapping membership

learn.summary: For learners aged 11-13, the goal is to move from recognising triangles, quadrilaterals and circles to DERIVING and justifying their properties (interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, side relationships) and reasoning about how shapes relate hierarchically. The signature idea is class-inclusion classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it has all their defining properties and more. The documented core obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, denying 'a square is a rectangle', and often miss the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational: diameter = 2 × radius and circumference = π × diameter, with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, builds from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic (or adjustable) shapes so a learner can watch one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties, with hands-on construction, measurement and comparison supporting the same ideas.

activities.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist
feedback: If a learner says the shape 'stopped being a rectangle' when it became a square, ask: which rectangle property did it lose? (It kept four right angles and opposite sides equal/parallel, so it is still a rectangle.)
If a learner insists the shapes 'look different', redirect to checking the square against EVERY rectangle property one by one rather than judging by overall appearance.
activities.rationale: Prototype/partition thinking is robustly documented: learners who know definitions still deny 'a square is a rectangle'. Watching one shape acquire a more general class's name-tags while keeping the general tag makes inclusion visible rather than asserted. The continuous morph requires a dynamic geometry tool (or an adjustable model such as a linkage/geoboard) with name-tags that light up as each shape's properties are met; a set of physical cutouts can support a compare-across-shapes version (holding a long rectangle beside a square and checking shared properties) but cannot show the live transformation, and a static family-tree/Venn reference can support the idea but cannot display the morph itself.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).

KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Start with a 'long' rectangle and list which names currently fit it: note that, of the names parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, only 'rectangle' and 'parallelogram' apply (it is also a quadrilateral).
Change the shape by moving its corners/sides until all four sides are equal, keeping the four right angles.
Observe that 'rhombus' and 'square' now apply too — while 'rectangle' never stopped applying.
Say in your own words why the square never stopped being a rectangle: it kept every rectangle property and simply gained the extra property of four equal sides.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special case of a rectangle (and of a rhombus): it satisfies every defining property of the more general class and adds more, so it belongs to both classes at once.

activities.title: Derive diagonal and symmetry properties by folding and measuring
feedback: If a learner claims a parallelogram's diagonals are equal, ask them to measure both diagonals of a clearly non-rectangular parallelogram — they differ. Equal diagonals belong to the rectangle, not the general parallelogram.
Praise justifications that cite a fold or measurement ('I measured both halves and they matched, so the diagonals bisect') over 'it looks like it'.
activities.rationale: A common error is attributing the wrong property to the wrong class by appearance (e.g. giving a parallelogram equal diagonals by confusing it with a rectangle). Construction and measurement give learners a reliable method to establish and distinguish properties. Paper/card cutouts are approximations with real thickness; treat them as stand-ins for the ideal zero-thickness plane figures.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Construct or cut out a parallelogram, a rectangle and a rhombus (paper/card approximations of the ideal flat figures).

Draw the diagonals; fold and measure to test: do the diagonals bisect each other? Are they equal in length? Do they meet at right angles? Also fold along each diagonal and along each line joining midpoints of opposite sides to test which are lines of symmetry.

Record for each shape which diagonal and symmetry properties hold, e.g. a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other but are NOT generally equal, whereas a rectangle's diagonals ARE equal and a rhombus's diagonals meet at right angles; a non-square rectangle's lines of symmetry join midpoints of opposite sides (its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry), a non-square rhombus's lines of symmetry are its diagonals, and a parallelogram that is neither has no line of symmetry.
State each property as something you checked by construction/measurement, not something you guessed from the picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties should be derived and verified, not read off appearance; different classes have genuinely different diagonal/symmetry properties, which is how you can tell them apart and justify inclusion.

activities.title: Measure several circles to let π emerge as a constant ratio
feedback: If a learner predicted the ratio would be larger for bigger circles, point to their own table: the ratios should be roughly the same for every circle, close to 3.14 apart from measuring error, with no trend by size — the true ratio is fixed, so π is a constant, not size-dependent.
If radius and diameter are confused, have them lay the radius against the diameter and confirm the diameter spans twice the radius across the centre.
Note that small measuring errors make the ratios differ slightly; the pattern 'a bit more than 3 every time' is the point, not a perfectly identical decimal.
activities.rationale: Measuring several circles and comparing the ratio lets π be felt as an invariant rather than memorised, directly confronting the misconception that π depends on circle size. A resizable circle with a live circumference ÷ diameter readout held near 3.14 is an optional model that reinforces the same invariance when physical objects aren't available.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Collect several circular objects of different sizes (tins, lids) and some string or tape.
Before measuring, PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference, and say WHY — in particular, predict whether the answer changes with the size of the circle.
Wrap and measure the circumference, then measure the diameter, for each object.
Compute circumference ÷ diameter for each and compare: the ratio should come out a little more than 3 (close to 3.14, within measuring error) each time, regardless of the circle's size.
Also check that the diameter is twice the radius (d = 2r) and state circumference = π × diameter in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference are related multiplicatively: d = 2r and C = πd, where π is a constant ratio (≈ 3.14) that does NOT depend on the size of the circle.

activities.title: Always / sometimes / never and the inclusion chain
feedback: If a learner accepts 'a square is a rhombus' but denies 'a square is a parallelogram', walk the chain: a square is a rhombus, every rhombus is a parallelogram, so a square is a parallelogram.
If a learner answers 'a rectangle is a square' as always true, show a long rectangle: it lacks four equal sides, so it is a rectangle but not a square — hence only sometimes.
Encourage justification by which properties are present/absent rather than by appearance.
activities.rationale: Targeting the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly addresses the documented one-directional/non-transitive error. Always/sometimes/never items (phrased in singular form so each verdict is well defined), categorisation and matching assess inclusion well, and prototype distractors ('a square is not a rectangle because it looks different') probe the core misconception. Used in teaching, these response formats can also surface reasoning for discussion, though a selection item alone does not elicit a learner's own justification.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Decide for each statement whether it is always, sometimes or never true, and justify by properties: 'A square is a rectangle', 'A rectangle is a square', 'A square is a rhombus', 'A square is a parallelogram'.
Trace the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram and explain why it follows that a square is a parallelogram (transitive reasoning).
Explain why 'a square is a rectangle' is always true but 'a rectangle is a square' is only sometimes true — the two directions are different.
Build or complete a family-tree / Venn diagram of parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, placing each shape in every class it belongs to.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion has a direction and is transitive: the more special shape belongs to the more general classes, but not the reverse; chaining inclusions lets you conclude square ⊆ parallelogram.

activities.title: 'Convince me a square is a rectangle' — a reasoning dialogue
feedback: Reward arguments that answer an objection with a property check rather than restating the conclusion.
If the learner concedes to a prototype objection, ask which rectangle property the square actually fails — it fails none.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue that repeatedly asks 'does a square have every property a rectangle needs?' and offers prototype counter-claims can surface and challenge partition reasoning and rehearse justification. It complements, and does not replace, the hands-on derivation and the dynamic morph activities, which can make the inclusion idea visible more directly.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Take the position that a square IS a rectangle and argue it to a partner or teacher who keeps pushing back with prototype objections ('but rectangles are long', 'they look different').
For each objection, answer by checking the square against a specific defining property of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel).
Conclude with a property-based statement: a square has every rectangle property and adds four equal sides, so it is a special rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A convincing justification of inclusion is built from checking defining properties, and it withstands appearance-based objections.

constraints: Build from hierarchical (inclusion) definitions and explicitly contrast them with partition definitions; a partition definition (e.g. 'a rectangle must have two long and two short sides') is the source of the core misconception and should be surfaced and corrected, not used.

Properties should be explored by construction, folding and measurement, then stated as checked for the shapes tested (within measuring accuracy) and, where possible, justified by reasoning from the definitions so they hold in general — avoid letting learners assert properties from appearance alone.

Paper/card cutouts have real thickness and are approximations of ideal zero-thickness plane figures; a flat screen is also a model. Distinguish the represented ideal shape from its physical or pictured representation.
Measurement of real circles yields ratios near 3.14 with small variation from measuring error; the invariance ('always a bit more than 3') is the learning point, not a perfectly identical decimal.

A static hierarchy/Venn reference is a useful support but cannot display a shape morphing while inclusion persists, and a fixed cutout cannot morph; pair either with a dynamic or adjustable model (or a deliberate compare-across-shapes activity) so inclusion is experienced, not only read.
Recognition-only response formats (picking the right option) do not by themselves elicit a learner's own justification; require them to state property-based reasoning in their own words.

When using always/sometimes/never, phrase items in singular form ('a rectangle is a square') so the verdict is well defined; a universally quantified statement is simply true or false, not 'sometimes'.

Optional interactive features — draggable corners, live name-tags that light up as properties are met, a diagonals overlay toggle, a resizable circle with a fixed C÷d readout — make the mechanism concrete when available, but are not mandatory; paper, string and construction tools serve the same objectives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding 'nothing essential'. These are plane figures plus one circle ratio, so 2D/physical work is well matched; this is a scope judgement, not evidence that a 3D representation could not help any learner.

The legacy claims that the square/rectangle question 'cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone' and that a static image 'cannot teach' inclusion are comparative claims not established by the cited sources; retained only as the narrow, true point that a static reference and a fixed cutout cannot display the continuous morph, while a dynamic/adjustable model can.

Corrected the morph activity and summary: a fixed paper cutout cannot continuously morph a rectangle into a square, so the continuous transformation is credited to dynamic geometry/adjustable models, with cutouts supporting comparison instead.

The always/sometimes/never activity uses singular-form statements so each a/s/n verdict is well defined; universally quantified statements ('every rectangle is a square') are simply true or false and were not used in learner-facing items.
The objective lists triangle interior angles, but like the original row no dedicated triangle angle-sum derivation activity is included; this is a scope gap to flag, not an introduced error.

Self-audit of mathematical content: d = 2r, C = πd, π ≈ 3.14 constant across sizes, parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not generally equal, rectangle diagonals equal, rhombus diagonals perpendicular, and the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram are all internally consistent and used as stated; no arithmetic or geometric error found to correct.

assess.poeTask: Give the child several circular objects (tins, lids) and string or tape. Ask them to PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference — and to say WHY — BEFORE measuring. Then wrap and measure each: the ratio is always a little more than 3 (π), for every size of circle. Whether they predicted the ratio would depend on the circle's size is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Is every rectangle a square? Why is that direction different from 'every square is a rectangle'?
List the properties of a parallelogram — are its diagonals equal? How could you CHECK rather than guess?
A square is a rhombus and a rhombus is a parallelogram — so is a square a parallelogram? How do you know?
For a circle, how do the radius, diameter and circumference relate — and which stays about 3 times another no matter how big the circle is?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes to both. A square IS a rectangle because it has every defining property of a rectangle — four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel — and simply adds the extra property that all four sides are equal, so it is a special rectangle. A square IS a rhombus because it has the rhombus's defining property of four equal sides, adding right angles, so it is a special rhombus. The reasoning must be property-based inclusion (the square satisfies all the properties of the more general class), not 'they look different'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partition/prototype classification — denies a square is a rectangle because rectangles are 'long' (two long, two short sides) or the shapes simply 'look different'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach hierarchical vs partition definitions; check the square against EVERY rectangle property; drag a rectangle dynamically until it becomes a square while its rectangle properties persist
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square is not a rectangle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no, a square isn't a rectangle' and justifies it by appearance or by a length restriction on rectangles

errorPatterns.pattern: One-directional / non-transitive inclusion — accepts an easy inclusion (square is a rhombus) but not the transitive or opposing-direction one (square is therefore a parallelogram), or thinks a rectangle cannot share square properties
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the inclusion chain explicit (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram) and reason transitively; use a Venn/family tree and always/sometimes/never tasks to distinguish the two directions
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On follow-up says a square is a rhombus but denies it is a parallelogram, or accepts every square is a rectangle yet insists a rectangle can never be 'square-like'

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. asserts a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the pupil derive the property by construction/measurement and compare classes (parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not equal; rectangle diagonals are equal)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a property (equal diagonals, right-angle diagonals) from how the figure looks, without constructing or measuring, and attributes the wrong property to the wrong class

responseLevels.gap: Classifies by appearance/prototype, denies a square is a rectangle, states properties only by looking, and treats each shape as an isolated category.
responseLevels.full: Reasons hierarchically from definitions and properties (a square satisfies all rectangle AND all rhombus properties, so is a special case of both), handles opposing-direction and transitive inclusions, derives and verifies properties (parallelogram diagonals bisect; C = πd, d = 2r), and transfers the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Lists correct properties of each shape and may accept the easier inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus), but cannot handle the opposing-direction or transitive inclusions, or derive/verify a property rather than assert it — knows the parts without the relational hierarchy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Answer each with yes or no, then explain: Is a square a rectangle? Is a square a rhombus? Use the properties of these shapes in your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who reasons hierarchically from properties answers yes-and-yes and justifies by property inclusion; a pupil reasoning from the prototype answers 'no' because the shapes look different or 'a rectangle must be long'. The square/rectangle question is the classic separator of hierarchical from partition/prototype thinking — it cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding angles (age 11+)
topic.description: Apply the properties of angles at a point (360°), on a straight line (180°), and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
evidence: Find a missing angle using the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180°
Use vertically opposite angles are equal to set up and solve an equation for an unknown
Combine multiple angle facts in a single diagram to find several missing angles step by step
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a diagram with several angles marked at crossing lines and some unknown, can they use the rules about straight lines and crossing lines to find all the missing angles step by step?

pedagogy.summary: This is the step up from knowing individual angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, on a straight line 180°, vertically opposite are equal) to CHAINING them across a single diagram to find several unknowns, and to setting up and solving an EQUATION for an unknown. Best taught by insisting that every step names the fact that licenses it (reasoning from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks), by keeping the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point), and by holding apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL, adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY. Diagrams are given not-to-scale so pupils must deduce rather than measure.
bestPractices: Require a named reason for every step ('angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' style mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises, tricks don't
Name the WHOLE before calculating: a straight line is a half-turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°); the unknown is the whole minus the known parts
Teach the crossing-lines diagram as two facts held apart — opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary — one diagram, two relationships
Present diagrams NOT to scale so pupils cannot measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts
Progress to letting an unknown be a letter and writing an equation (e.g. 2x+10 = 130 for a vertically opposite pair), linking angle facts to algebra
Build multi-step problems where one found angle becomes the input to the next, and ask pupils to carry the value forward onto the diagram
keyRepresentations: Crossing-lines ('hinged sticks') diagram for vertically-opposite versus adjacent angles
The whole as a fixed total shared among parts — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point
Not-to-scale multi-angle diagrams that force deduction over measurement
An equation written from the diagram (known + unknown = whole; or an opposite pair set equal)
commonMisconceptions: Treating vertically opposite angles as supplementary (subtracting from 180 to find the opposite angle)
Over-generalising that all four angles at a crossing are equal
Using the wrong whole — 360° where 180° applies, or vice versa
Measuring or reading the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing from facts

learn.summary: Pupils (age 11+) move from knowing isolated angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal) to CHAINING those facts across a single not-to-scale diagram to find several unknowns, and to writing and solving an equation for an unknown angle. The core discipline: name the fact that licenses every step (reason from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks or from F/Z mnemonics), keep the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point) for line/point calculations, and hold apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL (found by equality, not subtraction), adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.

activities.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
feedback: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles equal — found by equality, not by subtracting); each adjacent angle is 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so 180−130). Check: 130 + 50 + 130 + 50 = 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°.
For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120 and x = 60.
If you gave 50° for the angle vertically OPPOSITE 130°, you treated an opposite pair as supplementary — opposite angles are equal; it is the ADJACENT angle that is 180−130 = 50°.
If you used 360° for an angle on a straight line (or 180° at a point), you named the wrong whole — a straight line is 180°, a full point is 360°; sanity-check the answer against that total.
If you found the first angle but stalled, write it onto the diagram and use it as the given for the next step — the facts are sound, the chain just needs the value carried forward.
activities.rationale: The objective is multi-step deduction and justification, so the task must require an actual chain where each found angle becomes an input and a named reason is stated at every step; a not-to-scale figure means measuring is unreliable so pupils must deduce from facts, and part (c) links angle facts to setting up and solving an equation.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
Pupils should apply the properties of angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
Angle measure is additive: a whole angle decomposed into parts is the sum of the parts, and unknown angles are found by writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown
learnerActions: Work from a not-to-scale diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, and a third ray splitting the opposite angle into two parts, one marked 40°.

(a) Find the three unmarked angles at the crossing. For each, write the exact fact you used (e.g. 'vertically opposite angles are equal', 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'). Then check that the four angles at the crossing total 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
(b) Find the remaining part of the split angle, carrying the already-found angle forward as a given.
(c) Two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130°; write an equation and solve it for x.

Before calculating, name which relationship applies: for an angle on a line or at a point, say the WHOLE (a straight line is a half-turn 180°, a point is a whole turn 360°) and take the unknown as the whole minus the known parts; but for a vertically opposite angle the unknown is simply EQUAL to its given partner, NOT whole-minus-parts.
Write each found angle onto the diagram so it becomes a visible given for the next step.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are deduced by combining named facts in a chain, where one result feeds the next; a vertically opposite angle is found by equality while line/point unknowns are found by subtracting from the whole, and the not-to-scale picture cannot be measured, so only the facts license the answer.

activities.title: Hinged sticks: why opposite is equal and adjacent is supplementary
feedback: If you expected all four angles to be equal, look at a wide, non-perpendicular crossing: two clearly larger angles and two clearly smaller, with each large–small pair summing to 180°.
If you subtracted the given from 180 to get the OPPOSITE angle, the hinge shows the opposite angle grows with the original — equal, not supplementary.
The opposite pair being equal and each adjacent pair summing to 180° are consistent: 130° + 50° = 180° on each side, and the two 130°s face each other.
activities.rationale: The dynamic hinge gives a direct counterexample to the dominant misconception (treating vertically opposite as supplementary) and to the over-generalisation that all four angles are equal, by letting pupils see opposite angles change together while adjacent angles trade off.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Model a crossing with two hinged sticks (or two rulers pinned at a point).

Open the crossing wider and watch the angle you are opening and the one directly opposite it: observe that they grow TOGETHER and appear to stay equal (the hinge illustrates this; the straight-line facts explain why they must be exactly equal).
At the same time watch an adjacent angle: as one opens the neighbour shrinks, and each adjacent pair still sums to 180°.
State in words why the two opposite angles must be equal, and why an opposite pair cannot both be found by 'take it from 180'.
Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different, to check that NOT all four angles are equal — only opposite pairs are.
Optional screen version: drag one ray so the linked opposite angle updates equal in real time while the adjacent value updates to keep the pair summing to 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: At a crossing there are two distinct relationships held apart: vertically opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary — they cannot both be 'subtract from 180'.

activities.title: Introducing the vocabulary on a labelled crossing
feedback: Opposite pairs: equal. Adjacent pairs along either straight line: sum to 180°.
A tap-reveal confirms the name of a relationship but does not set or check a solved problem; once the vocabulary is secure, move to the chaining task to practise applying it.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal diagram efficiently introduces the naming of relationships; it is a vocabulary scaffold and does not itself require solving or chaining, so it should precede, not replace, the multi-step task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, identify the vertically opposite pair and state the relationship: equal.
Identify an adjacent pair and state the relationship: sum to 180°.
Where available as a reveal, tap an opposite pair to confirm 'equal' and an adjacent pair to confirm 'sum to 180°'.
Name each of the four angles and say which relationship each neighbour has to it.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary — vertically opposite (equal) versus adjacent (supplementary) — is attached to the right pairs on a crossing before any multi-step problem is attempted.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the supplementary-for-opposite trap and match steps to reasons
feedback: For the opposite angle, the correct option equals the given angle; the 180−x option is the supplementary (adjacent) value and is the common error.
A step is only justified when paired with the named fact that licenses it; 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' labels do not count as reasons.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and matching items efficiently probe the key misconception and reason-naming, but they assess isolated facts; they do not require a learner to build and carry a genuine multi-step chain, so they supplement rather than replace the chaining task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Fill in a missing angle given one angle at a crossing or on a straight line.
Answer a multiple-choice item for the angle vertically opposite a given one, where one option is the supplementary value (180−x) — choose the equal value and reject the trap.
Match each found angle in a worked solution to the exact fact that justifies it.
Set a slider or chosen value for one angle and state the resulting opposite and adjacent angles.
activities.intendedInsight: These recognition and matching items are intended to rehearse the equal-versus-supplementary distinction and the habit of naming a reason; they check isolated facts rather than demonstrate a mastered multi-step chain.

constraints: Diagrams must be presented NOT to scale so pupils cannot reliably measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts, and a reminder that the picture is not to scale is appropriate.
Every step must be justified with a named angle fact (e.g. 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not with F/Z/Z-angle mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises.

Name the WHOLE before calculating line/point unknowns (180° on a line, 360° at a point) and sanity-check against it; but do NOT apply whole-minus-parts to a vertically opposite angle — it is found by equality.
Hold the two crossing relationships apart explicitly: vertically opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary; do not let pupils apply 'subtract from 180' to an opposite pair.
Tap-to-reveal / static diagrams introduce vocabulary only; they cannot set a problem or check a chained deduction and must not be the sole activity for the multi-step skill.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess isolated facts and the key trap; they do not elicit an independent multi-step chain with a stated reason at each step, which requires the construction task.

Live-recolouring, dragging rays and sliders are optional ways to make the equal/supplementary relationships visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and a physical hinged-stick model achieves the same demonstration.

The additive and equation-based steps rely on correct arithmetic: 180−130=50, 130−40=90, and 2x+10=130 ⇒ 2x=120 ⇒ x=60; check these when authoring items and do not offer wrong partial values as valid alternatives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

One cited source (National curriculum in England mathematics KS3) is marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activity 1 as an exact copy supporting the multi-step application principle; treat its claim as unconfirmed pending a fresh check and do not read it as verified evidence.

Fixed an over-generalisation: the original 'the unknown is the whole minus the known parts' was being applied to EVERY unknown; this is only valid for line/point angles, so the guidance now scopes subtraction to those cases and states that a vertically opposite angle is found by equality, preventing reinforcement of the subtract-from-180 misconception.

The original claims that a static image 'cannot' teach the skill and that a third dimension or a persona/conversation 'adds nothing' reflect catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (e.g. static diagrams are a vocabulary scaffold). No universal necessity of the interactive format is asserted.

Arithmetic independently checked and correct: opposite of 130° is 130°; adjacent 180−130=50°; split remainder 130−40=90°; 2x+10=130 gives x=60. No dubious alternative values were carried into learner items.

probeDeeper: Point to the angle opposite 130° and ask 'how do you KNOW it's 130 and not 50?' — forcing the equal-versus-supplementary distinction into a reason
'If I opened the crossing wider, what happens to this angle and to the one next to it?' — a dynamic counterexample separating opposite from adjacent
'The diagram isn't drawn to scale — why can you still be sure of your answer?' — pressing that the facts, not the picture, license the deduction
'You found this angle was 90° — where does that value come from, and what can you now work out with it?' — checking they can carry a result forward
assess.correctAnswer: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite equal); the two adjacent angles are 50° each (angles on a straight line sum to 180°). For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°. For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120, x = 60. Each step is justified by a named angle fact, not by measuring.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats vertically opposite angles as supplementary — subtracts from 180 to find the opposite angle ('they're next to each other so they add to 180')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the crossing as two relationships held apart — opposite EQUAL, adjacent supplementary — with the hinged-sticks model: as one angle opens, its opposite opens equally
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(c) gives 50° (or 180−value) for the angle vertically OPPOSITE the given one, instead of the equal value

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises that all four angles at a crossing are equal ('they're all made by the same two lines, so they're the same')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different; establish that only opposite pairs are equal, adjacent pairs sum to 180°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports all four angles as 130° (or all equal), ignoring the supplementary adjacent pair

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — treats a straight line as 360° or a point as 180° when setting up the calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the whole aloud before calculating — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point — and sanity-check the answer against it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts from the wrong total (e.g. 360−130 for an angle on a straight line), giving an out-of-range or impossible answer

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the first angle correctly but cannot chain — doesn't carry a found value into the next step, or makes an arithmetic slip mid-chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold by writing each found angle onto the diagram before the next step so it becomes a visible given; do not reteach the facts — the reasoning is sound, the chain just needs support
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets the first unknown right then stalls on (b), or the individual facts are right but the final chained value is wrong through a slip

responseLevels.gap: Cannot apply the facts reliably — treats vertically opposite as supplementary, uses the wrong whole, or measures the not-to-scale diagram; single angles come out wrong
responseLevels.full: Chains multiple facts to find several angles, naming the reason at each step, carries found values forward, and sets up and solves an equation for an unknown — transferring to a new configuration and justifying from structure not appearance
responseLevels.partial: Finds single angles using one fact each and can state the facts, but cannot chain them across the diagram, mis-handles the equation, or reverts to measuring — has the facts as isolated statements, not as tools that combine

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a NOT-TO-SCALE diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, plus a third ray splitting the angle opposite into two parts, one of which is marked 40°. Set them to: (a) find the three unmarked angles at the crossing and, for each, say the fact they used; (b) find the remaining part of the split angle; then (c) here two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130° — write and solve an equation for x. Watch whether they treat the opposite angle as equal or as 180 minus, whether they name a reason at each step, and whether they carry found angles forward rather than measuring the picture.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the facts gives 130° for the opposite angle and 50° for the adjacent, naming each; a child with the common error gives 50° for the OPPOSITE angle (treating it as supplementary) — a visibly different answer. The not-to-scale figure means a child who measures lands wrong, and the multi-step chain and the equation reveal whether the facts are merely recognised or can be applied and carried forward.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Angles with parallel lines
topic.description: Understand and use the relationship between parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles; use these to find unknown angles
evidence: Identify alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angle pairs in a diagram with parallel lines
Explain why alternate angles are equal using the concept of translation along the transversal
Find missing angles in a parallel-line diagram using a combination of angle relationships
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a Z-shape or F-shape formed by two parallel lines and a crossing line in a diagram, can they identify the equal angles and explain why they’re equal?

pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn that a pair of parallel lines cut by a transversal produces a structured set of equal and supplementary angles: corresponding angles are equal, alternate (interior) angles are equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary (sum 180°). The goal is to REASON with these relationships to find unknown angles and to justify WHY they hold — ideally by translating one crossing's four-angle cluster along the transversal onto the other, so equality is grounded in transformation, not in a memorised 'F' or 'Z' shape. Two documented obstacles dominate: pupils over-generalise to 'angles on parallel lines are equal', missing that co-interior angles are supplementary; and they confuse alternate with corresponding angles, unable to pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams. A subtler difficulty is perceptual — pupils accept lines as parallel only when they are similar in length and position, so off-set lines are not seen as parallel and the rules go unapplied. Teaching therefore stresses structural reasoning, precise language over mnemonics, and non-standard, off-set diagrams.
bestPractices: Ground equality in transformation: use tracing paper to translate the four-angle cluster at one crossing along the transversal so it lands exactly on the other, showing corresponding/alternate angles are equal
Distinguish equal pairs (corresponding, alternate) from supplementary pairs (co-interior) explicitly, e.g. colour-code the two 'families' so the 70°/110° split is visible
Insist on precise language and full reasons ('x = 45° because alternate angles are equal') rather than 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics, which do not support reasoning
Use non-standard and off-set diagrams so pupils learn to identify pairs in rotated figures and still perceive off-set lines as parallel
Build multi-step angle-chasing on secure basic angle facts (straight line 180°, vertically opposite, angles at a point) and require a stated reason at each step
keyRepresentations: Parallel lines + transversal with all eight angles, the two crossings' clusters colour-linked
Tracing-paper / translation-along-the-transversal overlay demonstrating equal angles
Colour-coded equal vs supplementary angle families
Off-set and rotated parallel-line diagrams (non-prototypical)
Angle-chase worked example with a reason justifying each step
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising 'angles on parallel lines are equal', so treating co-interior (supplementary) angles as equal
Confusing alternate and corresponding angles, and failing to identify them in non-standard diagrams
Relying on 'F'/'Z' mnemonics that give the answer without supporting reasoning
Not perceiving off-set lines (little overlap) as parallel, so not applying the angle rules
Applying parallel-line angle rules to lines that are not actually parallel

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12-14 learn that when a transversal crosses a pair of parallel lines it produces a structured set of equal and supplementary angles: corresponding angles are equal, alternate (interior) angles are equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary (sum to 180°). The aim is to REASON with these relationships to find unknown angles and to justify WHY they hold — grounding equality in the translation of one crossing's four-angle cluster along the transversal onto the other, rather than in a memorised 'F' or 'Z' shape. Teaching must separate the equal family (corresponding, alternate) from the supplementary family (co-interior), insist on precise language and full reasons, and use off-set and rotated diagrams so pupils still perceive genuinely parallel lines as parallel and apply the rules.

activities.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal
feedback: If the slid copy lands on the lower cluster (within tracing accuracy), the translation shows that corresponding angles are equal; then use vertically opposite angles to explain why alternate angles are equal too.
If a pupil relies on the 'F'/'Z' look, ask them to describe what MOVEMENT maps one angle onto the other, so the reason is the translation, not the letter shape.
When the lines are not parallel, point out that the copy no longer fits and the readings diverge — this is the evidence that parallelism is the condition for the equalities.
activities.rationale: Grounding equality in the translation of the four-angle cluster along the transversal gives a structural reason for the result and directly addresses the over-generalisation and parallel-perception obstacles; tracing paper makes the transformation concrete.
sourceClaims: Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Draw (or use a prepared diagram of) two parallel lines crossed by a transversal, marking the parallels with matching arrows.
Trace the four-angle cluster at the upper crossing onto tracing paper, then slide the tracing straight down along the transversal until it lands on the lower crossing.

Observe that every angle in the slid copy lands on the matching angle at the lower crossing (as closely as tracing allows; in the ideal diagram the fit is exact). State which pairs this shows are equal: corresponding angles directly, and alternate angles by combining this with vertically opposite angles at the same crossing.
Now draw a second diagram where one line is deliberately NOT parallel to the other; trace and slide again, and record where the copy fails to fit and how the readings differ.
Write a one-sentence conclusion: equality of these angle pairs depends on the lines being parallel.
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding angles are equal because one crossing's angle cluster can be translated along the transversal onto the other, which is a transformation, not a shape to recognise. Alternate angles are then equal because each one is vertically opposite a corresponding partner. These equalities break when the lines are not parallel.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs into equal and supplementary families
feedback: If a pupil labels the co-interior angle 70°, ask them to check it against a straight line: the co-interior angle and the adjacent equal angle together make 180°, so it must be 110°.
Correct colouring with the 70°/110° split visible shows the two families are being kept apart — exactly the distinction the over-general rule erases.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the equal family from the supplementary family with a worked 70°/110° split targets the dominant over-generalisation that 'angles on parallel lines are equal'.
learnerActions: In a given parallel-lines-and-transversal diagram, point to one marked angle (e.g. 70°) and name its corresponding, alternate, and co-interior partners.
Colour the equal family (corresponding and alternate) in one hue and the supplementary family (co-interior) in another.
For a 70° starting angle, label each partner with its value: the equal partners read 70°, and the co-interior partner reads 110° because co-interior angles sum to 180° (180 − 70 = 110).
Explain in words why the co-interior angle is 110° and not 70°, referring to the straight line or to the equal angle that sits on a straight line with it.
activities.intendedInsight: Not all angles made with parallel lines are equal: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles are supplementary, so a 70° angle produces both 70° partners and a 110° partner.

activities.title: Identify pairs in off-set and rotated diagrams
feedback: If a pupil says the rules 'don't apply because the lines don't look parallel', redirect them to the arrow marks: matching arrows mean parallel, so the rules do apply.
If a pupil applies equality to an unmarked, non-parallel diagram, point out there is no parallel condition shown, so the equalities are not guaranteed.
activities.rationale: Non-standard, off-set, and rotated diagrams counter the perceptual error that only similar-looking lines are parallel and the inverse error of applying the rules to non-parallel lines.
sourceClaims: Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Work with diagrams where the parallel lines overlap only a little, are off-set, or are rotated away from the usual horizontal layout, with the parallels marked by arrows.
Before applying any rule, check the arrow marks to confirm the lines really are parallel.
Pick out and name each requested angle pair (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) despite the unusual orientation.
Also examine a diagram whose lines are NOT marked parallel and explain why the equal/supplementary rules may not apply there.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallelism is judged by the marking arrows and definition, not by how similar the lines look; the angle relationships hold in rotated and off-set diagrams whenever the lines are genuinely parallel, and must not be assumed when they are not.

activities.title: Multi-step angle chase with a stated reason at each step
feedback: Accept an answer only when each step carries a correct, precise reason; 'because of the F shape' is not a reason — name the relationship.
If a step is unjustified or a basic fact is misused, isolate that step and ask which angle fact licenses it before continuing.
activities.rationale: Requiring a stated reason at every step and resting multi-step work on secure basic angle facts develops the structural reasoning that mnemonics bypass.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and 'apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles' to derive and use angle results.

Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Given a diagram combining parallel lines, a transversal, and other lines, find an unknown angle that requires two or more steps.
At each step, write the angle fact used as a full reason, e.g. 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal' or 'y = 180 − 45 = 135° because angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Use secure basic facts where needed: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles at a point sum to 360°.
Check the final answer by an independent route (e.g. a different pair of angles) where possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are found by chaining relationships, each justified by a stated reason, building on secure basic angle facts rather than by pattern-matching a letter shape.

activities.title: Predict, reason, then check (diagnostic)
feedback: A pupil answering 110° with a supplementary/straight-line justification shows secure understanding of the two families.

A pupil answering 70° with 'angles on parallel lines are equal' reveals the over-generalisation — separate the equal family from the supplementary family and use straight-line reasoning to show the co-interior angle is 110°.
If a pupil only states that the relationship holds without saying why, press for the structural reason (translation or straight line).
activities.rationale: A predict-reason-check task makes the stated reason the diagnostic focus, surfacing whether a pupil holds a blurred 'all equal' rule or genuinely distinguishes equal from supplementary pairs. The stated correct value 110° follows from 180 − 70 = 110.
learnerActions: Look at two parallel lines cut by a transversal with one angle marked 70°; the teacher points to its co-interior (same-side interior) angle.
PREDICT whether that angle is equal, bigger, or smaller than 70°, and state WHY before checking.
Check by sliding a tracing-paper copy of the 70° angle (or an equal partner) along the transversal and reasoning via the straight line: the co-interior angle is 180 − 70 = 110°.
Answer the follow-up: would the answer still hold if the lines were not quite parallel, and why does parallelism matter?
activities.intendedInsight: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary (110° here), distinct from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs; a correct justification distinguishes the two families and depends on the lines being parallel.

constraints: Pupils must produce full reasons, not just answers: 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal', not 'F angle'. 'F'/'Z' mnemonics give an answer without supporting the reasoning and should not stand in for a stated relationship.

Keep the equal family (corresponding, alternate) explicitly distinct from the supplementary family (co-interior); a single 'angles on parallel lines are equal' rule is a misconception to correct, not a shortcut to accept.

The angle rules apply only when the lines are genuinely parallel; require pupils to check the parallel marking before applying equalities, and do not apply the rules to unmarked or non-parallel lines.

A static labelled reference diagram (with tap-to-reveal partners and relationships) is a useful lookup aid but cannot animate the translation that justifies equality or let pupils un-parallel the lines; treat it as a scaffold, not the full lesson.

Tracing-paper cutouts have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness lines and angles they represent; use them to demonstrate the translation while noting the idealisation.

Matching and multiple-choice items (e.g. sort pairs into 'equal' vs 'supplementary', find a missing angle, with a co-interior item offering a tempting but wrong '70° (equal)' option and a non-standard diagram) can probe the core over-generalisation and assess identification, but a recognition-only format does not by itself elicit the pupil's own constructed reasoning or the felt translation — pair it with tasks that require a written or spoken reason.
Multi-step angle-chasing depends on secure basic angle facts (straight line 180°, vertically opposite, angles at a point); shore these up first.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit arithmetic: for a 70° marked angle, co-interior partner = 180 − 70 = 110° (correct); the equal (corresponding/alternate) partners = 70°. These are consistent throughout.

Neither cited source claim explicitly states that co-interior angles are supplementary or names the 'angles on parallel lines are equal' over-generalisation; the equal-vs-supplementary family-separation activity (activity 2) and the predict-reason-check diagnostic (activity 5) therefore carry an empty sourceClaims, resting on the curriculum/pedagogy description. Activity 5's translation check-step is nonetheless consistent with the source's recommended tracing-paper technique, but no source claim directly supports its stated rationale.

The source material does not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium; the original catalog fit judgements ('3D adds nothing', a dynamic model is 'ideal', a quiz 'cannot deliver' understanding) have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

A dynamic sliding model with live readouts and an un-parallel control is an optional, helpful way to make the translation and the parallel-condition visible; it is presented as an interaction example, not a mandatory mechanism — tracing paper on paper achieves the same reasoning.

The original 'correctAnswer' noted an equivalent framing: the 70° angle equals the alternate/corresponding angle that lies on a straight line with the co-interior angle; this is retained as an alternative justification route and is mathematically sound.

assess.poeTask: Draw two parallel lines cut by a transversal and mark one angle. Ask the child to PREDICT whether a specified alternate angle will be equal, bigger, or smaller — and to say WHY — before checking. Then slide a tracing-paper copy of the first angle along the transversal onto the second: it fits exactly, showing they are equal by translation. The stated reason for the prediction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Which angle in this diagram IS equal to the 70° — and how do you know it's equal rather than supplementary?
Slide a tracing-paper copy of the 70° angle along the transversal — where does it land, and what does that prove?
If I drew the two lines so they weren't quite parallel, would your answer still hold? Why does parallelism matter?
Explain WHY alternate angles are equal — not just that they are.
assess.correctAnswer: 110°. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles between parallel lines are supplementary — they add to 180° — so 180 − 70 = 110°. (Equivalently, the 70° angle is equal to the alternate/corresponding angle that sits on a straight line with the co-interior angle, and angles on a straight line sum to 180°.) The reasoning must distinguish co-interior/supplementary from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs.
