topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Drawing triangles accurately
topic.description: Draw and measure line segments and angles accurately, and construct triangles from given conditions using the drawing approaches the standard calls for: ruler and protractor for two sides and the included angle (SAS) or two angles and the included side (ASA); ruler and compasses for three sides (SSS), using intersecting arcs; and dynamic geometry software; check each construction by measuring the remaining sides and angles (to within about 1 mm and 1°). Interpreting scale drawings is covered in Scale drawings and maps; deciding whether conditions give one, many or no triangles is covered in Which triangles are possible
evidence: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, angle A = 40° and AC = 5 cm using a ruler and protractor, then measure BC and the other two angles
Construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm using a ruler and compasses, drawing intersecting arcs from each end of the 6 cm base

Construct a triangle with angles of 50° and 60° at the ends of a 7 cm side in dynamic geometry software, measure the third angle (70°), and drag the vertices to show that the triangle can move or rotate but cannot change its shape or size while those ASA conditions hold
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 7 cm and 5 cm and a 40° angle between them, could they draw it accurately with a ruler and protractor — and then measure the third side to check?

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (age 11-13) accurate drawing and measuring with ruler and protractor is extended in two directions: constructing a triangle from a given specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. The construction half carries forward the protractor hazards of Y6 — chiefly reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. The scale-drawing half introduces a distinct and heavily-documented conceptual hazard: children reason ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and drop or muddle units when converting between drawing and reality. Effective teaching keeps the placement/estimate-first routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.
bestPractices: Keep the estimate-first protractor routine (is the angle bigger or smaller than a right angle? then choose the scale that agrees) and centre-on-vertex / zero-on-line placement, now to nearest-degree accuracy

Sequence SAS-style construction: rule one side from the ruler's zero, set the included angle at its endpoint, measure the second side, rule the third to close; treat a non-closing triangle as a signal of accumulated error
Teach scale as a MULTIPLIER: write 'real = drawn × scale factor' (and drawn = real ÷ factor), draw children's attention explicitly to the multiplicative and away from the additive relationship
Keep units explicit and precise — say 'each 1 cm represents 2 m' and carry the units through the conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area
Use pictorial/scale-plan models, which research shows reduce the tendency toward additive strategy, and demand a reasonableness check on the real length
keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule to disambiguate the two scales (to nearest degree)
Base-then-included-angle-then-side SAS construction sequence
Scale statement 'real = drawn × scale factor' with a worked ratio (e.g. 1 cm : 2 m)
Scale plan / map with a stated scale for measuring and converting real lengths
Double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m (to make the multiplier visible)
commonMisconceptions: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference rather than multiplying by the scale factor — the classic additive-strategy error, most common in the ratio/proportion literature
Drops or muddles units in a scale conversion, or treats 'size' loosely (confusing length scale with area scale)
Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, measuring/drawing the supplement of the intended angle
Misplaces the protractor centre or zero-line, so measured angles are consistently a few degrees out
Accepts a nearly-closing constructed triangle as accurate rather than as evidence of accumulated placement/measurement error

learn.summary: KS3 (age 11-13) learners extend accurate ruler-and-protractor work in two directions: constructing a triangle from a specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. Construction carries forward the protractor hazards of earlier years — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement) and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. Scale drawing introduces a well-documented conceptual hazard: reasoning ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and dropping or muddling units when converting. Effective teaching keeps the estimate-first placement routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.

activities.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
feedback: If your measured third side or remaining angles differ noticeably from about 6.7 cm, 47° and 78°, do not accept them as 'close enough'. This is evidence of accumulated error: recheck the protractor centre on the vertex, the zero-line along the side, and which scale you read
If you set 125° where 55° was asked, you read the wrong scale and drew the supplement; re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and pick the scale that agrees

If the sides or angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence on another figure. Use the self-check of measuring the third side and the remaining angles against their expected values
activities.rationale: On a dual-scale protractor, pupils struggle with which scale to read and with vertex/baseline placement. Estimate-first strategies reduce these errors. Comparing the measured third side and remaining angles with expected values reveals accumulated inaccuracy; closure alone is not a check, because an SAS triangle always closes when the endpoints are joined. An interactive canvas can make this routine concrete: the protractor shows both scale numbers with a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, the ruler measures from zero, and a tick confirms that the measured third side and angles are within tolerance. The same routine works with a physical ruler, protractor and paper.
sourceClaims: On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.

activities.title: Scale conversion as a multiplier, not an addition
feedback: If you added a constant (e.g. treated '1 cm represents 2 m' as '+2'), compare 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 with 4.5 × 2 = 9: the scale says every 1 cm is 2 m, so you multiply
If you dropped the units and just wrote '9', restate it as 9 m and carry 'm per cm' through the working so the result has the right units
Avoid the vague word 'size': say which dimension (side-length) you mean, since length scale and area scale are different
Check against reality for the actual object and scale given: does the converted length make sense for what the plan depicts?
activities.rationale: The additive strategy — computing a difference and applying it rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature, geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable, and pictorial models reduce it. Scale factor is a multiplier and teaching should draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one, refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)', and avoid the imprecise word 'size'. A live converter bar and a scale slider that shows the real length multiply while the drawn length stays put can make the multiplicative structure felt, but a ratio table, double number line, or physical scale map serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

Scale factor is a multiplier: teaching should 'ensure children's attention is drawn to the multiplicative relationship between side-lengths and not to the additive relationship'; shapes are similar only when every dimension is scaled by the SAME factor (adding a constant to each dimension does not produce a similar shape); refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)' and avoid the imprecise word 'size', which can be confused with area.
learnerActions: On a printed or on-screen scale plan labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m', measure a wall to the nearest millimetre (e.g. read 4.5 cm)

Convert to the real length by multiplying: write 'real = drawn × scale', so 4.5 cm × 2 m per cm = 9 m, carrying the units through the whole conversion. Equivalently, with the unitless scale factor of 1:200, 4.5 cm × 200 = 900 cm = 9 m
State the scale in words: 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply'
Use a double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m to keep the multiplier visible
Check the real length is reasonable for the object (e.g. a 9 m wall in a room)

Explore what happens when the scale changes, as a thought experiment about the scale factor: imagine the same drawn length read at a different scale — if 1 cm represented 5 m (a 1:500 scale) instead of 2 m (a 1:200 scale), the real length multiplies, so the same 4.5 cm would stand for 22.5 m while the drawn length on the plan stays the same. Apply the reasonableness check to whatever object and scale are actually given — at 1:500 the plan would depict a correspondingly larger space
activities.intendedInsight: Scale is a multiplicative relationship: real length = drawn length × scale factor (and drawn = real ÷ factor). Changing the scale factor multiplies the real length while the drawing is unchanged; adding a constant does not model scale.

activities.title: Feeling the scale factor by zooming from plan to real room
feedback: If the expansion feels surprising, it is because scale multiplies: each small step on the plan stands for a much larger real distance
Always come back to the numeric conversion — the zoom builds intuition, but the answer still comes from drawn × scale factor with units
activities.rationale: The spatial 'zoom from plan to real room' is an optional enrichment that can make a scale factor feel concrete; the core conversion remains numeric and planar, so this supports rather than replaces the measuring-and-multiplying work. Offered as an alternative with a different (intuition-building) purpose, not as the main vehicle. Its intuition-building efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: Starting from a floor-plan with a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm represents 2 m), zoom from the plan into a representation of the actual-size room to experience how a small drawn length corresponds to a large real one
Connect the visual expansion back to the number: a 4.5 cm wall on the plan becomes a 9 m wall in reality at 1 cm : 2 m
Return to the plan and do the measuring and conversion numerically
activities.intendedInsight: A scale factor can be made viscerally real by seeing a drawn length expand to its actual size, reinforcing that the real object is the drawing multiplied by the factor.

activities.title: Check scale reasoning and protractor scale choice (recognition practice)
feedback: If you picked the additive option (6.5 m), recall that each 1 cm represents 2 m, so the relationship multiplies: 4.5 × 2 = 9 m
If you picked the answer with no units, remember the real length is in metres (9 m)
For the scale item, estimate the angle against a right angle first, then pick the agreeing scale
activities.rationale: Fixed-response items can test scale conversions and scale-choice decisions with targeted distractors. This is recognition practice and consolidation; on its own it does not elicit or assess a learner's actual construction accuracy or their independent assembly of the conversion, which require doing and explaining.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Answer a conversion item such as: a wall measures 4.5 cm on a plan at 1 cm : 2 m — what is the real length? Choose from options that include an additive distractor (6.5 m from adding) and a units-dropped distractor ('9' with no units) alongside the correct 9 m
Answer a 'which scale reads this angle?' item: given an angle estimated smaller than a right angle, decide which of the two protractor scales to read
Explain in words why you multiply rather than add, and why the units matter
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising additive and units-dropped distractors and choosing the correct protractor scale reinforces the multiplicative structure and the estimate-first habit; recognising the right answer among options is not the same as independently constructing or converting, so this consolidates rather than replaces the full task.

constraints: Construction accuracy is a doing skill within the KS3 curriculum: it is built by actually ruling sides, placing a protractor, and measuring. A static diagram or tap-to-reveal picture can serve as a reference for the scale statement and protractor routine but does not itself elicit placement accuracy or the learner performing the multiplicative conversion.

Recognition-only items (choosing among options, naming the right scale) do not elicit independent construction of the triangle or independent assembly and explanation of the scale conversion; use them to consolidate, and assess the full skill through a performance task.
A zoom-from-plan-to-real-room experience is optional enrichment for intuition; the core conversion is numeric and should still be carried out and explained with units.
Keep units explicit throughout a conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area — length scale and area scale differ.

Interactive affordances (ghosted dual-scale numbers, a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, a live converter bar, a scale slider from 1:200 to 1:500, a green tick when the constructed triangle's measured third side and angles are within tolerance) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete. They are helpful options, not required, and the same learning is achievable with a physical ruler, protractor, paper, scale maps, ratio tables and double number lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static image and conversation as 'poor' and a 2D interactive as 'ideal' / the only way to 'defeat' the two hazards. These are catalog fit preferences; the exact sources support the teaching principles (estimate-first routine, multiplicative scale, pictorial models) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium. Medium-specific necessity claims have been softened to scoped proposals.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 4.5 cm × 2 m/cm = 9 m is correct. The 22.5 m figure is also correct — 1:500 denotes 1 cm : 5 m, so 4.5 cm × 5 m/cm = 22.5 m, consistent with 1:200 denoting 1 cm : 2 m. It is presented in activity 2 as a scale-factor thought experiment (same drawn length, different scale) illustrating that the real length multiplies while the drawn length is unchanged, not as a graded item or a claim about a specific room's wall. 55° is less than a right angle and its supplement is 180 − 55 = 125°, matching the dual-scale hazard. The additive distractor 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 m is one plausible incorrect-strategy illustration.

The KS3 statutory source claim was removed from the activity sourceClaims arrays because it states the curriculum objective/topic rather than the specific teaching principle in each rationale; the objective itself is preserved in the activity content. Legacy reteach prerequisite IDs and quiz-step vocabulary were removed per rewrite rules, with the underlying reteach moves preserved as feedback.

probeDeeper: Your drawing shows 4.5 cm here — how do you turn that into a real length? Why multiply and not add?
If the scale were 1 cm to 5 m instead, would this wall be longer or shorter in real life? By how much?
Before you read the protractor — is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle? So which of the two numbers is it?
How do you know your triangle is accurate — what would you check?
assess.correctAnswer: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately (side ruled from the ruler's zero, 55° set with centre-on-vertex and the correct protractor scale, second side measured, third side ruled to close) to about ±2° / ±2 mm; measures the wall on the plan to the nearest millimetre and converts by multiplying by the scale factor (drawn length × 2 m per cm), keeping units, and explains 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply.'

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference instead of multiplying by the scale factor when converting between drawing and reality
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the multiplier explicit — 'real = drawn × scale factor' on a ratio table / double number line; draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one; use pictorial models, which reduce additive responses
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a 4.5 cm wall at 1 cm:2 m gives an answer got by adding (e.g. treats the '2' as +2, or scales dimensions inconsistently), rather than 4.5 × 2 = 9 m; on 'similar shape' checks accepts adding the same amount to each side as an enlargement

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing or measuring the supplement of the intended angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate the estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a square corner?') then pick the agreeing scale; rehearse on a single-scale/numberless protractor until scale choice is automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets 125° where 55° was asked (or reports an angle as its supplement), so the SAS triangle is wrong or fails to close

errorPatterns.pattern: Constructs by eye rather than to the given spec, so the triangle does not close or the sides/angle are off — a lapse of the drawing skill under the tighter accuracy demand
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach from scratch: rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence and the 'does it close?' self-check on a couple of figures
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The triangle nearly-but-not-quite closes, or sides/angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, despite the child knowing the routine

responseLevels.gap: Cannot construct to the given spec and converts scale by adding or with no units; reads whichever protractor scale.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately to the nearest degree/millimetre, measures precisely, and converts drawing↔real by the multiplicative scale factor with units, explaining the scale and checking the real length is reasonable — and transfers correctly to a different scale.
responseLevels.partial: Constructs the triangle and can measure on the plan, but converts scale inconsistently — adds instead of multiplies, or drops units — or slips on the protractor scale; has the component moves (measure, multiply) without reliably assembling and explaining the conversion (lists parts without the relational whole).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler, a protractor, and a printed scale drawing of a room or map labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m'. Say: 'First, draw a triangle accurately with two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm and an angle of 55° between them. Then, on this plan, measure this wall and tell me its real length, and explain the scale you used.' Watch the construction and how they convert — do not talk them through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The constructed triangle and the stated real length together reveal the reasoning: a child who thinks multiplicatively converts by × scale-factor with units intact; a child who thinks additively adds a constant or muddles units, and a dual-scale slip yields the supplementary angle and a triangle that will not close. Right answers are hard to reach by an additive route — the numbers diverge.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Congruent triangles
topic.description: Know and use the criteria for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), use standard labelling conventions for sides and angles of triangle ABC, and determine whether two triangles are congruent
evidence: State which congruence criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS) applies to a given pair of triangles
Use the notation △ABC ≅ △DEF and match corresponding sides and angles
Use two non-congruent triangles that share two sides and a non-included angle to explain why SSA is not a congruence criterion
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown two triangles where all three sides of one match all three sides of the other, can they explain why those triangles must be identical in shape and size?

pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 students learn that a triangle can be pinned down by just three of its six measurements — but only in the right combinations: SSS, SAS, ASA (and their consequences AAS, and RHS for right triangles). The deep idea is DETERMINATION: which sets of data force a unique triangle, which allow more than one, and which allow none. The two hardest points are (a) SSA — two sides and a NON-included angle — is ambiguous (the 'swinging side' can meet the base in two places, giving zero, one or two triangles), and students wrongly assimilate it to SAS because both are 'two sides and an angle'; and (b) AAA fixes only the SHAPE (similarity), not the size, so equiangular triangles need not be congruent. Alongside this sits the correspondence convention: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so the order of letters encodes which parts are equal. Teaching is most effective when students physically construct triangles from given conditions and discover for themselves when the data over- or under-determine the figure.
bestPractices: Have students CONSTRUCT triangles from given conditions (ruler, protractor, compass or dynamic geometry) so they discover empirically when data force a unique triangle and when a second triangle appears
Make the included-vs-non-included distinction explicit: for 'two sides and an angle', always check whether the angle is BETWEEN the two sides (SAS, unique) or opposite one of them (SSA, ambiguous)
Demonstrate the 'swinging side' for SSA with a compass arc so the two intersection points — two valid triangles — are seen, and analyse the zero/one/two outcomes
Separate congruence (same shape AND size) from similarity (same shape, possibly scaled): show that AAA equal angles give similar but not necessarily congruent triangles
Drill correspondence notation — the order of letters in △ABC ≅ △DEF names the matching vertices, sides and angles — and derive AAS from ASA (a second angle forces the third)
keyRepresentations: Dynamic triangle constructor / compass-and-ruler construction from given conditions
The 'swinging side' compass arc showing SSA's two intersection points
Side-by-side SAS (angle between) vs SSA (angle opposite) diagrams
Correspondence map △ABC ≅ △DEF with matched tick-marks and angle arcs
A one/none/many outcome table for given measurement sets
commonMisconceptions: Treating SSA as a valid criterion by conflating it with SAS — not checking whether the angle is included between the two sides
Believing AAA (equal angles) proves congruence, confusing congruence with similarity
Assuming any three given measurements determine a unique triangle
Mismatching corresponding parts — ignoring that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes the correspondence
Not realising AAS works (because the third angle is forced) while SSA does not

learn.summary: Students aged 12-14 learn which combinations of a triangle's six measurements (three sides, three angles) force a UNIQUE triangle: SSS, SAS, ASA, plus the derived AAS, and RHS for right triangles. The core idea is DETERMINATION — which data over-determine, under-determine, or exactly fix a figure. Two hard points: (a) SSA (two sides and a NON-included angle) is ambiguous — the free 'swinging' side can meet the other arm of the angle in two places, giving zero, one or two triangles — yet students wrongly treat it like SAS because both are 'two sides and an angle'; (b) AAA fixes only SHAPE (similarity), not size, so equiangular triangles need not be congruent. Alongside sits the correspondence convention: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so letter order encodes matching parts. The strongest learning comes from physically constructing triangles from given conditions and discovering for oneself when data over- or under-determine the figure.

activities.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles
feedback: If you predicted exactly one triangle and found two, that is the key surprise — the identical SSA data gave two genuinely different triangles. This is why SSA is called the ambiguous case.

If the compass arc crossed the 40° angle's other ray at two points, each crossing completes a valid but different triangle; if it just touches that ray at a single point there is one triangle (the tangent / right-angle case); if it crosses the ray at only one point because the other crossing falls behind the corner (this happens when the swinging side is at least as long as the base), there is also one triangle; if the arc never reaches that ray there is none.

When you fixed the angle BETWEEN the two sides (SAS), the third vertex was forced to a single location — the swing collapsed to one locked triangle. Notice you changed only where the angle sits, not the lengths.

If you justified 'one triangle' by naming SAS or 'two sides and an angle are given', check whether the angle is actually between the two named sides. Here it was opposite the 6 cm side, so SAS does not apply.
activities.rationale: Determination is a manipulable idea: fixing two sides and an angle and swinging the free side directly shows how many crossings occur (two for the 9 cm/6 cm/40° data; changing the swinging length can also show the one-triangle and no-triangle outcomes), and toggling the angle between included and non-included shows why SAS locks but SSA does not. Prediction-then-test makes the ambiguity felt rather than told.
sourceClaims: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.
learnerActions: Set up a fixed 9 cm base line. At one end, mark a 40° angle, drawing the second arm of that angle as a long ray rising from the corner. Pin a 6 cm 'arm' at the FAR end of the base (so the 40° angle sits OPPOSITE the 6 cm side, not between the two sides).
BEFORE moving anything, predict in writing: how many triangles can you complete, and WHY?

Swing the 6 cm arm (physically, or draw a compass arc of radius 6 cm centred at the far end of the base) and mark every point where the arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle (the ray rising from the angled corner) — each crossing is a possible third vertex.
Count the crossing points and draw each complete triangle you find.

Reconfigure with the40-degree angle between the6cm and9cm sides. Fix both sides on the two rays and join their free endpoints; compare this lockedSAS construction with the freeSSA arc. Rotated or reflected copies are still congruent, not different-sized solutions.
State in your own words why moving the angle from 'opposite' to 'between' changes the number of triangles.
activities.intendedInsight: Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT determine a unique triangle — the free side can swing to meet the other arm of the angle in up to two places. When the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides (SAS), the triangle is locked. 'Included' is the word that matters.

activities.title: Construct from conditions: when do data fix a triangle?
feedback: For AAA you should have been able to build two triangles with identical angles but different sizes — equal angles fix the shape, not the size, so they are similar, not necessarily congruent.
For AAS, once two angles are known the third is forced (angles sum to 180°), so AAS carries the same information as ASA and fixes a unique triangle.

If every attempt 'worked' as a single triangle, revisit SSA and AAA carefully — valid AAA data always allow different sizes, and SSA data may give zero, one or two triangles depending on the measurements, so check whether a second triangle was possible.
Compare your outcome table with the construction you actually drew; a mismatch usually means a measurement was placed in the wrong position (e.g. the angle not truly between the two sides).
activities.rationale: Constructing triangles from given conditions lets students discover empirically which data over- or under-determine a figure, and separates congruence (same shape and size) from similarity (same shape, scaled) through a concrete size-changed counter-example rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: HSG.CO.B.8: 'Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.' The standard lists exactly and only ASA, SAS and SSS as the triangle congruence criteria.

SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.
learnerActions: Using ruler, protractor and compass (or a dynamic geometry tool), attempt to construct a triangle from each data set: SSS (three given sides), SAS (two sides with the angle between them), ASA (two angles with the side between them), SSA (two sides with an angle opposite one), and AAA (three given angles).
For each, record whether you got exactly one triangle, more than one, or none.
For AAA, construct a second triangle with the same three angles but longer sides; compare it to the first.
Fill in a one/none/many outcome table listing each data set and its result.
Explain for AAS why giving two angles and one side forces a unique triangle even though you were not told the third angle directly.
activities.intendedInsight: CompatibleSSS,SAS,ASA,AAS orRHS data determine a triangle up to congruence. Invalid measurements may determine none;SSA can allow zero,one or two, and validAAA data allow different sizes with the same shape. Reflected or rotated copies count as congruent, not new non-congruent triangles.

activities.title: Correspondence notation: △ABC ≅ △DEF
feedback: If you wrote the vertices in an order that pairs a long side with a short one, the statement is wrong even if the triangles are congruent — reorder so matching parts line up.
Mark corresponding parts (ticks and arcs) before writing letters; this prevents reading off the wrong equal pairs.
A correct statement lets you list all three equal side pairs and all three equal angle pairs purely from the letters, with no diagram.
activities.rationale: Correspondence notation is a convention that must be practised: matching letter position means matching part, so a correct statement lets learners read off all equal sides and angles. A static labelled reference of the criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS), with SSA shown as a non-criterion, and correspondence notation serves as a vocabulary anchor alongside this practice.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.

SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.
learnerActions: Given a pair of triangles with matched tick-marks on equal sides and arcs on equal angles, identify which vertex matches which.
Write the congruence statement in the form △ABC ≅ △___ so that the letter order pairs matching vertices.
From your statement, read off which sides are equal and which angles are equal, without looking back at the diagram.
Check: does the position of each letter in the two names point to a genuinely matching part? Mark the corresponding parts first, then write the statement.
Given a WRONG statement whose letters pair non-matching parts, correct it and explain what went wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of letters in a congruence statement encodes the correspondence: matching positions name matching vertices, sides and angles. The statement is only correct when every paired position is a genuinely equal part.

activities.title: Classify and reason: one, none or many?
feedback: For validSAS data, the included angle fixes a unique triangle up to congruence. ForSSA, inspect the actual measurements: there can be zero,one or two triangles, so a single solution is possible. The9cm/6cm/40-degree example has two; do not generalise that count to everySSA case. RHS is a valid special right-triangle criterion.
'Same angles so congruent' is a similarity-vs-congruence error: equal angles fix shape only, so the triangles may be different sizes.
Reasoning that merely names a criterion without saying why the data force (or fail to force) a unique triangle is incomplete — the justification is the point.
activities.rationale: Identifying the applicable criterion, judging one/none/many, and matching corresponding parts are assessable with selected-response and matching formats, and incorrect answer options can embody SSA-as-SAS and AAA-as-congruent errors. This format can check reasoning efficiently but does not itself elicit independent construction or the hands-on swinging experience, so it should follow the construction work rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

HSG.CO.B.8: 'Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.' The standard lists exactly and only ASA, SAS and SSS as the triangle congruence criteria.
learnerActions: For each given data set, answer: which criterion applies (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) — or none — and does it produce one triangle, none, or more than one?
When shown 'two sides and an angle', state explicitly whether the angle is between the two sides (SAS) or opposite one of them (SSA) before deciding.
When shown three equal angles, decide whether the triangles must be congruent, and justify.
Match corresponding parts in a △ABC ≅ △DEF item.
For each answer, write one sentence of reasoning that names WHY the data do or do not fix a unique triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which criterion applies and whether a data set fixes a unique triangle requires checking the included/non-included distinction and separating congruence from similarity — not pattern-matching 'two sides and an angle = SAS'.

activities.title: Construct a right triangle from hypotenuse and one side
feedback: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; check that the5cm length isBC, not a second leg.
Only one intersection lies on the chosen ray. A mirror image acrossAB is congruent, so it is not a second non-congruent solution.
activities.rationale: Restores the statedRHS objective with a concrete compass construction, complementing the preservedSSA/SAS contrast. This activity is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: DrawAB=3cm and a perpendicular ray fromA; the angle atA is90degrees.
Draw a circle centred atB with radius5cm. Its intersection with the chosen perpendicular ray locatesC, soBC is the5cm hypotenuse andAB is the3cm side.
Compare two constructions with the same data and explain why they are congruent, including reflected or rotated copies.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side determine a right triangle up to congruence: this isRHS, not arbitrarySSA.

constraints: A static labelled panel of the cases and correspondence notation is a useful reference and vocabulary anchor, but a fixed image cannot let the learner swing the non-included side and see a second triangle appear; use it alongside, not instead of, construction.

Selected-response/matching items can check which criterion applies, the one/none/many judgement, and correspondence matching, and can use incorrect options that embody SSA-as-SAS and AAA-as-congruent errors — but recognition items do not elicit independent construction or the hands-on swinging experience, so pair them with hands-on construction.
For the SSA swinging-side task, require a stated REASON with the prediction; the reasoning (appealing to the non-included angle / swinging side) is the diagnostic part, not the bare count.
When demonstrating SSA, note that the swing can give zero, one, or two triangles depending on the measurements; the 6 cm/9 cm/40° setup is one specific case (two triangles), not a universal count.
In the swinging-side construction, the free arm meets the OTHER arm of the given angle (the ray from the angled vertex), not the base line itself; describe the crossing on that ray.

Distinguish congruence (same shape AND size) from similarity (same shape, possibly scaled) explicitly; AAA equal angles give similarity, which is a legitimate and useful relation, not merely a 'failed congruence'.
Paper/card strips and compass arcs are approximations of the ideal plane figure (real card has slight thickness); treat the drawn or physical triangle as a representation of the abstract triangle.

An optional interactive constructor can provide hinged rods, an angle setting, an arc/crossing counter and a correspondence readout. Ruler/protractor/compass work also permits constructing and comparing the triangles; no comparative learning-effectiveness claim is established here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Correction applied: the original poeTask/recommendation described the swinging 6 cm side as meeting 'the base', which is inconsistent with the stated geometry (9 cm base, 40° angle at one end, arm pinned at the far end). The arm's arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle; actions, feedback and the audit were corrected accordingly.
Self-audit: AAS is correctly derived from the angle sum (two angles force the third = 180° total), consistent with the sources; retained as stated.

Self-audit on the specific SSA triplet (9 cm base, 6 cm arm, 40° opposite the 6 cm side): an editor arithmetic check gives perpendicular distance from the pinned end to the 40° ray ≈ 9·sin40° ≈ 5.79 cm; since 5.79 < 6 < 9 two solutions are expected, matching the source's 'two triangles'. This was computed by the editor, not re-verified against fresh sources; the general SSA outcome remains zero/one/two, and activities frame the count as learner-discovered.
RHS is listed as a criterion but is not developed in any activity; if RHS production is assessed, add an explicit right-angle–hypotenuse–side construction/example.

The source row's 3d and conversation entries claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' and the concept 'cannot' be taught by an in-role exchange. These universal-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated; construction/manipulation is proposed as effective without asserting other media are useless.
Reteach-prerequisite links and the assessment diagnostic structure live in the source assess field and were not altered here; internal identifiers are omitted from this guidance.

assess.poeTask: Set up a fixed base line with a 40° angle at one end and a 6 cm 'swinging' side pinned at the far end (a card strip or compass arc). Ask the child to PREDICT how many triangles can be completed, and to say WHY, BEFORE they swing the side. Then let them swing (or compass) it and observe the two points where it meets the base — two different triangles from the same SSA data. The stated reason for the prediction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If the 40° angle were BETWEEN the 6 cm and 9 cm sides instead, how many triangles then — and why does moving the angle change everything?
Someone says 'these two triangles have all three angles equal, so they must be congruent' — do you agree? What could be different about them?
Write the congruence statement △ABC ≅ △___ for these two triangles — which vertex matches which, and how do you know?
What is the smallest set of measurements you would need to be SURE there is only one triangle?
assess.correctAnswer: More than one (here, two). This is SSA — two sides and a non-included angle, the ambiguous case: the 6 cm side can swing to meet the base ray in two different positions, so the measurements do NOT determine a unique triangle. Only SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS, and RHS for right triangles) force a unique triangle; SSA in general does not. The reasoning must appeal to the angle being non-included / the side being able to swing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats SSA as a congruence criterion by conflating it with SAS — 'two sides and an angle always fix a triangle' — without checking whether the angle is included
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the swinging-side compass demo so two triangles appear from the same data; train the habit of checking whether the angle lies BETWEEN the two sides; have them construct both triangles themselves
errorPatterns.distractor: Exactly one — two sides and an angle always fix a triangle (SAS).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'exactly one triangle' and justifies it by naming SAS or 'two sides and an angle are given'

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes equal angles (AAA) prove congruence — confuses congruence with similarity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast congruence (same shape AND size) with similarity (same shape, scaled); show AAA fixes shape only, enlarging one triangle to break congruence while angles stay equal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, claims two triangles with all three angles equal must be congruent

errorPatterns.pattern: Mismatches corresponding parts — ignores that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes which vertices, sides and angles correspond
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground the convention: matching position in the two names means matching part; mark corresponding parts before writing the statement
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes a congruence statement whose letter order pairs non-matching sides/angles, or reads off the wrong equal parts

responseLevels.gap: Applies the criteria as memorised letters without meaning — treats any 'two sides and an angle' as fixing a triangle and confuses congruence with similarity.
responseLevels.full: Determines whether given measurements yield one, none or many triangles by reasoning about the included angle and the swinging side, distinguishes congruence from similarity, uses correct correspondence notation, and transfers the reasoning to a new configuration.
responseLevels.partial: Names SSS/SAS/ASA correctly and can match corresponding parts, but cannot explain why SSA is ambiguous or why AAA gives only similarity — lists the valid criteria without reasoning about what determines a unique triangle.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I give you two sides of a triangle — 6 cm and 9 cm — and an angle of 40° that is NOT between them (it sits opposite the 6 cm side). Is there exactly one such triangle, more than one, or none? Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who understands determination recognises SSA as ambiguous and reasons via the swinging side / non-included angle; a student who pattern-matches 'two sides and an angle = SAS' answers 'exactly one'. The non-included angle is the hinge — the correct answer requires the included/non-included distinction and cannot be reached by reciting 'two sides and an angle fix a triangle'.

sources.claim: HSG.CO.B.8: 'Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.' The standard lists exactly and only ASA, SAS and SSS as the triangle congruence criteria.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, High School Geometry — Congruence (HSG.CO.B.6–8)

sources.claim: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.
sources.source: Illustrative Mathematics, 'When Does SSA Work to Determine Triangle Congruence?' (task 340, aligned to G-CO.B.8)

sources.claim: KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.

dependencies.reason: Congruence criteria are exactly the sets of conditions that determine a unique triangle, and explaining why SSA fails uses the two-triangle case
Determining congruence requires constructing triangles from given conditions
Triangle congruence criteria require standard labelling conventions

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Which triangles are possible
topic.description: Decide whether given side and angle conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and explain why, predicting with a freehand sketch and testing by construction (ruler and protractor, compasses, or dynamic geometry software): three sides give exactly one triangle when each pair of sides adds to more than the third, and none otherwise — if the two shorter sides add to less than the longest, the construction arcs do not meet, and if they add to exactly the longest (e.g. 3, 4 and 7), the arcs touch only on the base line, so the sides lie flat in a straight line rather than forming a triangle; three angles must add to 180° and then fix only the shape, not the size, so many triangles fit (none if the sum is not 180°); two sides with the included angle, or two angles with the included side, give exactly one triangle; and two sides with an angle that is not between them can give two, one or no triangles
evidence: Show that sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm make no triangle (the arcs do not meet) and that 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm make none either (the arcs touch on the base, giving a straight line), while 3 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm make exactly one
Explain that angles of 50°, 60° and 70° fit many triangles of different sizes, while angles of 100°, 50° and 40° fit none because they add to 190°
Sketch freehand, then construct, two different triangles with AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle A = 40°, and explain why making the 40° angle the one between the two sides gives only one triangle
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to make a triangle from straws 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm long, could they predict that it can't be done and explain why — and say why 'angles of 50°, 60° and 70°' could describe lots of different-sized triangles?

dependencies.reason: Knowing that a triangle's angles add to 180° explains why three angles must sum to 180°; soft because this GB topic is not in the US route, where the angle sum is used informally until 8.G.5
Testing whether conditions give one, many or no triangles is done by attempting the SSS, SAS and ASA constructions with ruler, protractor, compasses or software
Conditions are stated with triangle notation (AB, angle A), and explaining 'included' versus 'non-included' angles relies on it
